div.p: Vettrp.
EULALIE.

------- Her voice is like the mocking-bird's upon the myrtle tree, Her eyes are like the summer stars that frolic on the sea; Oh, 'tis rapture to look at her ; And it sets my heart abeat, Just to catch the pretty patter Of her merry little feet. The fairies spun her tresses on a spindle made of pearl, Then dipped them in the sammer shine and put them up in curl; Led when I see them flutter, As she dances in the wind, I wish I were a butter- fly, or—something of the kind. I know that Cupid did it, and I think it was a sin To carve a cunning dimple in the middle of her chin; . . . .

_ For rt is a'crime to covet— So says the Law Divine— Yet I look at it, and love it, And I want it all for mine. She whispers that she loves me! Now, be it understood, The tidings are delightful—l'd believe them if I could; But in her vocabulary With its tantalising flow, The truth will often tarry Far behind a "yes" or "no." She smiles at me! She frowns at me! She knows I can-
not fly; 0, Cupid, come and aid me with an arrow on the sly, That when the orange bowers Are blowing, Ealalie May wear the snowy flowers In a bridal wreath for me! —The Manhattan.

div.head: Tarietis.
div.p: Tarietis.
The cyclone is the biggest wind instrument heard of as

yet. Why is Q rather impertinent? Because it is always in- When are writers like cattle? When they are absolutely -driven to the pen. Why is a selfish friend like the letter?? Because, though the first is in pity, he is the last in help. "Why do you always come after tea ?" said a young lady. I come after T," was the response, "in order to be -nearer U." Oaght there not to be a dewy fragrance in our lives, in our words and ways, that may silently witness to the reality of the source of our freshness. It is one of our special pri- vileges to do this.—Havergal. " To.morrow," says the proverb, "comes never, and the same tempter who leads you to put off doing what is right to' a more convenient season,' will be as ready to suggest an excuse to-morrow as to-day."— Whateley. Angels of Life and Death alike are His; Without His leave they pass no threshold o'er; Who, then, would wish or dare, believing this. Against His messengers to shut the door.—Lonofellcnc. Christianity is not a philosophy or a scholasticism. It is the light of life—plain truth for plain people; and it com- mends itself to every husgry heart arid to every man's con- science in the sight of God.—R. Ellis, D.D. Counsel—" Then you think he struck you with malice aforethought?" Witness, indignantly—" Yoa can't mix me op like that. I've told you twice he hit me with a brick. There wasn't no mallets nor nothise of the kind about. A wealthy London merchant is reported as having said— "l always feel happy when I am advertising, for then I know that, waking or sleeping, I have a strong though silent orator working for me; one who never tires, never sleeps, never mattes mistakes, and who is certain to enter the house- holds from which, if at all, my trade must come." And still, to the end of time, the clear waters of the un- failing springs, and the pasture lilies in their clathed multi- tude, and the abiding of the burning peaks in their nearness to the opened heaven, shall be the types and blessings of those who have chosen the light, and of whom it is written, "The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills righteousness."—Ruskin. Hoare.—So far as home is a sacred place, a vestal temple, a temple of the hearth watched over by household gods, be- fore whose faces none may come but those whom they can receive with love; and roof and fire are types only of a nobler shade and light—shade of the rock in a weary land, and light as of the Pharos to the stormy sea—so far as it vindicates the name and fulfils the praise of home, and wherever a true wife comes this home is always round her. —llaskzn. A teacher was hearing a class in spelling and defining words. The word "orphan" had been correctly spelled, but none of the class seemed to know its meaning. After asking one or two of them, she said encouragingly, "Now, try again. lam an orphan. Now, can't some Of you guess what it means?" 'The blank look upon their faces remained, until one of the duller scholars raised his hand, and said, with no intention of being saucy, "It's someone who wants to get married and can't." The late Dean Stanley was once travelling in a railway carriage, when a blustering man exclaimed, "I should like to meet the Dean of Westminster. I'd pat a question to him that would puzzle him." "Very well," said a voice out of another corner," now is your time, for I am the Dean." The 1 man was rather startled, but presently recovered, and said, " Well, sir, can you tell me the way to heaven?" "Nothing easier," answered the Dean, "you have only to turn to the right and go straight forward." A friend was talking to Wordsworth of De Quincey's articles about him. Wordsworth begged him to stop; he hadn't read them, and had even dismissed the man from his mind, and did not wish to ruffle himself about the unavoid- able. "Well," said the friend, "I'll tell you only one thing he says, and then we'll talk of other things. He says your wife is too good for you." The old poet's dim eyes lighted up, and he started from his chair, crying with enthusiasm, • "And that's true! There he's right," his disgust and cons , tempt visibly moderating. ROME POLITENESS.—If we want anything of our children, or our servants, we should not, merely be- cause we have the authority to comma ad. give a bold order ;. but why not use the gentle erlease, will you do this ?" "I should like you to do that." "Oblige .me with that." When service is rendered we are not to take it in silence, curtly, rudely, because we have a right to the service; but it is easy to say "Thanks," or "I am obliged," -or " Oh, that is very nicely done." These little every.day courtesies are called the small change of life, but we should •be badly off in trade if we had no small change and must always deal with tweaty-dollar bills; while the small change mounts up to the great sum in a lifetime. If parents have plenty of this small change of politeness on hand, it will be put in circulation in the family. The children will pay it out to each other, to servants, to playmates, and with it family peace and family affection will be largely purchased. Home is the place where true politeness tells.

ANTIQUARIAN DISCOVERY.—The Times Vienna correspon- dent writes :—An interesting antiquarian discovery has been made near the village of Cele., in Moravia. There is a mysterious mound, which stands near the village in a south- • easterly direction. Hofrath von Hochstetten, the keeper of the Imperial and Royal Museum for Natural History, • recently sent his assistant, Herr Szombathy, to examine the spot. Four strong labourers cat three feet down into the mound and found some skeletons. The skeletons were in layers, which were only separated from each other by a layer of earth scarcely two feet thick. Further examinations ,showed that the skeletons in the different layers were placed in different directions, at right angles to one another and diagonally, but always close together, and that they com- prised persona of all ages and of both sexes. The skulls are broad, with large brain cavities, and Herr Szombathy -assumes that they belong to a north Slav race, and, to judge by the size and structure of the bones, to a strong race. The bones were brittle, and when exposed to the air and sun ,crumbled into dust. The corpses were probably placed there, •at the same time, at a period of war or plague. Jow; Wocur AND Woot.—le considerable attention is being directed at present to the career and opinions of Wyclif, the follorring extract from his writings, in reference war, may possess some interest:—" Friars now say that ttops can fight best of all men, and that it falleth most properly to them,-cince they are lords of all this world. Thus they say, Christ bale His disciples sell their coats and buy them swords; but whereto, if not to fight? Thus friars make a great array, and stir up many men to fight. But Christ taught not ED apostles to fight with a sword of iron, but with the sword of God's word, which atandeth in meek- ness of heart and in the prudence of man's tongue. And as Christ was the meekest of men, so He was most drawn from the worW, and would rot judge or divide a heritage among men; and yet Ile could have done that best. Angels have withstood fiends; and many men with right of law with- stand their enemies,andyet they kill them not, neither fight with them. Men of the gospel, by patience and the pros- pect of rest and peace, have vanquished through the suffer- ing of death, just as we may do now. But here men of the world come and say that by this wise kingdoms would be destroyed; tint here our faith teaches that, since Christ is our Goa, kingdoms should be thus established, and their -tlamies overcame. Well Indeed I know that men will scorn 1s doctrine; but men who would be martys forth° law of God will hold thereby." A JaParrass FAIAIL= AT Sna.—We had a large number 4f Japanese passengers, who seemed to fill every nook and cranny foeard. A pleasant-locking family, fearful of he closeness of the steerage, had boat their soul t a lordly dwel- ling-house ever the hatches amidships. They had piled their luggage round., and planted themselves in the middle The walls Were not very high, but at least they served to. mark the limits of their domain. There they eat, the father blandly smiling at the fair scene around, the mother tidy- ing up, raid the little boy with his head shaved save for two locks over either ear, which were nicely oiled and combed. I was very glad to think, as I looked upon this family acene, that we were going to bave such fine weather that the captain was making preparaoons for spending the night t on the bridge. It would be a terrible thing if the vessel rolled and pitched, breaking down the house of cards, in- extricably mixing up the little boy with the luggage and apoiling his hair. Worse still, if cruel seas were to come ever and wash the decks. Presently, as we came nearer ts the bar, and could faintly hear the boom of the Pacific rollers on the rugged coast, a tarpaulin was slung over a pole covering in the scene of domestic felicity. They had a i lantern, and, peeping through a chink, I discovered them amiling more vigorously than ever. Never bad they been eo comfortable on board ship, and they were more than ever , pleased that this happy thought had occurred to them, and - that they had not pigged in with their countrymen b the I I hold.-27a English Illustrated Jragazine.

part of the country that I have visited has the dry weather produced so little effect as here. The grass lands about Gar- stang are greatly in need of rain, but cattle and sheep are looking well, and reports of the milking season are satisfac- tory. The gooseberry crop appears to be a very good one in most places. A correspondent, writing nearly a week ago after a return from Kent. says he was told that they were sending two or three tons of this fruit nearly every night from Long Stanton Station, and in three weeks time from the date of his visit it was expected they would send 12 or 13 tons away every night if they could get hands to pick them. A Lincolnshire correspondent writes :—• Black and red cur- rants, gooseberries, and raspberries are likely to be scarce here, as the late frosts killed them. Apples are in full bloom. We have plenty of young rabbits and hares, and pheasants and partridges are laying.'"

the education there given consists more of mathematics and modern languages, while the landwirthschaftaschulesupphes an equivalent education in which mathematics and lan- guages are to a certain extent replaced by the natural sciences and the principles of agriculture. The schools are not exactly State institutions, but they receive a State sub- vention in aid of the funds of the district or associaticn by which they have been organised. The Provincial Adminis- tration controls all matters relating to the entrance and leaving examinations, and to the personnel of the teaching eta Reports to the Ministry of Public Instruction must, be sent yearly through the Provincial Administrati an. Thesis landwirthscbafteschulen are organised on a basis di a three ye us' course of instruction, but it is allowed to have under the same management a preparatory school for those boys who are intended for students but who are not yet qualified by previ ma education to enter the higher school. The organisation of the teaching in the preparatory school is not prescribed by the Government, but it must be sub- mitted to the local authorities and approved by them. Every province of the Prussian Monarchy, with the excep- tion of the province of Saxony,now pos-e3ses at least one of I these schools. Particulars as to the constitution and work- ing of some of these schools are given, and Mr. Jenkins gives it as his opinion that the educstion given at these schools doss not exceed in scope, depth, or breadth the instruction given in English country schools, at some of which the principles of agriculture are taught with no inconsiderable Mass.

Lower agricultural education is given at farming schools, of which there are two types—those in connection with the iotermediate agricultural schools and those estahlished in country districts in connection with a farm, and where practical instruction is combined with theoretical and general education. In the kingdom of Prussia there are 32 such schools; in Saxony three, and in Wurttemberg four, all combining practice with school instruction. The total state grants to these schools is £6,698, and the provisional gran* £10,376 per annum. The course of study at these schools varies from 1 to two years, and the results are ex- czeiingly good. We shall complete the report on Germany in our next article, and shall then give a summary of the Commis- sioners' visit to France.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES,

An International congress on the subject of the phyl- loxera will be held at Turin from the Bth to the 15th of August. The travels of Colonel Prshewalski in Thibet and on the Yellow River in 1879 and 1880 have been translated into German by Baron E. von Stein Nordheim, and published by Costenoble of Jena. It contains numerous illustrations and a map.

- The Atheneum says that the last novel written by Charles Reade, entitled " A Perilous Secret," will be published by Messrs. Bentley early in July. Mr. Reads finished the novel two or three month before his death and told his godson, Mr. Charles Liston, "This will be my last novel; put at the end, 'The °amain drops." Mr. Bentley published his first novel, "Peg Woffington," and the last will now appear from the same house.

Tics PLANET VENUS is just now the centre of attraction for Parisians. She LI 80 brilliant that she is not only the marvel of the night, but is visible even in daylight. The astronomers at the Observatory are doting themselves exclusively to her, and M. Flammarion, who is famous for having passed his wedding night in a balloon, has discovered a chain of mountains on her equator, while M. Thouvenot has discovered white spots at her poles, which he knows are very high clouds.

The Athenzum has the following :—Shaksperean students will be glad to learn that the Church of Stratford-on-Avon is no longer in danger from those who have been agitating lately for a very reckless restoration. The fabric has been for some years out of repair, and at the suggestion of Mr. C. E. Flower the services of the Society for Protecting Ancient Buildings have been called into requisition. The Society's architect last week examined the building with the local authorities, and his report is awaited in many quarters with mach interest. Dr. Holub having surmounted his difficulties with the Cape Custom House, where the officials demanded duty on his explorer's outfit, has now started for the Transvaal ; thence he means to penetrate the interior of Africa. His collections of the fauna and flora of that continent he intends to divide among the scientific societies which have contributed to the expenses of the expedition. During Dr. Holub's involuntary stay in Cape Colony he made some studies of the ornithology of the Somerset mountains, and has sent home the specimens there collected. From Engineering we learn that M. G. A. Hire, the well- known French astronomer, has devised an apparatus for giving the absolute actinic power of the sun. It consists of an alembic of copper containing sulphuric ether, alcohol, or sulphuret of carbon, and exposed to the solar rays. The dimensions are so chosen that the quantity of heat received in unit time is proportional to the quantity of liquid vola- tilised and condensed by the alembic. By means of Reg- nanit's formuhe the solar heat absorbed by the known sur- face is calculated from the quantity of liquid condensed.

div.head: CURIOUS BANQUET.
div.p: A CURIOUS BANQUET.

On the Bth of February a sheep was stunned and rendered insensible without stopping the action of the heart; a tube was then inserted in the jugular vein, and through this some blood was allowed to flow. Then a solution of the boric acid raised to blood heat was made to flow into the vein from a vessel suitably placed above its level. This solution, as I was told, contained only 4- ounces of the acid, the sheep weighing above 701bs. It was then allowed to flow with the blood for a few minutes, simply projected by the or- dinary action of the heart. Then the larger vessels of the neck were divided in the usual mariner, and the blood al- lowed to escape, carrying with it what remained of the solu- tion. The sheep thus killed was skinned and prepared in the usual manner, then placed in one of the cellars of the Society of Arts Rooms, in the Adelphi, in proper custody for verification sake. I saw it there about a month after its death. It was perfectly free from any odour of putrefar- tion, though here and there on the surface were :a few spots of mildew.

On the 2nd of April it was cut up in the usual joints, which were variously cooked—roasted, boiled, stewed—and served both hot and cold at the Adelphi Hotel, opposite the Society's rooms, where a party of about 25 gentlemen as- sembled to test it practically in the way of luncheon. There was a joint of ordinary vulgar beef for those who might hesitate to complete a meal on the injected mutton. I plead guilty of some timidity at first, and of seating myself within reach of the beef; but after a cautious beginning, and finding no flavour beyond that of pure mutton in the first dish, I made a complete circuit of both hot and cold. The others appeared to have begun with similar feelings, but, strange to say, the beef remained uncut, while there was considerable havoc among the mutton joints. I used my palate very critically, but failed to detect any flavour beyond that of pure and very tender mutton in the hot roast, the cold roast, or the stew, but was just able to detect a slight softness of flavour like that of distilled water in the boiled leg. Mr. Barff (son of Professor Barff), who has been working for some time past upon his boroglyceride, and is familiar with the taste of boracic compounds, told me that he detected a slight boracic flavour in the boiled , mutton, but none in the roasted. There can be no doubt about the success of this method of preserving meat, though we have yet to learn the effect of daily partaking of small quantities of boric acid on the system. Mr. Barff spoke very positively of its perfect harmlessness, basing his assertions on rather severe experi- ments, the particulars of which I have not apace to detail. His testimony Is the more valuable, as this process is rather a rival to that of the borozlyceride, in which he is com- mercially interested. The marvellous element of the success of this method of preserving meat is the very small quan- tity of the antiseptic that acts so effectually. Besides the cooked joints at the Adelphi Hotel there was a large dish of uncooked chops offered for home testing. I secured two of these for further study of the mildew patches above described which had excited my curiosity, as they presented what appeared to be a curious contradiction. A detestably damp outhouse where boots and shoes and every- thing else speedily become covered with green mildew was conveniently available. I placed the chops there, and at the end of six days (i.e. on the Bth of April, or just two months after the slaughter of the sheep) they were com- pletely coated with a thick deposit of the rich green fun- gus. They were apparently putrid and unfit for food, but gave out no particular odour beyond that of the mildew itself. The fungus was washed off and the chops cooked. They were excellent, very tender, and not perceptibly " high " or "gamey." This is the greatest puzzle of all. The modern theory of putrefaction is that it is due to the action of fungus or fungoid or microzoic germs of some sort, which, abounding in the air, are deposited on the animal substance, feed on it, grow, and by their excreta produce the putrescence. Here we have a case in which fungus germs are freely deposited and flourish luxuriantly on the out sur- faces of meat seven weeks old, and yet they fail to taint it with any degree of the ordinary putrescence of flesh. Can it be that boric acid is a selective antiseptic? Is it a sub- stance that destroys germs of bacteria bacilli, micrococei, &c.; but does net affect the purely vegetable germs of mildew fungus? Supposing this to be the case, then we must conclude that the mildews are not concerned in putre- faction. If boric acid is thus selective, it will not arrest Ivinous fermentation, as salicylic acid is said to do.— Gentleman's Magazine.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

Pricking out—which signifies the removal of plants from the place where they are sown, and planting them at such distance as will afford space for them to develop until ready for planting in permanent quarters—has been impeded by the continuous dry weather. Our various kinds of winter vegetables have been waiting for some time to be dealt with in this way. Some of the very forward we felt almost com- pelled to deal with a week ago, and it has involved mach labour in watering and shading. The latter expedient is the most beneficial, as the plants can be induced by its aid to hold up their heads with very little water. By thus in- tercepting the sun's rays evaporation is partially interrupted. However heavily plants may be watered they will droop on sunny days if not shaded. Shading a few hundred plants is not a difficult task. Four or more pieces of quartering should be driven into the ground at the corners of the bed, and in the middle if the length demands it; on the top of these strips of wood should be nailed lengthwise and cross- way. If the covering material is in one piece, it should be fixed on a piece of wood, to serve as a roller, so as to make its removal a momentary act. The distance of this skele- ton frame from the ground need not be more than one foot. Old pieces of sacking can be nailed all round, to prevent the wind sweeping under. A simple structure of this kind if placed at one end of the garden need not be disturbed, for it would be found useful at different times of the year, and if made a permanency we would nail boards round the sides. If the hoe is run between the rows of onions, parsnips, &c., daring the sunny weather, the labour of hand weeding will be reduced to a minimum. Just now we are unable to pro- ceed with hand weeding, as the binding nature of the ground prevents the roots from coming out, and for this purpose rain would be acceptable. To all appearance, rain is much needed for every crop in the garden, and especially for seed- lings, whose roots have not penetrated but a few inches below the surface of the soil.

THE Pamir Gennxiy."-Liiefore planting Dahlias a few spadefuls of soil should be taken from where it is intended to be planted. Then procure some manure and mix with the bottom, at the same time spreading some on the top, so that it may mix with the soil as it is placed round the plant. When the plants are removed from boxes into the open ground there is a great deal of root disturbance, con- sequently some steps should be taken to shade the plant during sunny weather. If there is any doubt about slugs being present, it will be advisable to place some cabbage or lettuce leaves, soaked bran or brewer's grains at a short dis- tance from the plant to allure the slugs. These decoys should be examined late at night and the slugs picked up. They are very partial to Dahlias, and will eat a moderately thick stem through in a night. As a further security, each plant may be girdled round with either soot or fresh lime. ' Each plant should be loosely tied to a stake to prevent the wind from blowing them over. Stakes should also be fixed to other plants that are likely to require them. At present, the plants may stand all night, but a moderate breeze when the foliage is wet will drive them on their sides. The first to suffer are the herbaceous Larkspurs and Phloxes. Some of the Carnations will be now sufficiently advanced to require tying, and in doing so it is as well to tie the material round the stick first, to prevent it from slipping. Guard against drawing the-more busy plants together too tightly so as to appear bundled. Ta Wmnow.—The plants in the window get very dry just now if the pots are full of roots. It would be an ad- vantage to sereen the pots from the sun by placing a neat board on its edge in front of them or a temporary shelf may be placed below the window ledge, so that the rim of the pots will only be level with the edge of it. This is also an excellent contrivance at any time for plants that are getting ISO broad or too tall for the window.

-- FEEDING AND HOUSING DUCKS. It may, at the outset, be accepted as an axiom that no one should keep clacks, at least for breeding, who has not a sheet of water, large or small, to give them. Ducks are aquatic birds, and though ducklings can be reared without water, yet to keep them for breeding, or even for any length of time, it is absolutely necessary that they have water. I We have often reared ducks for killing, and they have never bad more than as mach water as could be contained in a tub sunk in the ground, but the eggs were from birds that were kept under more natural conditions, and consequently did not come under the same influences as if we had attempted to breed from birds in confinement. But in suitable places a small pond or lake can very easily be made, and if there Is room then the matter is easily put right. The corres• pondent who some two or three weeks ago asked a question as to the feeding and housing of clacks, did not say what accommodation he has for keeping them, and we assume that he has sufficient ground space so as to enable him to go in for breeding, but if noto then if he will let us know, or should anyone else desire the same information, we shall be pleased to tell how ducks can be reared for the table in small places. - - -

Granted, therefore, a suitable place, one where there is a reasonable supply of water, the first question is that of housing, but fortunately this is not a very troublesome one. Ducks are very hardy birds, and do not need the same amount of care in this respect as do ordinary poultry, con- seqaently houses are neither so costly nor yet so elaborate as are the others. Where a good roomy shed can be given, very little more is needed, for there is not the same ob- jection to damp as in the case of fowls. We do not mean that decks thrive as well on a cold, damp soil as on a dry one, bat simply that there is not the same need for attention to the question of dryness. In fact, this cannot be secured where there is water, for the ducks will soon have all the place soaking if it be dried half a dozen times a day. Such a shed as we hive named is all the better if a low one, say about three feet high, or even less, for ducks roost on the ground, and do not need perches, though if the shed is al- ready bnilt and is higher it makes no matter, but it should be roomy and well ventilated. Foe a floor we prefer not to have a wooden one, as that soon begins to rot and gets saturated with excrement, so that the atmosphere of the house becomes charged with ammonia. We prefer to have the earth excavated out, and filled in with broken brick or slag, and the top covered with coarse sand or fine gravel. This will drain the water off very quickly, and the floor will always be fairly dry. The sand or gravel can be re- newed, as often as is necessary, say two or three times a year, and thus there will be no danger from saturation of the ground. If a house has to be built, and so large a one is not required, then it is easy to build a low shed, but in all cases unle=a it is to be a movable house, it will be better to go upon these lines, and it is jest as easy to make it ornamental as not, so that in parks or near lawns where ap- pearance is a matter of consideration, there is no difficulty in keeping the duck-house in unison with the surroundings. Should it have to be a movable one, it is still preferable to make it without a floor, continuing the sides down to the ground, but in that case straw will have to be used instead of the send. Where a wooden floor is regarded as indis- pensable, the precaution should be taken to Out plenty of moles in it, so that the water may get quickly through, and to have it raised three or four inches above the ground. Ducks are very stubborn in one point, and in one point only, and that is they object to lay where they are wanted, preferring to select some quiet, out of the way place, where they think their eggs will remain undiscovered. In this respect they show mach greater wisdom than do hens, for the latter go on to the nest provided, and are content, as a rule, to lay away, asking no question about, and making no attempt to hide the eggs. But not so with Mistress Duck, and many have been the wearisome hunts we have had to find oat their nests. For this reason, it is a capital plan to have a good-sized yard formed around the duck house, in which they can be kept until after they have layed, which will mean ten or eleven o'clock in the morning. This can he formed of 2ft. wide netting, and will be very inexpensive, Unless it is done, the ducks will give no end of trouble by laying in all sorts of places. One large deck yard we know of is kept entirely covered with straw, which is renewed several times a year, and the owner informs us that this is the most valuable manure he can possibly get, and, for the same reason, all straw oat of duck houses, should be pre- served, as it will come in splendidly for garden or farm work. Of course, straw could not be put down in places where appearance is studied, for it is not very pleasing in appearance, and there the arrangements must be altered to sait the circumstances. Coming next to the question of feeding, ducks are not very difficult to please in that respect, and, except for spe- cial purposes there is nothing better than the ordinary food as given to laying hens. In the morning they should have a feed of soft food, made of barley meal, thirds,or pollard, Indian meal, or any other kind of meal, though we must warn our readers not to use Indian meal entirely, or even principally. It is much too fattening in its nature and will soon put a stop to the laying; but a little of it, say one-fourth, mixed with thirds, makes a very good food. Then, in the evening, about an hour before going to roost, they should have a good feed of some sound grain, say barley, or wheat, or oats, or buckwheat, all of which singly or mixed can be freely given. Ducks are very voracious eaters, and they make the food bill a heavy one, but if they have plenty of room they for- age a great deal, and do not need so much food as they other- wise would. Still, in any case, they are heavy eaters, and a dozen ducks will consume at least twice as much food as any dozen fowls. But they are more profitable if kapt in a suitable place and given proper attention, so that they re- pay any additional cost which they may entail. When fat- tening a different system of feeding is required, bat as we have previously described this in our columns, we will not repeat it now. Sdll, if any readers of The Guardian spe- cially desire it, we shall be happy to give it again. So far as the choice of breed is concerned we have no- thing to add to what we have already said. If eggs alone are wanted then undoubtedly the Pekins are the best; if rapidly maturing and first-class eating fowls, as well as good layers, then the Aylesburys stand first, with the Cayugas next; or if large birds the Ronens are to be preferred, though they do not mature quickly. All are hardy and can be kept in almost any place, and the chief drawback to the Aylesburys and Pekihs is that their white plumage soon gets soiled in places where smoke and dirt abound. If this is objected to the dark plumage of the Rouens, or the black feathers of the Cayugas, make either of them to be prefer- red. There is just one thing more that need be said, and that is fowls and ducks should never be kept together. The habits of the one are entirely antagonistic to the other, and hens especially suffer if the ducks are with them. _ _

With the advent of hot weather it will be very difficult indeed to prevent hens of the sitting varieties getting broody, as this is a natural state of things with them. Should they not have brought up a brood during the spring they may be allowed to do so now, but if they have done this then it will be as well if they can be kept on laying for a few weeks longer. Hens vary very much in their desire for sitting, and whilst some can be easily broken off we have known others that were tried with all sorts of things in vain, in the attempt to get them off being broody, for if they could not get anything else they would sit on half bricks or stone cobbles. Perhaps the best thing is to keep changing them from one house to another, but even this will fail at times, and if it does the only thing will be to let the birds have their own way. Such plans as starv- ing, or sousing in cold water, are cruel in the extreme, and should not be resorted to. They are not only cruel but seldom effectual.

CHAPMAN & Co.—All others are frauds.—Advt. On the removal of the Wellington statue it was found that a starling had built its nest in the head. The nest had been built on the crown of the duke's head, and entrance to it was effected from under the ends of the great plume at the point of the hat. It was allowed to remain. MR. GLADSTONE.-80, seeming as if flaccid from want of sleep, he lies in wait. The men on the other side gird at his Government. Mr. Gorst pelts him with the pebbles of perennial blame; Lord Randolph Churchill, light and agile as a bull.fighter, stings his broad hide with pointed darts; and Sir Stafford Northcote, from the opposite corner of the gangway by the Mace, says the most disagreeable things with an amount of blandness which might put Ah Sin to the blush. Then the lax figure which seemed to sleep sud- denly sits bolt upright, chin in the air and hands clasping his knees. And now the tribe of draughtsmen who evolve portraits of Mr. Gladstone—with the aid of photographs— out of their inner consciousness might observe that there are only three fingers on:the left hand; the first finger is no longer there, the knuckle being concealed with a circular black patch kept in its place by a narrow black riband drawn back and front of the palm. All traces of fatigue pass away as the eyes, large and luminous, keen and gray, rest with anger upon the enemy. The nostrils dilate, the lips—still close—work impatiently, the body leans forward, the hands gride upon the knees pressed outwards. In a mo- ment Mr. Gladstone is upon his feet! Say it is a field night, and that he has come from some political reception. He wears evening clothes and a flower. And when he comes down to the House, decorated with the spoils of the garden, the reporters sharpen their pencils, and members wait about the lobbies to hear lam. By what process the Liberal chief rumples the fronts of his dress-shirts is a secret as close as that of the age of the world. With a couple of quick steps he comes to the despatch-box at the corner of the table, and for an instant beams upon the House. Then he opens the flood-gates of his oratory, and deluges the Commons with superb eloquence. The timbre of his voice is delightful, gliding, mellow, dropping to the soft sound of well-stirred reeds by the river, rising to the full volume of the storm beating and bellying the sails of a ship at sea.—Scenes in the Commons.

EARLESTOWN. THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH DISPUTE. ANOTHER DISCHARGE OF THE ORGANIST. The many phases of the Earlestown Church dispute, and the varied complexions it has assumed since it originated some six months ago, have excited especial curiosity as to what feature it would next present to the parishioners of St. John the Baptist Church. The position of affairs seems to have been gradually going from bad to worse, and the nominally peaceful settlement arrived at after the arbitrae- tion by the Rev. Canon Hopwood has been a long way short of accomplishing what it was fondly hoped it would do. Al' most every individual in the parish welcomed the decision, but many persons exoressed the opinion that the last of the "dispute" had not been heard of, and these anticipatoing, , we regret to say, have been fully realised. The more respect- able Darishioners have practically been driven away from the church and now attend other places of worship in the neighbourhood. The Sunday school has been disorganised by the discharge of teachers, while beyond the vicar, (the Rev. T. R. Matthews), the curate (the Rev. H. E. Smith), and the sexton or church cleaner, there is not a single church officer about the parish. According to the athitra- tion decision of the Rev. Canon Hopwood, the pist was to be condoned and a fresh start made, and this was virtually agreed to by all the partiesconcerned, but it seems the vicar has made "a fresh start" in a somewhat peculiar vial. First, the discharge of the choir; secondly, the refusal to have any sidesmen, and consequently inability to obtain wardens; and thirdly, the discharge of the Sunday school teachers have all been matters of comment throughout the district, but this has been further eclipsed by another dis- charge of Mr. H. J. Darman, the organist. Last week end Mr. Darman received the following note from the Vicar: "The Vicarage. Earlestown, June sth, 1834. Dear sir,—l hereby inform you that your services se organist and choirmaster at St. John the Baptist Cu0r,„011 will Cease on the sth of July next.—Yours faithfully, T. r. MATTHEWS, Mr. M. J. Durman."—Upon the receipt of this communication Mr. Durman had a oonversation with the Vicar, and the latter stated that his reason for discharging him was that he (the Vicar) could not be responsible for th! payment of his salary. He added that during the month May £2 only was the total amount collected for five San: days, and he therefore could not guarantee the payment OK the salary. He also intimated that if Mr. Dorman did not wish to serve a month's notice he could give 111;) his post at once; but Mr. Darman did not give any &finite reply at that moment. On the following Sunday there were - not more than 30 adult persons present at the forenoon service, the congregation being principally composed of tile school children. The latter conducted themselve6 in a noisy and irreverent manner, and so incliner ent have the parishioners become that Sunda! , • after Sunday there is no elderly person to keep then quiet. On Sunday forenoon the vicar was compelled to ON.- rect the lads from the reading desk, and on one occasion dal" ing the service he had to leave the chancel and walk UP On aisle to rebuke the children. Mr. Durman again presided , the organ, bath in the forenoon and in the evening;. several members of the choir were in their accustoms" places. Owing to the continued absence of the Rev. 0. E. Smith (curate) through illness, the vicar (the Rev. ' ' Matthews) conducted the service, and preached o new, n occasions. We understand that only as was collecr;.. throughout the day. On the Monday Mr. Darman lieu another conversation with the vicar, and intimated to hins • that he had decided to at (once give up his post, find r , would not again preside at the organ in St. John's Chore'. . This decision of Mr. Darman is likely to be followed by the , abstention of every member of the choir, and a difficult,' en, , to the musical part of the service will thus be occasional* , The parishioners and public generally are now becoming so accustomed to these extraordinary occurrences that WY , are not easly surprised, but still it is customary to a 0 v".... "When and what shall the end be?"

HOUSE OF LORDS—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4-0. The House resuming after the VVhitsun recess. Lord Raglan and Lord Langford, the latter an Irish representa- tive peer, took their seats. Tun CONFERENCE :Replying to a question by Earl Stan- /013e, Earl GRANVILLE said that although very great pro- gress had been made in the communications with France With reference to Egypt he could only say the Govern.nent hoped to make a perfectly full statement in the course of next week. He appealed to Lord Stanhope whether it would not be better to reserve expression of opinion on the course taken by the Government till the full statement promised Was before them. Such a Statement would give Parliament au opportunity of taking action to prevent the country from being committed to any course the Government might be it- °tined to adopt. Lord Sexamscrav expressed the greatest satisfaction at receiving this pledge, and would not alloy it by criticising a policy of which the details were not yet known. Some conversation took place between Cord Northbrook and Lord Salisbury on the state of the navy, and at half. Peel five their lordships adjourned till Friday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. The Manchester, Bury, and Rochdale Tramways (Eaten- eion) Bill was ordered to be read a third time. MISCELLANEOL-S.—A proposal by Sir E. REED that the Cardiff Corporation should be empowered to contribute a anm of £lO,OOO for the purposes of the University College Of South Wales and Monmouthshire was, after some debate and on a division, agreed to by 185 votes against 141. The Proposal received the support of all the Welsh members who aPoke.—A Bill dealing with the Thames sewage was, on the Motion of Sir H. WOLFF, and with the consent of the Go- vernment, referred to a Select Committee.—A new writ was Ordered to be issued for Lincoln to fill the vacancy created ...sbY the death of Mr. Hinds Palmer—At the instance of Mr. rtylands, Mr. SHAW LEFEVRE promised to lay on the table a eopy of the agreement entered into with the Crown at the time when her Majesty came to the throne, in which the Government undertook to maintain and keep in repair Certain Royal palaces —Lord EDMOND FITZMAITRICE in- formed Mr. Stanhope that the Government were not aware of the existence of any treaty by which Russia was author- ised to occupy Sarakhs, on the western banks of the Heni Rad. There was a report that Russia was about to take Possession of the right bank of the Herißud at Old Sarakhs, and to make it over to the Turcomans. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN —Sir Joule HAY gave notice that on the Supplementary Estimate to be presented on ac- Count of the Egyptian campaign he would move a vote of thanks to the troops.—Replying to Mr. E. Gibson, Lord E. Prrattannlce said that in the despatch of the 21st May General Gordon had received full permission to adopt at the drat proper moment measures for his removal from Khar- toum, and for that of the Egyptians who had served him. The Government had not heard that the depatch had reached General Gordon.—This answer was received with loud laughter from the Conservative benches.—Replying to Mr. Bourke, the PRIME MINISTER made a statement with resPect to the negotiations with France identical with that given in the other House by Earl Granville. The Premier added a word of "respectful counsel" to members and gen- tlemen elsewhere to he upon their guard against erroneous and misleading statements, sometimes made with consi- derable confidence, as to the nature of the arrangements in contemplation.—ln reply to cross-examination by Sir S. Northcote and Mr. Bourke, Mr. GLADSTONE repeated the atatement of his belief that in the course of next week he Would be in a position to make the promised communica- tion. THE NEWRY RIOTS—Lord ARTHUR HILL asked whether the attention of the Chief Secretary had been drawn to the rePort by the Dublin correspondent of the Times as to the circumstancee attending the Newry riots.—Mr. T. O'Coeneon interposed with the question "whether the correspondent of the Times is not the well-known editor of the Orange organ."—Mr. TREVELYAN said that was true, and proceeded to read an official report. which placed a very different corn- Plexion on the affair. THE FRANCHISE BILL IN COMMITTEE. The consideration of the Franchise Bill was resumed in Committee at Clause 4—restriction of faggot votes—which was discussed in much detail.—Mr. C. BENTINCK, in the first place, moved to omit sub-section 4, which deprives of the franchise all owners of rent-charges except the owners Of the tithe-rent charge of a rectory or a vicarage.—Mr. GLADSTONE opposed the amendment, and vindicated the Conservative character of the clause, and ultimately the amendment was negatived by 162 to 77.—0 n the second ' eub-section, which provides that where there are two or. More joint tenants, or tenants in common of the same estate, one only should be entitled to vote.—Sir M. HICKS BRACE ' Pointed out that the language of this clause left it entirely to chance as to which of the tenants should be entitled. He formally moved to leave out the first word of the sub-sec- tion.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL admitted the apparent (lit- Acuity, but pointed out that they were proceeding on the lines of the Act of 1867, and it was worth remembering that not a single case of difficulty had arisen under it —The amendment was negatived.—After further discussion the clause was passed. On Clause 5, which issimilates the occupation qualifica- tion by providing that every man occupying any land or tenement of a clear annual value of £lO should be entitled to vote for such qualification in a county or borough.—Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON moved to reduce the franchise to £s. The ATTORNE (-GENERAL objected.—Mr. M`LAREN Would have supported the amendment if it would have been likely te bring in voters not already included, but its only object aPPeared to be to introduce faggot votes.—The amendment Was withdrawn, and the clause agreed to. Clause 6, providing that a voter should not vote in the ' county in respect of occupation of property in a borough, ' Was also agreed to. On Clause 7, defining household and lodger qualifications and other franchises and application of enactments relating 'thereto—Mr. RAIKES moved to insert the words "the occu- pation of a dwelling-house containing not less than two habitable rooms," the object being to restrict the 'qualifica- tion of dwellings of this character.—Mr. GLADSTONE Pointed Out that this amendment would introduce into a great enfranchising measure a disfranchising provision of LIM most sweeping character.—Mr. S. LEIGHTON and Sir E. ' WATKIN supported the amendment.—The ATTORNEY- WIRERAL pointed out that the bill was not one dealing with sanitary subjects. bat was an enfranchising measure.—The amendment was negatived without a divisiou.—Mr. MICK- INVOSH moved an amendment providing that non-payment Of Poor rate should be no disqualitiaation for the franchise. The LORD ADVOCATE opposed the amendment, which on a division was rejected by 194 to 9.—Clause 7 was then agreed to, as use also clause 8. On clause 9, which gives the definition and application of tile Rating Acts, Sir M. litcxs-Bgacx proposed to amend the second paragraph, which makes every person rated in respect of any lands and heritages which comprise any dwelling-house, when applied to by the assessor to give an accurate written list of the names and designations of all Men other than himself being inhabitant occupiers of such dwelling-house, liable on summary conviction to a penalty Of £5 if he fail to do so. He wished to protect the owner by the insertion of the word "wilfully."—The ATTORNEY- aRNERAL opposed the amendment, and it was withdrawn.— E. CLARKE proposed instead the insertion of the words I:without reasonable excuse."—The Committee divided, and the amendment was rejected by 192 votes against 95.--A. Proposal by Mr. Warten to reduce the penalty under th 3 clause from £5 to 40s in Scotland was accepted by the Attorney-General amidst Opposition cheers.—Mr. WRITLET luoved to insert words providing that the dwelling-house to Which the clause referred should be separately rated.—The amendment was negatived, and the clause as amended was agreed to. Clause 10 having been agreed to without amendment, Sir M. Moro-Mann proposed as an amendment to clause 11, relating to construction, that " clear yearly value " should mean in England rateable value.--The ATTORNEY-GENERAL showed that the amendment would not conduce to unifor- mity, beeaass rateable value in England varied in different eountiet—After some debate the Committee divided, and the amendment was rejected by 176 to 81. Clause 12, the last in the bill, was then agreed to amidst loud cheers. Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the new clauses stood next on the paper ; therefore this would be a convenient time to re- Port progress. Progress was then reported and the House resumed. MISCELLANEOUS.—The LORD ADVOCATE moved the second reading of the Burgh Police and Health (Scotland) Bill, ex- plaining that its object was the consolidation of numerous existing Acts. If the measure was read a second time he sheald move its reference to a Select Committee. (Hear, hear.)—The bill, after some observations from Sir R. Cross and Mr. Anderson, was read a second time, and referred to a Select Committee.—The House went into Committee on the R,.,eyal Courts of Justice Bill, and progress was reported.— The Marriage Legalisation Bill WAS read a second time.—ln Committee on the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill Clauses 1 and 2 were agreed to. and progress was then reported.— Oti motion of Mr. Feweere, the Post Office Protection sill was discharged, to be introduced in the House of Lords. --Mr. C. SYKES moved the second reading of the Fisheries (Oyster, Crab, and Lobster) Act (1877) Amendment The bill was read a second time amidst cheers. The House adjourned at 1-20. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 2-10. DISESTABLISHMENT IN WALES—Mr. DILLWYN postponed his motion in favour of the Disestablishment of the Church ~ Wales to this day four weeks. (Hear', hear.)--Nir. "atrroN, on the same day; will bring forward his motion With reference to bills from the House of Lords. TEE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACIES.—Mr. Anderson was in- formed by Lord E. FITZNIATIRICE that representations had keen made to the Government of the United States sugges- tive of the duty of friendly Powers in regard to dynamite ,Conspiracies ; but the reply to the last communication oad not yet been received. He could not give any Pledge that the correspondence should be laid on the table. THE FRENCH IN MADAGASCAR —ln reply to Mr. A. Bart- lett, Lord E. Frrzmarmtcs said the Crovernment had not leceived any confirmation of the statement that the French 'forces invading Madagascar are to be increased by troops 10101 Tonquin, and that a march on the capital is to be undertaken. As to the steps which were being taken to ob- Min compensation for the losses sustained by Britfsh sub- , jects, his lordship said the consular staff had been largely jacreakied, and referred the hon. member to a previous reply r which he had made.—Mr: ASHMEAD-BARTLETT said he tt,b9uld call attention to the inaction of the Government in "is matter on the diplomatic fund.
L

TURKISH TROOPS POR EGYPT.—LyTd. R. CETTRCHILI. asked the Prime Minister whether, as in the case of negotia- tions with France, he will undertake to place before the House any negotiations or communications which have passed or may be passing between Great Britain and Turkey with respect to the despatch of Turkish troops to Egypt or , the Soudan before any action can be taken by Turkey upon r sum] negotiations or communications?—Mr. GLADSTONE said in the present disturbed state of the Soudan he could not undertake to communicate to the House on all occasions the measures which the Government were taking; but in the present instance he did not think that this difficulty arose. The noble lord had asked a question about the state- ments which had been made that England had proposed to Turkey to send troops to the Soudan. There was no founda- tion for that report. There had been some communications upon a subject which was mentioned in a Blue Book already before the House, with reference to certain ports in the Red Sea, but they had made no progress. THE FRANCHISE BILL —FEMATE STIFFRAGE

. The House then resumed the Committee upon the Fran- chise Bill, the new clauses being considered. Mr. ECROYD moved to insert after clause 3 the following new clause :—" Every man who is the owner cif a copyhold estate or of a leasehold originally created for a term of not less than 40 years in any land or tenement in the United Kingdom of a clear yearly value of £4 or more shall be en- titled after the passing of this Act to be registered as a voter, and when registered to vote at an election in like manner as a freeholder."—Mr. GLADSTONE said it might be desirable in the future to introduce some such change as this, but for the present it was one of a series of amend- ments of small importance which, if they were all intro- duced, would seriously imperil the progress of the Bill, and could not, therefore, be entertained.—Several Conservative members described this as a curt way of disposing of the amendment, but on a division it was rejected by 168 to 76. Mr. ECROYD then moved that the Committee insert a new clause providing that every man qualified to be registered as a voter in respect of the ownership of any freehold. copy- hold, or leasehold estate in a county or borough shall, after the passing of the Act, when duly registered, be entitled to vote in respect of such qualification at an election in the county or borough wherein the estate is situated, whether he be or be not also entitled to vote at such election in respect of an occupation or lodger franchise.—Mr. GLADSTONE said they could not accede to the proposal, which meant a com- plete establishment of the double vote.—On a division it was rejected by 236 against 122. ' •

Mr. BRYCE moved for the insertion of a clause reducing the term of residence which qualifies a man for the franchise from twelve to six months.—Mr. GLADSTONE said it was a question which would come up better on a Registration Bill, and he hoped, therefore, it would not be pressed.—The amendment was negatived without a division. At half-past. five Mr. WOODALL'S motion for the enfran- chisement of women was reached. The hon. member moved this in a speech which the Prime Minister justly character- ised as eloquent and able. He marshalled with great skill all the arguments in favour of woman's suffrage made familiar to the House through a long series ot sessions. He disclaimed all intention of imperilling the Franchise Bill, and observed that it had not been pointed out in what way the adoption of his motion would hurt the Franchise Bill.

Mr. GLADSTONE, who followed, said there were two ques- tions involved in the proposal. One was whether woman should be enfranchised, and the second whether such en- franchisement should be effected by the introduction of a clause in the present bill. On the first point he contented himself by observing that the question was one of great difficulty, upon which nothing hasty ought to be done, and above all, it should be considered separate from party con- flict. With respe3t to the second question, he entertained the opinion himself, and declared it on the part of his col- leagues, that it was "not fit, but unfit" to attempt to effect this enfranchisement by the introduction of a clause in committee on the present bill. It would be a breach of duty on his part to consent to such a course. The ship was already loaded with as much cargo as it could fully bear, and amid loud cheering he declared that if the clause were carried the Government would disclaim all further res- ponsibility for the Franchise Bill. He freely admitted the question was one for full consideration, and neither himself nor other members of the Cabinet would attempt to bind their colleagues to the matter supposing it were taken out of the vortex of political warfare. But as the matter now stood he should offer the proposal the strongest opposition in his power.—lt was just ten mintues to seven when the Premier concluded, and on the motion of Lord JOAN MAN- NERS progress was reported, and the sitting suspended. Upon resuming at nine o'clock the House was immediately counted out.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS...--WEDWESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS...--WEDWESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock.

LOCAL TELEPHONE ACCOMMODATION. - Mr. WHITLEY gave notice that to-morrow he would ask the Postmaster- General whether he is aware that the Postoffice has refused to allow the same advantages of telephonic intercommunica- tion to Liverpool and Birkenhead, which are divided by the river Mersey, as are allowed to Manchester and Salford, which are divided by the river Irwell ; and whether he is prepared to reconsider the application of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Company to establish communication between the two licensed areas, so as to give to the people of Liverpool and Birkenhead the facilities which are enjoyed by Manchester and Salford.—Mr. BRIGGS also gave notice that to-morrow he would ask the Postmaster-General whether he is aware that the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company are desirous to open all offices in the various towns in their district, whereby for a small payment the public may converse with subscribers to the Telephone exchange; whether he is aware of the existence of such accommodation in cities on the continent of Europe and America, where the telephone is in use ; whether the Postmaster-General insists upon the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company charging Is each time such facility is afforded; and whether be can see his way to so relax these terms as to enable the company to afford the public the great convenience referred to.

THE REPORTED FALL OF BERBER.—Sir H. MAXWELL asked the Secretary to the Admiralty (in the absence of Lord Fitzmaurice) if he could give the House any informa- tion whether the reported fall of Berber was confirmed or otherwise 2—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, said any news of that sort would not be likely to come to the Admiralty. He had not heard of it.—At a later period of the sitting, Lord E. FITZMAIIRICE, replying tu, Mr. Arnold, said on June 9 Mr. Egerton telegraphed that Major Kitchener telegraphed from Korosko a Berberan report, unconfirmed to him from other sources, that Berher had fallen. On the 9th a mes- senger arrived at Suakim, who had left Berber on the 3rd, and had seen Hussein Pasha Khalifa. The messenger re- ported to Major Chermside that steamers were working be- low Berber, and barges up to Khartoum, that the road west of the Nile was fairly safe, that provisions at Berber were cheap, and there was no particular danger there. On the 10th of June Mr. Egerton telegraphed that Major Kitchener telegraphed that Berber was surprised and nearly the whole garrison massacreed nine days ago. "This news," Mr. Egerton says, "is difficult to believe, being sent by pass from the Mandi's Emir to K halifa's sons, and news brought by Chermside's messengers being of later date."—ln reply to Lord R. Churchill, Lord E. FITZMAIIRICE said the Foreign Office had received no news in reference to an attack on Wadi Haifa. NEW WRIT —On the motion of Mr. WINN, a new writ was ordered to be issued for Mid-Surrey in the place of Sir H. W. Peek, Bart., who has accepted the Chiltern Hun- dreds.

SCOTCH ECCLESIASTICAL BILL.—Mr. J. A. CAMPBELL, in moving the second reading of the Ecclesiastical Assessments (Scotland) Bill, said the measure was designed to remove a grievance occasioned by the present state of the law, which operated greatly to the injury of the church in Scotland. The bill was not supported as a party measure, Liberals as well as Conservatives having petitioned in its favour • nor did it propose to deal with more than 914 of the parishes of Scotland, although the number of Established Church parishes in that country was L5Ol. The bill only applied to Vae rural districts, leaving the burghs untouched.—Mr. A. ELLIOT moved as an amendment that no measure would I be satisfactory which proposed to continue for the provision and maintenance of ecclesiastical buildings belonging to one religious denomination any system of compulsory general assessment.—Mr. R. BRUCE seconded the amendment.—The bill was supported by Sir J. Hay, Mr. A. Balfour, and Mr. Dalrymple, and opposed by Mr. Dick Peddie, Mr. Anderson, Sir E. Colebrook, and Sir A. Gordon.—Lord C. CAMPBELL did not think the bill would effect the object in view, or that I the time chosen for its introduction was a favourable one.— Mr. Williamson and Mr. Ramsay also opposed the The L0311)-ADTOCATX, speaking on behalf of the Govern- ment, said they could not accept the measure, but felt bound to give their support to the amendment. The bill admitted that it was not just in principle to assess the bur- dens it dealt with on land, and proposed to make the rates voluntary up to a certain point, at which it stopped short, leaving the assessment compulsory on the part of a certain class of persons. He could not see what principle there was in this.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE urged that if it were desired, not only to reject the bill, but to pass the amendment, those who did so would be establishing a dangerous principle that would have a much wider effect than appeared on the face of it, and might be used in a manner that would be highly objectionable.—AfLr a few remarks from Mr. LEWIS, who charged the oppponents of the bill with insincerity in desir- ing the removal of a grievance which, when offered to them, they refused to accept, the House divided, the numbers be- ing:—For the second reading, 103; against, 160; majority, sT.—Colonel ALEXANDER moved that the debate be ad- journed.—The SPEAKER, pointing to the clock, which indi- cated a quarter to six, sal' I the debite stood adjourned under the standing orders, applicable to Wednesday's sittings. The House adjourned at 5-55. HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH SYSTEM.—Mr. Fawcett was subjected to a good deal of questioning as to telegraphic and telephonic communication in Lancashire.—Mr. WHIT- LEY wished to know whether Liverpool and Birkenhead could not be allowed the same facilities for communication as are enjoyed by Manchester and Salford, but though the proposition is a ressonable one, the Postmaster was unable to agree to it, because, unlike Manchester and Salford, Liverpool and Birkenhead each has its own postal and tele- graphic system. Mr. Briggs then enquired whether the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company could be al- lowed to open call-offices for the use of tke public at a less charge than one shilling a time; but Mr. Fawcett did not see his way to granting this concession. Mr. Jacob Bright next took up the cause of the Telephone Company, with a view to procuring for it liberty to organise a cheap telephone system between distant towns in Lancashire and Cheshire ; but the Postmaster, having regard to the public interests,

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JTJNE 14, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JTJNE 14, 1884.

again declined to meet the views of the Telephone Com- pany. MADAGASCAIL.—Sussia's progress in Central Asia is a matter on which Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett is manifesting con- siderable anxiety, but neither on this subject nor as to the claims of British subjects in Madagascar was Lord E. Fitzmaurice able to satisfy the member for Rye last night and Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett gave notice that he would call attention to the ignorance and inactivity of the Government as to affairs in Madagascar. THE BRADLAUGH QUESTION.—A conversation was raised on the Brad laugh case through a question being asked by Sir H. D. Wolff as to whether' ill face of the opinions he had already expressed, the Lord Chief Justice would be allowed to preside in the matter of the The Queen v. Brad- laugh.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL administered a sharp rebuke to the member for Portsmouth for his personal references, and informed him with emphasis that Her Majesty's Government could not, and certainly would not take any steps whatever to interfere in any way with the selection of the Judges who were to try any particular case. THE ABYSSINIAN MISSION.—IO reply to Mr. Bourke, Lord E. Frrahreunrcg stated that beyond what he read on Wed- nesday no further information had been received at the Foreign Office in regard to Berber, but in regard to Admiral Hewett's mission a telegram bad been received at the Ad- miralty, dated Adowa, 3rd June, stating that the mission had been successful and that the Admiral would leave for the coast on the 4th of June. A treaty was signed securing free transit through Abyssinia from that day, and also a slave trade treaty. THE FRANCHISE SILL : REJECTION OF THE WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE CLAUSE.—Lord J. MANNERS resumed the debate on Mr. Woodall's amendment to the Franchise Bill, and promised his cordial support to the proposal.—Mr. LEATHAM as strongly took the opposite view, and challenged Mr. Woodall to get upon his side the women of England if he could, and then his motion would have some degree of sub- stance.—Mr. STANSFIELD followed, and complained that the Premier had placed those who thought as he did in a painful position. He could see no danger in the clause itself to the bill, and thought the peril must lay within the Cabinet. —The debate was continued at great length by Mr. Newde- gate. Lord Folkestone, Baron de Worms, Mr. Cowen, Mr. Bryce, Mr. Labouchere, Sir W. Lawson, who dared the Go- vernment to throw up the bill if the clause were carried, Mr. GOSCHEN, who dwelt upon the fact that the measure would enfranchise women lodgers as well as house- holders, and Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, who supported the clause. _ _ .
--„,. The committee divided on Mr. Woodall's clause. For 135 Against 271
Majority for the Government 136 The result was received with cheers.—On the motion of Mr. GLADSTONE progress was then reported, and the House resumed.

NATIONAL DEBT (CONVERSION OF STOCK) BILL.—On the motion for going into Cornmi,tee on this Bill, Mr. HUB- BARD moved an amendment, which was negatived, and the House went into Committee.—On clause 1, Mr. W. FOWLER moved to report progress —The CHANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER opposed, and the motion was negatived by 58 votes against 23.—Mr. W. FOWLER then moved an amend- ment that only one stock of 21 per cent, at par should be issued.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER opposed the amendment as fatal to the Bill.—After discussion, the amendment was withdrawn.—Several other clauses were also agreed to, and progress was reported.
, ships at Massowah. Several deaths from heat apoplexy have occurred.
Tiii-E-L.ECTIONS IN EELGIUM.-A MINISTERIAL
CRII3IS.

BnussEts, Tyrone:v.—The partial elections to the Belgian Chamber of Deputies took place here to-day, and result.i in the victory of the Clerical party by a majority of Lan votes. The Liberals, who had a majority of 20 votes in the Chamber, have lost 26 seats, and the Clerical party will have a majority in the new Chamber of 32 votes. In the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg all the Liberal candidates have been re-elected by a large majority. At Antwerp it is expected that the Catholics will have a majority of 1,000 votes.

. BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY MIDATIGHT.—BrusseIs was again to-night the scene of serious disorder. The principal quar- ters of the city were invested by a mob, who created great disturbances by singing, shouting, and hooting. Street fighting occurred at several parts. A party of people broke the windows and shutters of a Roman Catholic library, and, making their way into the house, tore down the Papal arms, besides doing other damage. Five arrests were made by the police. RESIGNATION OF THE BELGIAN MINISTRY.

BRUSSELS, THURSD&Y.-It is officially announced that the Ministry tendered its resignation to the King yesterday. ADMIRAL HEWETT'S MISSION. ADEN, THURSDAY.-A telegram has been received here from Admiral Hewett, announcing his safe arrival at the coast on his return from Abyssinia. Her Majesty's gunboat. Ranger, has arrived here. NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT._.

- WELLINGTON (NEW ZEALAND), THIIIODAY.—Tbe HOU9O of Representatives has passed a vote of want of confidence in the Ministry. In consequence of the defeat of the Gov- ernment, Parliament is expected to be dissolved.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. BERBER AND KHARTOUM.

CAIRO, SUNDAY—The English and Egyptian military authorities here give no credence to the news from Suakim reporting the fall of Berber, Sir Evelyn Wood has received a telegram from Major Trotter at Wadi Haifa, stating that a man named Abdallah Ameer arrived here from Dongola on the 4th inst., and reported that Khartoum was strongly fortified, and that there was a plentiful supply of wheat in the city. A steamer had come out on the Nile and was daily firing upon the rebels along the banks. The Nile was rising well, and the rebels, fearing the arrival of an army from Cairo, were about to retire te Kordofan. The position of affairs at Sennaar remains unchanged. Nubar Pasha has telegraphed to the Governor of Dongola to send messengers to El Obeid, with a view to obtaining the release of the Austrian mission at that place. Orders have been received from London that Lieutenant-General Stephenson, com- rnander-in-chief of the British forces in Egypt, must be consulted concerning all movements of troops be- longing to the army under command of Sir Evelyn Wood. The Khedive this afternoon reviewed the troops prior to their departure from Suakim and Upper Egypt, which is fixed as follows --The fifth battalion will leave here to- morrow evening for Suez, where it will embark on the fol- lowing day for Suakim, together with the small detachment of artillery. The cavalry will proceed on Tuesday to Siout by rail, and thence by road to Assouan. A detachment of artillery will at the same time leave by rail for Siout, and thence by river to Assouan. PORT SAID, SATURDAY.—The remainder of the Marines here have been ordered to Suakim. They will be replaced at Port Said by a detachment of the Cameron Highlanders, stationed at Hamlett. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The party under Captain Hammill and Major Marriott have returned to Wady Haifa after having made their way to the Third Cataract. They report that the country they traversed was tranquil, and the people ex- pressed delight at the defeat of the rebels at Debbeh by the Governor of Dongola. Major Chermside telegraphs as fol- lows from Suakim :—A paid scout of mine left Berber six days ago, after returning to that place from Khartoum, whither he had been sent in a boat by Hussein Pasha Khalifa. During a short stay of three hours at Khartoum, he was met by an Englishman, who banded him a bulky letter. Between Berber and Suakim the scout was pursued and killed by the rebels, who seized the letter, which was too big to be swallowed. His companion, however, suc- ceeded in escaping, and reports that all was quiet at Khar- toum. The town was in the hands of the Government, and provisions were cheap. Khartoum and Berber are, he de- clares, less closely invested than Suakim. Digma's reports are'only credited eastward of Kokreh. Another paid spy from Digma'a camp reports that the False Prophet has retired from Kordofan inland. The messenger who brought the news to the rebel camp has been imprisoned by Digma. Tele- grams from Korosko state that dissensions have arisen among the sheikhs under Maior Kitchener. The Bedouins refuse to proceed beyond Korosko or to engage in any warfare, that being outside their country. An unofficial telegram has been received that a battle was fought by the defenders of Berber on the 2nd of June. The result was not known. Mr. Cuzzi is well treated by the rebels. MOVEMENTS AT SUAKIM.

SITAKIM, MONDAY.—This place was subjected to a sharp attack last night, and the firing on both sides was very heavy for about an hour, but no casualties are reported on either side. The Iris arrived to-day with 250 marines. Her Majesty's gunboat Coquette has arrived from Massowah, having been delayed on her voyage by an accident to her machinery. She brings news that Admiral Hewett's treaty bas been accepted in principle by King John, and that the details are not likely to cause difficulties. Admiral Hewett was expected CO return to Massowah shortly after the Coquette left.

div.head: REPORTED MASSACRE AT BERBER.
div.p: REPORTED MASSACRE AT BERBER.

CAIRO, TIJESDAY.-A report has reached here to-day stating that Hussein Khalifa Pasha, the Governor, and his whole family, together with the men of the garrison faith- ful to the Khedive, and all the European traders remaining at Berber, were massacred by the rebels nine days ago. Cent°, TUESDAY, 9-35 P.M.—The report of a massacre at Berber is based upon a telegram from Major Kitchener at Korosko, according to which a person calling himself the Ameer of the False Prophet, has written a letter containing the intelligence. Sir Evelyn Woed gives no credence to the news.

div.head: RUNOURED FALL OF BERBER..
div.p: THE RUNOURED FALL OF BERBER..

- A " Times " second edition, on Thursday, contained the following telegram from its own correspondent :—" Haifa, June 11, midnight News has reached here that Berber has fallen. This event is supposed to have happened about twelve days ago. It is stated that the troops fought until their ammunition was exhausted, and then the rebels entered the town and massacred nearly all the soldiers and inhabi- tants. Hussein Pasha Khayla, the Governor of Berber, and the chief of the Fagara tribe are reported to have been badly wounded, and are prisoners with 50 other survivors. There were in Berber 1.300 soldiers and 500 Fagars as a garrison. I am informed that the rebel general, Anair Abullah, had collec- ted around Berber a force of 100,000 men. It is also stated that after the fall of Berber 30,000 Arabs were dispatched to invest Dongola, the Governor apparently ignorant of the fall of Berber, for he has telegraphed here that no news has come down the river. Fifty Bashi-Bazonks with their chief who were waiting here to take horses to Dongola, bolted the Inight before last, apparently in the direction of Dongola. The armoured steamer Nassif Kher arrived here this after- noon. but left immediately with Captains ilaminill, Tyr- whitt, and Marriott. ' THE RUMOURED TURKISH EXPEDITION.: CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.-The Porte has received no invitation from the British Government to take part in an expedition to the Soudan. The Ottoman Government de- clines to appoint a delegate to the Conference unless the whole Egyptian question be submitted to the representatives of the Powers or a previous understanding concerning Egypt be arrived at between England and Turkey. GERMANY, ENGLAND, AND EGYPT. BERLIN, TUESDAY—Lord AMpttiffl, the British Ambassa- dor, was received by Prince Bismarck yesterday, and had a long conversation with the Imperial Chancellor. It is be- lieved that the interview, which was at the ambassador's special request, had reference to the question of the Con- ference. THE ABYSSINIAN MISSION. ADOWA (vie ADEN), Max 29.—The King arrived on the 25th. The Admiral presented Queen Victoria's letter and Captain Speedy Lord Napier's. Kivg John said that but for the English he would not now hold the crown. He owed much to them, and knew that they only advised for Abys- sinia's benefit. He placed himself unreservedly in their hands. The King's sentiments may be sincere, but through his suspicions of the exact nature of the mission, fostered by unscrupulous Eorepeans, who are jealous of England's interest in the country, we have been virtually kept prisoners for five weeks. It is owing entirely to the tact and patience of the Admiral that the mission has come to a successful termination. Only the signature of the treaty is now required, and then the Admiral and his party will return to the coast immediately. Great sickness prevails in the
