div.head: FIGHTING IN ZULULAND.
div.p: FIGHTING IN ZULULAND.

- - DURBAN, SATURDAY.— Further collisions have occurred in the Reserve between the Usutos and the Loyals, in which the former, who were the aggressors, were defeated. The Boers, aided by a strong force of Usutos, have invaded Usibepu's territory. THE ILLNESS OF THE PRINCE OF 'ORANGE.

THE HAGUE, THIIR—SMIY.—The Prince of Orange was prevented from sleeping last night by an incessant cough, and is in consequence suffering from drowsiness to-day, although the intestinal symptoms are satisfactory. His Royal Highness is in a very weak state. THE CRISIS IN NORWAY.

CHRISTIANA, SIINDAY.—The new Conservative Ministry has entirely broken down. The King has had several com- munications with Professor Broch and Mr. Sverdrup, the leader of the Liberal party. Last night, at a meeting of the Liberal majority of the Storthing, a compromise was dis- cussed, the principal point being that the King should sanc- tion a new bill which would be introduced for the admission of Ministers to seats in the Storthing. ELECTION RIOT IN HUNGARY. . .
VIENNA, disturbance broke out at an election meeting at Miedspeel, Hungary,' yesterday, and in the fight- ing which ensued five persons were killed and Tour woun- ded.
THE VIENNA MURDERS.

VIENNA, MONDIY.I-IT-Te. 'final proceedings in the trial of Hermann Steil macher began to-day. The prisoner confessed to the murder of the detective Bloeck, which, he said, had been committed in furtherance of Anarchist designs ; but he denied having been concerned in the murder of, the money- changer, Herr Eisert. Several witneSses, however, deposed that they recognised Kammerer as one of the assassins of Herr Eisert ; and evidence was also adduced to the effect that a pencil found on the murdered man's premises corres: ponded exactly with eleven other pencils discovered in Steil- macher's lodgings. VIENNA, TITESDAY.—The Anarchist, Herman Stelmacher, charged with the murder of Detective Bloech and with be- ing an accomplice in the murder of the money changer Eisert, has been found guilty on all counts of the indictment and sentenced to death. GERMANY.—THE NEW PARLIAMENT _BUILDING.

.--.— BERLIN, MONDAY.—The foundation stone of the new Ger- man Parliament House was laid this morning by the Empe- ror William, who was accompanied by the Crown Prince and Princess and their sons and the other members of the Prussian Royal Family. Prince Bismarck read the docu- ment drawn up by the Emperor which was sabsequently de- pesited in the cavity of the foundation stone. In this docu- ment the emperor points out how, through the glorious successes which bad attended the arms of the United Ger- man races, the Empire had attained a pitch of greatness un- dreamed of, and how by the enthusiasm of the people and the confidence prevailing between the Federal Governments, Germany had gained strength to protect by her own power, the Constitution and the National development, and to take into her own hands the care of the National prosperity. Notwithstanding the unfavourable weather, the ceremony passed off very successfally.—The newspapers to-day state that the Transvaal Deputation intends to conclude a com- mercial treaty with Germany, by which the latter will be placed on the most favoured nation footing. THE PRINCE OF WALES. WIESBADEN, SIINDAY.—The Prince and Princess of Wales and the young Princesses and suite attended divine service this morning at the English church. Since the Prince's arrival the weather has been unfavourable, preventing any excursions in the neighbourhood. DIPLOMATIC RUPTURE BETWEEN SERVIA. AND

div.head: BULGARIA.
div.p: BULGARIA.

BELGRADE, SATURDAY.—M. Zankoff, the Bulgarian Pre- mier, has caused the Prefects of Widdin to occupy the fron- tier post of Bregovo, near Negotine, driving out four Servian Guards, who had occupied the post since the Treaty of Ber- lin. The Skuptschina to-day unanimously approved the action of the Government, and declared that it was ready to rise in defence of Servian rights. SOPHIA, MONDAY.—The Bulgarian Government made a last attempt the day before yesterday to prevent a rupture with Servia. The Servian diplomatic agent, however, in- sisted upon the execution of the demands contained in the last Servian note. It is estimated that the number of Ser- vian emigrants, including women and children, in Bulgaria does not exceed forty. BELGRADE, Tunsnev.—Diplomatic relations between Ser- via and Bulgaria are now broken off. SOFIA, WEDNESDAY.—M. Gueschoff, the Bulgarian diplo- matic agent, having, in reply to his inquiry, received infor- mation from his Government that the diplomatic relations between Servia and Bulgaria had been broken off, has now left Belgrade. It is officially stated that the number of Ser- vian emigrants at present in Bulgaria is about forty. No party of emigrants has ever crossed the Servian frontier, and nothing is known here of the alleged incursions of Bul- garian marauders into Servia. The announcements to this effect in Servia are declared here to be devoid of foundation

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Broad Arrow stales that, all things being equal, the expedition for the relief of General Gordon will be on its way to Khartoum in six or seven weeks. Mr. Samuel Morley, speaking at Bromley. Kent, on Tues- day night, said they were not safe about the Franchise Bill. Two million new voters were entitled .to vote whether a Re- distribution Bill were passed or not. THE LATE DEAN OF BANGOR—The members of the North Wales Elementary Scholarship Association have de- cided to establish a scholarship to the memory of the late Dean Edwards, who was president of the association.

THE LABE DISTRICT.—ESaIWaite, One of the most pic- turesque of the Cumberland and Westmoreland lakes, which has been closed to the public for the past seven years, as a result of legal proceedings taken by Colonel Miles Sandy s in 1875 to maintain his rights, will, it is now announced, be open to the public in future as before. FATAL ACCIDENT To EXCIIRSIONISTS.—On Sunday after- noon the funnel of a Thames steamer bound for Kew came in contact with Battersea Bridge, and felt among the pas- sengers, severely injuring Martha Higson and Martha Ellen Coniston, two excursionists from Manchester, who were re- moved to the hospital. The accident has since resulted in the death of Mrs. Martha Higson. Her married daughter, Mrs. Marther Ellen Coulson, lies in a precarious condition.

THE ORGANISED ATTIMPT TO 11117RDER NEAR CORE.—On I Tuesday, 24 prisoners were charged before Captain Stokes, stipendiary magistrate, at Cork, with having formed part of ' the mob of sixty persons who assembled with arms and at- tempted to take the life of John Creed, at Donoughinore on the 2nd inst., on which occasion Creed received several ;hot wounds. Twelve of the number, including two women who organised the attacking party, were returned for trial at the assizes. The other eleven were discharged for the present. FATAL QUARREL OVER A PENNY—The Leicester police have aporehended a man named Alfred Chapman, an iron turner, charged with killing an ostler, named Arthur Cockeril I. Chapman and several others were playing bagatelle in a public-house, when Chapman bet a penny that a certain stroke could not be repeated. Chapman lost, but declined to pay, and a quarrel ensued. Chapman knocked two men down, biting one on the cheek and arms; he then knocked deceased down, breaking his leg. Cockerill was removed to the infir- mary, where he expired. ' A DISCOVERY.-.A diver engaged in diving operations off the coast opposite Gibraltar, under Apes Hill, with the ob- ject of obtaining the whereabouts of a recent wreck, has discovered from eighty to one hundred large guns, mostly 24 and 32 pounders, and also two large anchors. They are supposed to have belonged to some large line of battle ship which sank in the old war, possibly after the battle of Tra- falgar. As there was no apparatus for the purpose, none of the guns were brought up, so that it has not been possible to ascertain their nationality. ORANGEMEN V. NATIONALISTS AT NEWRY.—Newry was in a state of great excitement on Sunday. The Nationalists succeeded in holding their meeting, but the counter demon- stration was proclaimed. This action am the part of the Lord Lieutenant gave rise to much indignation, and the authorities fearing serious consequences, caused large bodies of police to patrol the town. The military were called out, and grave fears were entertained that the peace would be broken. The meeting of the Nationalists passed off quietly, but on returning home serious rioting took place. The Orange Hall was attacked, and the inmates had to defend themselves. Military and police also came to their assis- tance. Several persons were injured. The police succeeded in arresting four of the Nationalists who were caught in the act of throwing atones. They also entered the Orange Hall and arrested several Orangemen. slum ciumpAGNE.—The champagne districts of the Conti- nent produce some 300,000,000 bgttles annually. Only one- half of this quantity is exported, and yet England and America alone are said to consume more than twice this vast production. From whence does the balance come? From the apple orchards on both aides the Atlantic I Yes, it is these apple orchards that are responsible for most of the cheap champagLea.

1 Baker Pasha has left London for Cairo, whither he has 1 'kr IC E H AND S I suddenly been ordered to take up his command in the Egyp- ..1.11 Han army. J. H. m-Dartby, proposed by Mr. A. Geoghegan, and seconded by Mr. Kilkelly, was returned unopposed for , .11 1i ICE Athlone on Thursday. J.l_ AND XT It is reported from Madrid that twelve workmen have I\TI C E H AND been killed by the falling in of one of the tunnels on the -:-1 Austrian line.

Mr. Francis J. Summer, of Glossop and Hayfield, died in London on Thursday morning. The deceased gentleman was one of the largest landowners in North Derbyshire. was a deputy-lieutenant and magistrate, and had been twice Mayor of Glossop. ACCIDENT AT IRON WORIIS.—Six workmen were seriously injured on Thursday at the Yorkshire Steel and Iron Works, Penistone, by the explosion of a vessel containing molten steel, which had by some misfortune been overturned into a pool of water. Three of the men are not expected to re- cover. FATAL ACCIDENT—TWO farmers, named respectively Duff and M'Laren, were driving near Blairgowrie on Thurs- day evening, when the horse took fright. Both tbe men were thrown out; Duff was killed instantly by receiving a kick on the head from the horse, and his companion was mortally injured. DEATH SENTENCE COMMUTED —The Home Secretary has taken the unusual course of reducing the sentence of death passed upon a man named Smith, at the Durham Assizes, for wife murder to one of penal servitude for ten years. The , deceased woman was a persen of the roost abandoned char- ! ocher, and when he committed the crime the prisoner was labouring under intense provocation. COLLIERY PROPRIETORS FINED.—At Bolton, on Thurs- day morning, Messrs. Entwistle and Co., of Cranberry Moss Colliery, near Darwen, were tined 40s and costs, for not pro- viding sufficient places of refuge in the Jig Brow. A boy went down the pit, although warned not to do so, and was killed by tubs of coal. It was shown that the places of re- fuge were both inadequate and neglected. A LION'S VAN OYERTHELOWN.—An alarming accident occurred to Wombwell's menagerie while on the way to Stourbridge on Thursday morning. The horses drawing the van of six lions were startled by a steam tram, and they swerved and overthrew the caravan with a crash upon its side. Great alarm was felt at first at the possible escape of the lions. The ironwork, however, kept right, and penned them in.

SALE OF ANTI-VACCINATORS' GOODS —At Leicester, on Thursday morning, the goods of twenty persons who had declined to pay fines for the non-vaccination of their chil- dren were gold by public auction. Chief-Constable Duns and fifty policemen were present to preserve order and to protect the auctioneer. The sale was very disorderly, bat no violence was used. At a meeting afterwards, resolutions were passed condemning the acts which permitted the break- 1 iag up of people's homes under such circumstances. SACRILEGE IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY.—For a third time a new bead has just been placed upon the carving of Major John Andre, in the beautiful fresco upon his tomb in West- minster Abbey. Exactly six cases of sacrilege have occur- red at this tomb. The heads of George Washington and of Major Andra, both being prominent in the fresco, have been three times stolen respectively. Americans are fond of tak- ing home samples of what they see in the "old country," and the tomb of this unfortunate English gentleman Ins, it is aupposed, specially suffered in this way. SERIOUS MISHAP TO A CUNARD STEAMER.—The Press Association Queenstown correspondent telegraphs :—Pas- sengers who landed here on Thursday morning from the I Cunard Line steamer Aurania, from New York, state that the previous evening, during a dense fog, the vessel ran on the Bull Rock, near Dorsey Island, on the south-west coast of Ireland. Considerable excitement prevailed among the passengers, and preparations were made to lower the boats, but the Aurania was backed off without apparent damage, arrived here safely on Thursday morning, and then pro- ceeded for Liverpool. THE DEVONSHIRE MYSTERY.—lnterest in the death of Mrs. Shortland has not subsided with the discharge of her husband. N3W he has been liberated, Mr. Shortland, who is a barrister, freely asserts that his careful sifting of all the facts convinces him that his wife's death by accident Was impossible, and by suicide extremely improbable. His be- lief is that she was murdered, or at all events rendered in- sensible before being put into the pond, and he intends to proceed to London forthwith to lay before the Home Secre- tary an elaborate statement he is preparing, with a view to the nil-opening of the coroner's inquest. PROVINCIAL MUSEUMS AND SOUTH KENSINGTON.—With a view to increase the aid and advantages which provincial museums and art galleries already derive from the Science and Art Department, South Kensington, Mr. Jesse Collings intends to move for the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire how far, and in what manner, the British Museum, the National Gallery, and other collections supported by State funds, may be made available for the promotion of science and art in the proviaces. Mr. Collings further pro- poses that the Committee should inquire into the expediency of placing all the national collections under the direct con- trol of one responsible Minister. MR. SRADLAUGH AND PERPETUAL PENSIONS.—Mr. Brad- laugh attended at the Treasury, on Monday, by appointment to be heard against the commutation of the Marlborough and Penn pensions, and handed in a memorandum of his objec- tion and evidence in support. He learned, however, that the Penn pension was commuted on April sth, and the Marl- borough pension commuted long prior to the Chancellor of the Exchequer's direction that Mr. Bradlaugh should be heard. All opposition being fruitless, Mr. Bradlaugh with- drew, expressing his regret that Sir James Carmichael should have written permitting the hearing at a time when such hearing bad become useless. _

Tait Wrru WIvES.—On Saturday afternoon, at the Dublin Commission, Dennis Molloy was put on his trial for bigamy, he having five wives living, one of whom he married at Liverpool. The prisoner presented a miserable object in the dock, but to his wives in court he cast tender glances. The same evidence as was given at the magis- terial investigation was heard. The prisoner was defended by counsel. His first wife, a grey-haired woman, was pre- I sent in court, and seemed to feel her position acutely. Mr. Curtis, prisoner's counsel, put in the plea that the accused was insane, and had been four times in a lunatic asylum. Dr. Banks was called, and said the prisoner had escaped from the lunatic asylum. The prisoner was found to be insane, and was ordered to be detained during the Lord Lieutenant's pleasure. On hearing the sentence, several of the prisoner's I wives burst out laughing. The Judge said there was no ac- I counting for taste. THE POPE AND FREEMASONRY.—On Sunday, by direction of the Roman Catholic Bishop ot Liverpool (Dr. O'Reilly), the encyclical letter of Leo XIII. on Freemasonry was read in all the churches and chapels in the diocese. At St. Peter's, Seel-street, Father Anderson, 0.8.11., before reading the letter, remarked that it was only fair to the Freemasons in England that it should be made known that they had protested at a meeting of their Grand Lodge against the serious indictment of his Holiness. Ile (Father Anderson) would remind English Masons that se long as they con- tinued in the bonds of Fellowship with Masons throughout the world, and encouraged and supported the different lodges by subscriptions, they could not consider themselves altogether irresponsible for the principles and acts of their foreign brothers. To free themselves from all blame they must repudiate publicly false teaching and break off all fraternal connection with those brethren. As for Catholics, they listened with respect and veneration to the words of the holy father, as the authorised teacher of faith and morals.

ATTEMPIRD TRAIN WRECRING*—A. dastardly attempt at train-wrecking was made on Saturday morning. The driver of the Dover express, when a few hundred yards from the bridge which spans the Medway at Rochester, noticed an obstacle on the line ahead of him. Seeing that he could not pull up the train in time, he put on pull speed and drove right through the obstacle, the engine and carriages pro- videntially keeping on the metals. The engine was damaged. A heavy iron rail had been fastened with ropes across the metals. Had the train left the line it would have fallen into the river.—On Tuesday a boy named William Pearce was arrested at Rochester on a charge of maliciously attempting to wreck the Dover mail train by placing a bar of iron on the line, near Rochester, on Saturday. Pearce, who is under 14 years of age, is employed as office boy in the London, Chatham, and Dover goods sheds at Rochester. The prosecution allege that the boy committed the act out of pure wantonness, but the evidence is believed to consist almost entirely of the fact that he passed the spot only a few minutes before the obstruction was discovered. Pearce will be charged before the magistrates at Rochester to-day (Sat. urday.)

SHOCKING MI7RDER BY A LUNATIC IN RADNORSHIRE —On Thursday an inquest WAS held on the body of the servant girl, named Mary Ann Hathaway, who was shot by her mistress, Mrs. Edwards, wife of a highly-respected ' farmer, residing at Castle Farm, near Rhayader. It appeared that for the past twelve months Mrs. Edwards has been sub- ject to fits of insanity, and under advice a woman was employed to look after her. On Sunday evening the nurse went to the chapel, leaving Mr. Edwards and Hathaway at home. During the evening Mr. Edwards and Hathaway went out on the farm to attend cows, leaving Mrs. Edwards in the house. On their return , they had supper. Mrs. Edwards went upstairs and called Hathaway up. Directly afterwards Mr. Edwards heard a scream and the report of a gun. He ran upstairs, and found Hathaway dead on the landing and Mrs. Edwards picking up his gun. He asked his wife what she had d,,one, and she replied, "Nothing at all; I want to be hung. It , transpired that while the deceased and her husband were absent, Mrs. Edwards found the gun, which her husband had hidden in the stables, and the cap she procured Thursday. GOLBORNE. • MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Golborne Parochial Com tnittee was held at the office at Brewis's Mill on Wednesday afternoon, Mr Brewis presiding. The other members present were Messrs. W. H. Harwood, William Mitchell, Jolla Fetrns, Isaac Taylor. William Garton, Thomas Pierpoint, John Davies, Roger Yates, Thomas Mitchell, and Bennie (clerk.) LIGHTING AND WATER COMMITTEE.—The Clerk read the minutes of a meeting of this committee held for the purpose of considering the gas account for street lighting from December 1883 to May 1884. The readings of the various meters were submitted to the committee and considered, as was also the amount of the account, £35 63 sd, and it was resolved that it be passed subject to the approval of the general Committee. It was also resolved that a dry meter be substituted for the wet one at the Co-ope•ative shop in Heath-street.--After a short discussion the minut-s were duly approved. HIGHWAYS AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—A meeting of this committee having been held for the purpose of con-

I s-idering work proposed in the High-street improvement, the Clerk read the minutes, which were to the effect that the consent of Mr. Fleetwood having been obtained to take down and re-build the butcher's shop m a line with the premises occupied by Mr. James Unsworth and Mr. H. L. Pennington, in High-street, and the Surveyor having been requested to obtain tenders for the work, the same were submitted and considered, and the committee recommended that Mr. Wake- field's tender of LIO 15s be accepted, on the condition that he included the wicket gate mentioned in Mr. Harrison's tender. —Mr. W. Mitchell thought that a great improvement would be obtained at a reasonable price.—The recommendation of the committee was confirmed —At the meeting of the Com- mittee the Surveyor pointed out work proposed to be done in front of property belonging to Mrs. Caunce and Mr. Thos. Heath, and it was approved by the Committee and the Sur- veyor was requested to obtain the consent of the owners thereto. The work proposed consists of paving with par- bold setts between the road boundary line and the buildings, and is brought about by raising the road.—The Clerk read a letter from Mrs. Caunce, dated /from Wigan, agreeing to the raising of the public highway, as pointed out to her, in front of the property occupied by Mr. W. Lowe, Mr. J. Beardsworth, Mr. J. Openshaw, Mrs. M. Wo-thington, and Mrs. Allen, High-street, Golborne, on condition that the Committee provided, and paved with setts, between the boun- dary line of the highway and the buildings, and that when the work was completed the highway parish would have no contiol of the frontage beyond the said boundary line.— The recommendation ef the Committee was adopted on the motion of Mr. Harwood, seconded by Mr. Davies. TEE ENCROAcEmENT QUESTION. The Clerk reported that Mr. Unsworth was willing to pay £lO to settle the Heath-street encroachment question.—Mr. Harwood: That was the 9UM recommended by Mr. Mitchell to be accepted, and I have no doubt that he will propose it.—Mr. W. Mit- chell said that he would be quite willing to make the propo- sition "that the sum of £lO be accepted on \behalf of the ratepayers from the property owners in Heath-street as com- pensation for encroachment."—Mr. Garton seconded.—The Clerk: Mr. Unsworth made the offer cn behalf of his son and daughter, who are the it-rested parties.—Mr. Harwood thought that the offer should be accepted. Mr. W. Mit- chell : It is an unpleasant subject a d I wish it could be settled successfully. They were, he said, bound to prevent encroachments.—Mr. Yates I think there will not be se many now.—lt was decided to accept the offer. WATER CONSUMPTION.—The Clerk reported that the water consumption for the four weeks ending the previous Saturday was 808,000 gallons, being 150,000 gallons more than the previous month. A COMPLAINT.—Mr. Davies said that he did not see why the inhabitants of Leigh-street should not have the street watered like the other parts of the town, as they contributed to the ratee.—The Chairman supposed that the reason one part was watered more than another was because there were more shops in some localities.—The Clerk said that they would require extra carts if they watered all the streets alike.—Mr.Fearns said that they required the dust laid in the public streets where there were shops.—Mr, Davies : It is the same in:prwate houses; they do not want to be cleaning down every day.—The Clerk mentioned several places that required watering.—Mr. Harwood: Of course, the whole township wants it.—Mr. Davies said that they were all en- titled to it.—Mr. Harwood : Where there is a great deal of road traffic there is more dust, and that wants attending to before any other part.—The Clerk: I should be glad if the committee would define the proper area. It would be more satisfactory to me.—Mr. Davies : We have got to study the comforts of the inhabitants as well as the rate.—Mr. Har- wood : Mr. Davies is not asking for it for himself, but for the promenaders of the West End. (Laughter.)—The sub- ject then dropped. OUTBREAK OF FEVER.—Mr. Yates : Are you aware about the fever in the township ? I think there should be some- thing said at this meeting about that. I believe there are , people who have fever in their houses who are going about the streets from house to house selling things, and I do not think that that should be allowed.—The _Chairman : And

ff;ncy schools will be a means of spreading the disease.— Mr. Yates: I don't want to mention any names but I know this is so, and in one instance one of the parties living in the house is going from house to house selling things, and entering both public-houses and private houses.—The Chair- man : Is not that more the policeman's business ?—Mr. Yates: Ido not know, but I thought I would speak about it.— the Chairman : I believe they are worse in Ashton than they are here. I have heard of nine or ten cases in one house.—Mr. Harwood : They say there is an increase in the number of patients, and I suppose there are some now awaiting their burial.—Mr. Davies: Are there no means of disinfecting the house where fever has taken place ? Mr. Harwood said that they could make a recommendation to the Board of Guardians, who would supply disinfectants if necessary—Mr. W. Mitchell thought that the medical officer would look after disinfecting fever.—M!.. Davies said that in some places it was compulsory to disinfect houses. He thought that the medical officer could order it to be. done.—Mr. Harwood, in answer to the Chairman, said that he would mention the matter to the Guardians. He thought himself that the schools should be closed. i .—The Chairman :- Someone with some knowledge and skill n applying the • disinfectants should be apmainted.—Mr. Fearns : The nuisance iespector.—The Chairman : Nuisance inspectors are often as ignorant as we.are.—Mr.Fearns The meical officer instructs and assists him. The subject then. dropped. This was all the business of public interest.

SIR CHARLES [IMRE ON THE FR&NCHISE BILL.—.Sir C- Dilke was the chief guest on Wednesday night at the dinner- of the Marylebone Liberal Association, and, in reply to tbs. toast of "Her Majesty's Ministers, he said that when the. Government were carrying on important negotiations he ad- vised the country to wait until the revelation was made br the Government itself rather than to accept viewa-as to their policy which were appearing both morning sad evening, Lord Salisbury at Plymouth had spoken very s:vongls- as to 1 a dissolution impendine, but. Sir Charles doubtad very muck whether, if his lordship intended to reject the, Franchise Bill, he would find a sufficient number of Conaervstive peers. ready to follow him in a struggle which every Radical in the country longed to join in. A great deo; had been Said about the casual references to redistribution made by Mr. Gladstone, but after 311 he (Sir Charles) d:dnot see how any portion of the country could suffer, mre particularly the metropolis, from anything which had been said. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 14, 1884.

THE Franchise Bill has this week made such rapid progress in the House of Com- mons as to take most people by surprise— particularly the supporters of the Women's Suffrage clause, who have had to make a fight for it before they were quite ready for the fray. As has been seen from the begin- ning, the Tories occupy an unhappy position on the question of the Franchise. According to their traditions, they were bound to oppose, "tooth and nail," the assimilation of the borough and county franchise; but that "education of the party" which Lord BEA- CONSFIELD as their political Schoolmaster undertook has gone so far that some of them —at any rate—could not be content with the old lines. They had got that " little learn- ing" which was "a dangerous thing" to them, and it has thus happened that, not daring to meet the Bill with a direct nega- tive, they have sought indirectly to mutilate it. They have had week by week what it is customary to call amendments," but whether their adoption would have " amen- ded " the measure is another matter. Take the point dealt with on Monday night on clause 4., which includes a proposal by the Government to prevent the creation of faggot votes by means of rent-charges. Mr.CA.vErr- DISH BENTINCK actually proposed to omit the sub-section in question; and this being de- feated, Mr. WARTON sought to give a vote to holders of rent-charges of the value of Zioo. Liberals have no love of property qualifi- cations, but now that men are to be enfran- chised all round, it would be seen that the Tories are making every effort to edge in property claims wherever they can. The amendment was, however, negatived without a division; and another motion bearing on the same issue was also rejected. On clause 7, Mr. RAIKES gave special evidence of brotherly feeling towards the poorest of the poor by proposing to exclude from the bene- fits of the Bill those who did not occupy "two habitable rooms." Mr. RAIKES, as an ex-Chairman of Committee, is looked upon as a leading light of the Tory party—a fact which Irishmen should not lose sight of in considering this question. The " amend- ment " was indeed aimed directly at Irish- men, for when Mr. GLADSTONE with a far- seeing eye proceeded to show that this was a "sweeping disfranchising proposition" which would affect the inhabitants of many one- roomed houses in Scotland, Mr. RAIKES coolly remarked that he was "not thinking of Scotland, but of Ireland." "Thinking of

Ireland !" Yes, with a view to preventing an act of justice being done to those who are voiceless, and who are therefore in most need of help. Having previously failed in the deliberate effort to deprive Ireland as a whole of the benefits of the Franchise Bill, the Tories, with Mr. RAIKES as their spokes- _ _
man, have sought to by this last move to ex- clude the Irish peasant, who will now know what i 3 the worth of Tory professions of at- tachment. He may indeed say with the poet—

Perhaps it was right to dissemble your love, But—why did you kick me down stairs? Happily for the occupants of one-roomed houses, the PRIME MINISTER, backed by the Liberal party, was in no mood to listen to the base suggestign. and the " amendment " was negatived without a division. Sundry points of a fairly debatable character were afterwards raised, but they were disposed of without materially interfering with the Bill, the ri Clauses of which were got through on Mon- day night amid hearty cheers from the Minis- terial benches.

On Tuesday evening the House was again in Committee on the Bill, commencing with the new clauses proposed by outsiders. Mr. ECROYD came forward with an ingenious proposal for conferring the franchise on coPY" holders, but Mr. GLADSTONE made it clear that he was not in favour of extending the property qualification in any direction, and showed that the amendment would not
remedy any injustice, as the bulk of copY- holders would be voters as householders. Mr.
TOMLINSON, the colleague of Mr. EcßoYo in the representation of Preston, urged that the declaraticn of the Government would be

received with "great dissatisfaction" in Lan- cashire, but we venture to say just the reverse. Lancashire working-men are too practical to be led away by a fancy franchise; and the House showed itself to be of a like mind, for the proposal was rejected by a la ge majority. Still to the fore as a " Protectionist, ' Mr- ECROYD next moved a clause having for its object the giving of a vote to persons resident in a county who might have certain property in a borough. In this way they were to obtain a second vote for the county. He contended that this was a fair thing to do, seeing that borough yoters sometimes had a county vote consequent upon their being possessed of freehold property. The PRIME MINISTER hinted that he was not to be moved by appeals as to the existing property qualifica- tion, remarking that there was a good deal to be said in favour of the "one man one vote principle ;" but he bowled the member for Preston out by showing that thrifty working- men for whom he professed such anxiety would not get the benefit of the proposal, seeing that it was not intended to applY it to those who had obtained their houses through building soci:Aies. "Fancy fran- chise "number two was therefore setaside bY 236 votes against 122. Mr. i3nYcE met with a sympathetic reception from the Go- vernment on proposing to shorten the quali- fying term from twelve to six months; but it was pointed out by the PRIME MINISTER that it was a question for a registration measure rather than the bill before the House. Mr. BRvcE then offered to withdraw his clause, which was ultimately negatived. Next came Mr. WOODALL'S important proposal for the enfranchisement of women—that is to say of such female householders as are at present entitled to vote for members of Town Coun- cils and School Boards He. made a power- ful appeal on their behalf, and, supported as he is by a considerable number of members on both sides of the House, he cannot be blamed for pressing the issue to a division. On the other hand, the Government have taken a prudent, consistent, and straight- forward course in opposing the introduction, in committee stage, of what cannot but be regarded as a new principle in the bill. From the first, the PRIME MINISTER has been. careful to explain that there was so much danger of shipwreck from "rocks ahead," visible ar‘d invisible, that it was their duty to avoid over-loading; and now, after getting so far in safety, the Captain is asked to risk everything by taking in a cargo which might prove as terribly explosive as dynamite itself. The Government must follow that course- which divides the party the least, and, as the Liberal party are not united on the question of the enfranchisement of women, Mr. GLAD- STONE did well to state, as he did on Tues- day • night, that not only could they not accept Mr. WOODALL'S amendment, but that its adoption would mean the overthrow cf the bill. In the face of such an issue, Liberals who would give Parliamentary votes to 'female householders, must wait for a more opportune time; it would be madness, under the present circumstances, to endanger ,the fate of the Reform Bill, to say nothing of the folly of walking into a trap which the Tories may have prepared for them. That this is the opinion of the majority of the supporzers of the Government was seen in the division which was taken at a late hour on Thursday night, Mr. WOODALL'S Women's Suffrage clause being rejected by a majority of 136.

Mr. PETER SMITH, Chemist, Of Runcorn, has been misapplying his energies, for instead of keeping peacefully to the pounding of drugs he has been taking wrathfUlly to pound- ing a policeman ; and the result is that, although he has increased his fame, he has consicerably lightened his purse. The long story of the encounter with " Robertus " will be found in another column. It would seem that Mr. SMITH was not without provocation; but he failed .to make good his counter-charge of assault and abusive language, and had to pay the piper. It is not a wise thing at any time to begin arguing with policemen, but it is the height of folly to commence an interchange of opinion when you are leaving a public- house at "one minute or so to ii o'clock" at night. Mr. SMITH must have been in a very sanguine mood on the occasion in ques- tion, or he would not have adjourned the debate from the street to the police office. "Bearding the lion in his den " is all very well as a figure of speech, but as a matter of fact it is best to leave the beard of the lion alone and to keep out of his den. Not content with having a shy at the policeman, Mr. SMITH went home, and, like a victorious general who .sets to work to write his despatch while hot from battle, he proceeded instead of creeping quietly to bed to pen an account for the benefit of the Superintendent of Police of his engagement with "P.C. 321." He made it out to his own satisfaction that "P.C. 321 " was a coward, and that PET ER SMITH was by far "the best man of the two." Indeed, he went the length of telling him he had struck " P.C. 32.1. with his fist—" " of course—admini- stering what, professionally speaking, might be called a gentle stimulant. We cannot bnt think that Mr. SMITH made a mistake In writing this letter; it would have been better if he had slept on the matter; for in that case he might not have written it at al, and he

could not therefore have witnessed against . himself. As for settling who is " the best man of the two," Mr. PETER SMITH, chemist, Should be a trifle above that; but if he should ' feel full of fight, and want to have it out with some one at "one minute or so to eleven," let him go not to Jericho, but to Khartoum ; he will have full scope there for his prowess in helping General GORDON to "smash up the MARDI ; " a Prophet is higher game than a Policeman.

"THE Educational Franchise with obser. \rations in its application on Italy and Bel- gium " is the title of a pamphlet just issued by Mr. JAMES HARGREAVES, F.C.$., F.A.S., of Widnes. Its object is to show the danger of conferring the" franchise upon illiterate persons, and the wisdom that Italy and Bel- gium have displayed in setting up an educa- tional barrier. While agreeing with much that Mr. HARGREAVES has,to say, we cannot help feeling that he is "a day after the fair." Does he want the nation to go back upon itself, and disfranchise those who cannot read and write; or would he apply his educational test to those only who want the county fran- chise? Such a distinction would not be tolerated; and disfranchisement is out of the question in face of the fact that, though we have had household suffrage in the boroughs for sixteen years, the country is not yet ruined. On the contrary, it is all the better for the wide extension of the franchise. "The illiterates" is best left alone; he is rapidly retiring with the schoolmaster at his heels.

RESIGNATION OF TECE VICAR OF DITTO.—We under- stand that the Ray. J. Cassels Brown, M.A., who has held the living of Bitton for the past two years and a half, has Placed hi 9 resignation in the hands of the Bishop. ...POLICE INSPECTION AT RIINCORN.—On Monday the hon.

Captain C. G. Legge Government inspector oeconstaba- lary, inspected the iuncorn• division of Cheshire County Police. There were on parade one inspector, two sergsants, and 19 constables, and they were put throngh drill by Ser- geant Lowndes Afterwards the inspector examined the books in the office, and he had no complaint of any descrip- tion to make. . RUNAWAY HORSE AT RUNCORN. -- Considerable excite- ment was caused in Bridgetstreet by the running away of a horse attached to a milk shandry belonging to Mr. J. Stokes, Of Rock Savage. While standing opposite Mr. King's shop, the horse was startled by a passing lurry, bolted, and the vehicle beeoming overturned, was dragged upon' its side for Some distance, the tankards being thrown out and the milk eats and the shafts broken. The horse was uninjured. A RUNCORN BANKRUPT.—The creditors of Mr. Thomas Egerton Tunna, grocer and provision dealer, of High-street, Runcorn, bankrupt, held their first meeting on Wednesday at the office of Mr. T. J. Ridgway, official receiver, Warring- ton. Several of the creditors who were not present were re- Presented by Mr. T. Myers and Mr. A. Thraves, of Liver- pool, and Mr. Whitehead, of the firth of J. Kerr and Com- pany, Manchester. Some discussion ensued with respect to the position of another grocer of Runcorn who had entered Into partnership with Mr. Tunna recently, but withdrew in few weeks. This was left over, being considered a matter for the trustee to investigate. Mr. John Balmer. chartered accountant, 25, Lord-street, Liverpool, was appointed trus- tee, there being three nominations. Subsequently the debtor underwent his public examination at the County Court, be- fore Mr. H. B. White, deputy registrar. The official receiver expressed himself perfectly satisfied with the examination, and it was concluded. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Board's Offices, Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. 2-Moss presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Norman, lebtva, W. Whittaker, W. H. Rogerson, W. Littler, and Salkeld (secretary). The secretary's report showed the interments during the two months ending May 25th nurnbered 61, against 60 in the corresponding period of last rear. The fees received during tffe same period amounted to £66 12s lid, against £63 lOs in the corresponding period ilaat year. On the recommendation of the Finance COM• tnittee, accounts amounting to £34 9s 2d were passed for Payment. The secretary was instructed to call a vestry Meeting on Thursday, the 26th last., for the purpese of ap- Pointing three persons to be members of the Board in place Of Messrs. James Handley, JP., Thomas Norman, and George Moss, whose term of office expire on that day, but they are eligible for re-election. The tender of Mr: John Pennington for repairs to the cemetery wall was accepted ; and Mr. Norman and the secretary were deputed to superin- tend the work.—ln reply to Mr. Littler, the Secretary said there was a tank near the chapel, and another near the workshop, containing an abandance of water which persons wiehing to water the plants on graves could use free of Charge. MAGAZINES, &C.--" The New Book of Kings" by Mr. .1. Morrison Davidson, author of "Eminent Radicals," is a Lively production issued at the price of sixpence by "The Modern Press," 14, Paternoster-row, London. It is Radical enaugh in its way—more sweeping than judicione as it seems to us ; but the reader will find facts as to our Kings which be cannot otherwise readily come at. " Cassell's, Family Magazine" for June is even more than usually readable. The frontispiece, 'Fair Margaret," is accompanied with a tew lines of verse obviously after the manner of the Laureate. Professor Blaikie has an admirable article on "Letting off the steam ;" and there is a valuable paper OR Household Surgery." "Within the Clasp "is continued, Slid there are two well-written complete stories :—" Mr. !Irowe's Heiress" and ‘Maddalena's Lovers." The chief illustration of "The Quiver "—the subject of which is a Pretty haymaker—is a charmiug rural bit well worthy of a frame, “Little Folks" is also quite up to the mark with "Mv little PLI93 "for the leading picture. The second parts Of "The Book of Health" and "Popular Gardening,' by Lee same firm (Caseell's), are to hand with contents that Make it a matter of surprise that so much good material can be given for so little money. "Gardening" has the merit, 105, of being well illustrated. "The English Illustrated atagazine " keeps up to its high standard in the way of en- graving. There is a capital portrait of Mrs. Siddons from a Painting in the National Gallery, while "Drawing-room "ances." and "Two Centuries of Bath" are well illustrated. The "Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall" pursues Lite Pleasant course, the engraving of the beautiful drawings Mr. Hemy being as heretofore the great feature. There 19, too, a racy article by Mr. H. W. Lucy—" By Sea and &and to Kiyoto." "Summer Tours in Scotland," an official guide issued by Mr. D. Mac Brayne, of Hope-street, Glatt- Few, is a mine of valuable information. It is profusely il- ,estrated with photo-lithographs, and is cheap at sixpence.

WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB: FEBSENTATIONS.—A meeting of the members of Widnes Football Club was held at the Norton Arms, Lugadale road, Widnes, on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. J. Burgess. and there was a fair attendance. The meeting had been called for the interest- ing purpose of presently: a testimonial of esteem and regard to the late capt.iin, Mr. Ireland, for bis admirable services to the club, and to fur. J H. Smith, a member of the club, who had shown great bravery a few months ago in rescuing a boy from drowning in the canal —The Chairman, after referring to the bright prospects of the club for the next reason, said Mr. Ireland had been connected with the club °ince its formation, and after occupying the position of sec- retary for several years, he became captain in 1882-3, fulfill- ing his duties in that capacity with g,reat satisfaction to the Club. By his resignation the club sustained a great loss, for be might tell them that during the first year of his cap- telincy the first team lost only one match. (Applause.) He • 'lad great pleasure on behalf of the members and friends of the club in asking Mr. Ireland to accept a purse of gold, and be hoped that gentleman would live long enough to see children occupying honourable positions in the club. (Hear, bear, and applause.)—Mr. A. Brown gave a sketch of t,be late captain's achievements on the football field ; and then the Chairman observed that Mr. J. H. Smith, Who was to be the other recipient of a present, ...W.as absent. It was thought by some members the club that that gentleman should be reminded Of his bravery in saving a boy from drowning ia the canal 4,nd a subscription was raised, with the result that a very nandsome silver medal was procured. Perhaps his brother, r. Fred. Smith, would accept it on his behalf. The medal "ure the followinginscrillion :—" Presented to J. H. Smith, 18. a token for bravery in saving life on December 15th, as•B3, by the members of the club."—Mr. Ireland expressed ",a thanks to the gentlemen who had so kindly thought fit tvey SilOW their apprecia,ian of his efforts to make football in d idnes what it ought to he—a success. Whatever he had „une for football he bad done for football alone and his own rraonal pleasure—not for any benefit which be might de- hereafter. (Appl lase.) He hoped the WI Iles Football tub had not reached its best. Althou.h they had been Itrifortunate in loin, ra lichee during the past season they •.tad shown themselves to be no, far bellidd some of the lead- Clubs in the No.v, of England. (applause )—Mr. ted• Smith sit;tably replied on bahalf of his brother, and e meeting terminated with the usual vote of thanks.

WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS..—TbeSe popular sports will take place at Farnworth on Friday and Saturday next, and if favoured with tine weather will be as successful as in former years. Entries close this evening. In addition to the usual athletic events, the committee have arranged for a gymnastic display by several members of the Liver- pool Gymnasium, which will enhance the interest in the proceedings. The refieehments will be pro- vided by Mr. John Smith, of the Griffin Inn, and the Star of Temperance Brass Band will discourse music from its usual place. Mrs. A. McClellan has kindly consented to distribute the prizes. TER TERRIBLE ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. Yesterday, 'Michael Murphy, captain; was brought up again at Rue- corn Mee Court, before Captain Hezlehurst, charged with ' doing grievous bodily harm to Wm. Stringer.--e-P.S. Wal- ley said the injured man was still in a weak condition and unableao appear. The prisoner was therefore remanded until next Friday, but he was admitted to bail, himself in r£loo and two swedes in £5O each on condition that he re- ported himself daily to the police.—Superintendent Leah said it was doubtful if Stringer would recover. He was much weaker than when the prisoner was formerly admit- ted to bail. CRUELTY TO A RoRSE AT RUNCORN.—At Rancor!? Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Redford was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an waft state.—P.C. Bryan stated that about 430 p.m. on Wednesday, the 21st nit, he was on duty in Helton, when he saw a small pony attached to a trap coming along. The defendant, who was accompanied by three women, was driv- ing. He noticed that the fore-feet of the animal were bloody and he called upon the defendant to stop, bet he did not do so until the constable bad followed him some distance. The constable then examined the horse and found that a nail projected from the foot about an inch, and was injuring the fetlock.. The feet were bleeding very much, and under- neath the flanks there was also blood as though the defen- dant ban been thrashing the animal to get her along.—P.C. Smith corroborated.—After hearing the defence the Bench inflicted a penalty of 10a and costs. WIDNES (377TH) STAIIR-BOWEET BUILDING SOCIETY. The members of this society held their annual meeting on Wednesday, when the directors presented their third annual report, in which they state they view with pleasure the steady advance of the society in public favour, 60 members having been added to the roll during the past year. There had been six appropriations during the past twelve months, amounting to £1,300, making the total amount appropriated up to the present £2,200. The statement of accounts for the year ended on the 30th April last showed that there bad b.eq received hi lebecriptions from member!, 41,02 t ade di, on aodOunto v.,;ous items £5B 4a so, r 5 VO tt nl appo.- itionments £96 03 83, balance in band £l6l 'cis 20, total £1,340 1881 d. The expenses during the year amounted to £Bl 12s sd, and the balance in the secretary's hands and at the bank was set down at £447 9s 83. The capital account had now reached £2,549 14s 10d. The report and balance sheet were adopted. DARING STREET ROBBERY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Burke, a plumber, resi- ding in Margaret-street. Widnes, was charged with stealing a purse containing 7s. 61. and some coppers, tram the per- son of Jane Curlet on Saturday night last. From the state- ment of Inspector Wood it appeared that Mrs. Curie!, in company with her husband had been making some pur- chases in 'a shop, and was proceeding. to Wellington-street through the entry leading from Waterloo road, when the prisoner came behind her and snatched her purse from her her hand. She screamed, and her husband, who was in front turned round, and pushed the prisoner who ran away. Mrs. Cadet followed him while her husband fetched pi policeman.—She aoked for the pores but he threatened to kick her if she fpllowed him —The prisoner Vended guilty, saying he had no recollection of the affair.—The prisoner, who had been before the B•moh four times for drunkenness was sentenced to two 'months' 'hard labour. RUNCORN POLICE Courer.—(Thursday : Before Mr. Brun- drit).— A Tippler's Farewell: An elderly man named Edward Lockley was brought up in custody charged with being drunk and incapable. P.C. Bryan said on the prel vious night he found the,prisener in Mersey-street so drunk that he had to obtain assistance and carry him to the police station. The magistrate imposed .a fine of 5s and 6s 4d costs, or seven days. The prisoner asked for time in which to pay the fine. His Worship referred the prisoner to Super- intendent Leah, who intimated that he would consider the prisoner's application. The prisoner (to Mr. Brundrit): I hope I won't come before you again, sir.—Mr. Brundrit : I hope you won't. I don't want to see you. I cart assure you. —Begging : Thomas McCarthy, a young man, was charged with begging on the previous night. Mrs Edgar, who Bites in Canal-street, saw the prisoner ask a woman for a piece of bread, and P.C. Bryan took him into custody, as be had no apparent means of subsistence. On promising to leave the town the prisoner wee discharged. RUNCORN COUNTY COVRT.—The monthly sittieg of this court was held on Tuesday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. There were 4 adjourned plaints, 90 original plaint% and 20 judgment summonses set down for hearing.—The only case of general interest was one in which Jos Hughes, of Kingsley, sued John J. Steward, auctioneer, of Frodsham and Chester, for the sum of £7 108. for injuries sustained through having been bitten by the defendant's dog.—Mr. Burton appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. A. E. Linaker for de- fendant—The plaintiff said that early in March, this year, he was passing the Horse Shoe Inn, Kingsley. where the deg' was kept, when it flew at him and bit him very severely. Dr. Robinson came and attended him. He was unable to work for three weeks.—ln reply to Mr. A. E. Linaker, the plaintiff said he was sure that it wan the defendant's dog which bit him.—David Worrall,labourer, Kingsley, said that early in January he saw a dog at the Horse Shoe Inn, Kingsley, when it attempted to bite him. He could not say whether the dog belonged to Mr. Steward or not —At or several other witnesses had been called on behalf of the plaintiff, hie Honour held that the plaintiff could not re- cever against Mr. Steward because he could not satisfy him that the dog was really the defendant's; or that Billington, of the Horse Shoe Inn Kingsley, where the dog was kept, was a servant within ate meanisg of the Act. His Honour then directed a verdict of non-suit. A SHARP HORSR TRANSACTION BY A RUNCORN MAN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Henry Watkin was brought up under A war- rant charged with having, on the 24th May last at Runcorn, stolen a horse, the property of John Wood.—Mr. Oliver Leak appeared for the prosecutor, who is a cab-owner and driver rediding in Liverpool, and said the warrant was taken eat on the 28th May but the police had been unable to find the prisoner, but he understood that he gave himself up on the previous day. He had written to the prosecutor to in- form him of this fact and requesting his attendance at court. He had not however put in an appearance.—P.S. Walley proved the apprehension of the prisoner On Tuesday morn- ing at Mr. Hitchen, solicitor's office.—Mr. Johnson, deputy- magistrates' clerk, stated the information had been laid on oath before Mr. Davies, and a warrant granted on the 28th May.—on this evidence the prisoner was remanded until Monday, and the prosecution will now be undertaken by the police.—Mr. Hitchen said he appeared for the prisoner and applied for bail. The prisoner was a respectable man and bad resided at Halton for a number of years. The applica- tion whs reftised.—The facts of the case are these. On the 24th May the prisoner went to the prosecutor and bargained for the purchase of a horse. After coming to an agreement the prisoner stated that he had not got any money with him but if the prosecutor would go with him to Runcorn where he lived he would pay him. They therefore brought the horse to Runcorn by train, and at the station the prisoner informed the prosecutor that he lived at Halton where he had unfortunately left his cheque book. The prosecutor agreed to accompany him there to obtain the,cheque. and on the suggestion of the prisoner the horse was put up at Tuckey's Stables. On arriving at Halton, the prisoner made the excuse that he could not find his cheque book, and the prosecutor returning to the stables two hours later aithoat having been paid found that the horse had been removed. It appeared that whilst he was with the prisoner, the latter's eon had been to the stable and taken the animal away.

div.head: WELCOME OF THE REV. A P. H. WILSON TO WIDNES.
div.p: WELCOME OF THE REV. A P. H. WILSON TO WIDNES.

On Thursday evening the weekly meeting of the Widnes C.E.T.S. was transformed into a congregational gathering to welcome the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson, who has recently come to Widnes to undertake the duties of curate at the Parish Church. There was a large attendance. The Vicar, the Rev. J.Wright Williams, presided, and he was supported by the guest of the evening, and Messrs. James Foley (lay reader). L. Killcross, N. Farrant, F. Neil, W. Treacy, een, and F. Cave.—The Chairman atid if there was one person who welcomed help in the parish it was himself, especially when it was likely to be effective. Some people made a mistake in regard to the work of the Vicar in the parish. Us had much work in Connection with the Measures in which the church was engaged, particularly in relation to the schools, while there had'been a good deal of labour in con- nection with the building, whose progress they viewed with considerable interest. This was all extra, and those who had not received visits as often as they thought they might have done must be thankful that they were not sick. He was glad to welcome his colleague, the Rev. A. P. Hamilton ;nd he hoped in a short time the congregation would ktow him so well that they would welcome him in every case with all their hearts. (Applause.) The speaker hinted that the rev, gentleman had with him a very substan- tial evidence of the favour in which his services were re- garded in that large and important North of England town—Barrow-in-Furness. (Applause.) Mr. Kilcross, in a short speech, referred to the sun. Iday School work, and said that owing to his , multifarious parochial engagements Mr. Williams had ' been obliged to forego many other meetings in which he would have been pleased to take a part. The Vicar would now have more liberty, and be felt sure the work of the Church and its organisations would be carried on with much efficiency. (Applause.)—Mr. W. Treacy, ten,, re- marked that the way in which the Vicar had had to work was well known to all of them, and they also knew how that work had been performed. (Applause.) He would now have associated with him a second clergyman, a fact which was gratifying to the whole parish ; and on behalf of all present he heartily welcomed the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson amongst them. kApplause.)— ! Messrs. Foley, Neil, Chadwick, Atherton, Farrant, H. N. I Wharton, Cave, and Dickson all addressed a few appropriate ' observations to those present.—The Vicar observed that the j help needed in the parish now came from three sources. , First the Church Pastoral Aid Society, to which he was largely indebted for the presence and help of Mr. Wilsoa ; 1. and secondly he was largely indebted to the Addition al Curate Society for his second work. Over and above this he was largely indebted to the manufacturers of the parish, particularly Messrs. Timmis, Gossage. Deacoo, Pilkington, 'Vickers and Sons, and a few others; and last but not least, to a lady whose name must always be received with respect

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 14. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 14. 1884.

and something more—Mrs. Deacon. (Applause.)—The Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson, who was heartily.applauded on ris- ing, said he believed one thing which greatly enabled him to decide to come to Widnes was the pleasure be bad in being present at a meeting of the Church of England 'rem- perance Society, because he wee so astonished to find so. inlay working-men and women banded together for the pro- motion of the temperance cause. Referring to the remark that there were in Widnes 600 professing numbers of the Church of England; the speaker said he was not one of those who believed that the church existed solely for a sec- tion of the people. He believed the church was the church of the nation and the church of 16,000 in the ecclesiastical parish of Widnes. (Agplause.) He hoped and trusted, and he believed he expressed the feelings of the vicar that there would not be a Coca where the Clergy of St. Mary's would refuse to visit a person of whatever denomination. Speak- ing of educational matters, Mr. Wilson said he was a bitter Opponent of everything in the shape of education where the Word of God was not taught. (Applause.) In conclusion he intimated that they would work together harmoniously, and though they might not have the same ideas, let them ever remember that' they Torked not for their own glory but for the salvation of souls and the glory of God. (Applause.) —During the evening several hymns were sung; Mr. W. White presiding at the piano. Miss Wilkinson and Mr. Far- rant gave a pianoforte duet.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES YESTERDAY.

Shortly before four o'clock yesterday afternoon an acci- dent occurred at the Widnes station of the Sheffield and Midland Companies. The pilot engine had brought a train of waggons from the goods-warehouse with the intention of pushing them into a siding below the station. In order to do this tde engine had to pass from the front to the rear of the train, and as it was passing the points on the down line ,four wheels left the metals, and boat lines were blocked for Upwards of an hoar. Several platelayers were engaged re- pairing ‘the lines at the spot where tbe mishap occnrred, but no satisfactory explananation of the accident could be ascertained. The train due from Warrington at 4-15 was unable to pass the obstruction; but the Passengers after a I delay of 10 minutes were changed into a local train, AO despatched to their destinatieu, One line was cleared,about a router-past five, and tinder the direction 01 Mr. Catte,n, the etationmaeter, be traffic ‘vas carried very slight r •on art delay. A break-d Own Cfane from the locomotive Depart Went was attached to the engin-; blat when in the act of raising it the powerful shafts of thli. crane smashed, and severe. of the men narrowly escaped injury. The engine was afterwards placed upon the metals by means of hydraulic jacks, and the lines were c.nnpletely cleared about balf-paet seven.

fraction over 2icl per day and a total of £55 Is 4d, the I profit claimed on the stone account in the same half-year being £B6 ls 3d. Inclusion of these casuals with ordinary Workhouse inmates will destroy all analogy between the • Union Workhouse and the Union Schools. There are still other difficulties in the way after reducing the number to 56,879. My own calculetion would be thetas, by the dietary tables three meals are due to one day's maintenance, a total of 300 meals counts 100 days. The number of days' mein- teitance is, bqwever, fixed on tne total number of days given by the relief lists. Now many of the ordinary inmates of a workhoute are people whose stay is of a Ci 311.11 or transient character, and there is much lees fluctuation at schools, Than inf ants nurtured at the breasts may eich count 182 doe in a lt elf-year. Wheether, then, the Master's average of 4s ni per week or my average of 6s Id per week is accepted, they are alike subject to this explanation. The" Master's payments" include £llB 12s 6d paid as salaries. making this total to be £291 2s 6d. It will be seen from Appendix B the sum for salaries is returned by me at £383 2s 61, and I am unable to explain the dis- crepancy. In other respects the accounts will, I think, be clear. 'fable 1 gives provisions, necessaries, and clothing, according to use and consumption, with the average cost of each and of toe whole. Table 2 similarly dells with salaries tend ration!. Table 3 with establishment expenses. Table 4, sundries, mainly applicable to Workhouse, to give the exceptional average thereof. Table 5 includes actual rates and insurance. Table 6, annual occupation value. The appendices will be found useful and explanatary. They include profits on labour for the year, divided to give the average for a half-year, and other necessary information "It is not an unusual thing to hear of the Padgete Pauper PALIC9 having increased the poor rate the tune of 61 in the £.' I have heard 51. named in discussion even at the Board, The need for calm thought will be evident wen I explain that provisions, necessaries, clothing, offi- cers and other s ee and ratons, furniture and property, repairs, erahlisemmt expenses, rates, insurance, anl rental or annuel value, all and everyihine included in connecion with your Padgate institution, affects the rates by just one siogle perm; in the pound. Dednct the rent and substitute the purchase money, or sum paid in redemption of mortgage, then every expense is met, and the property itself acquired foe a Mere fraction over 11. in the pound, which frac- tion will quickly disapnear."—The report wag teken es reed. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS:
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS:

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuisday. Preeent: Mr. 4hu Ashton (in the chair), R.v. J. Lockwood, Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, R. Ashton, J. Oba,lloner, G. Whitlow, W. Jackson, W. Fisher, W. %%Maker, C. Rigby, J. Weir, J. Darbyshire, Smith, Andrews, Hamilton, Stokes, Wallington, Warburton, Mc- Intyre, and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) Fttramiet, MATTERS.—The Deputy Clerk reported that the county treasurer had issued a precept for £963 Is 91. The Rev. J. Lockwood moved the adoption of the Finance Committee's minutes, which stated that the county rate was £535 6s Bd, constabulary general expenses, r £l7B 8s 10.1 ; constabulary, local expenros £247 88 10d; other items, £ll 17s 61; total, £973 Is 34 showing a decrease of £159 10a lid on the corresponding period last year.—The minutes were adopted. THE Masrgn.—On the motion of Mr. W. Weir, seconded by Mr. C. Rigby, It was unanimously resolved that Mr. Jones, the master, should be allowed £2O fcr.,his services in connection with the carrying out of the sewerage scheme for the workhouse. .

INSPECTOR BOLLINGSVORTFL AND THE BOARD —A. lettter was read from Inspector flottingworth tendering his resigna- tion as assistant relieving officer for Runcorn.—The Chair- Man observed that for many years it bad been the custom for the inspector of police at Runcorn to be assistant reliev- ing officer to deal with tramp cases.—Mr. Handley moved that the resignation be accepted, and that Captain liamersley be asked to allow the new inspector of police to undertake the duties at the same salary as formerlv.—Mr. Norman seconded the motion, which was carried. STATE OF THE HOUSE.—The Master reported that the number of inmates in the house was 172, as compared with 186 last year. There were 26 boys sad 31 girls in atten- dance at school, and six boys and 15 girls were receiving an industrial training. During the week 21 vagrants had been relieved.

div.head: NEW PUBLIC BUILDINGS FOR. WIDNES.
div.p: NEW PUBLIC BUILDINGS FOR. WIDNES.

An adjourned meeting of Widnes Local Board was held yesterday afternoon, for the purpose of considering the sub- jects of public offices and infectious diseases hospital Mr. Carey presided; and there were present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Pankhurst, Handley, Forster, Midwood, Webster, Houghton, Gaskell, Wright, .1. T. Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Dickson (nuisance inspector).—The Chairman read the notice convening the meeting, which stated that it was called to consider the proposed alterations to'the esti- mate for the new public offices, and to decide about going on with the work at once. Further, to consider the advisa- bility of erecting an infectious diseases hospital. The Chairman explained that the Board had to decide whether they would have a tower to the Town Hall or not. If they had to have a tower they must provide proper thickness of walls and proper foundations ; and the cost would be £1,397. The original esimate was for £3,925, but they would remember that Mr. Higginson said it was necessary to add somewhat to the size of the rooms, namely, nine feet in the length of the building, and an extra height propor- tional to that increased length. The cost for that errs work would be about £5OO, so that they would see that the building without the tower would cost abon £4,425. If they had to provide the tower to the height of the roof they would have to add £497 to that amount at least.—.lr. Webster: I thought the estimate for the offices was to be £3,500.—Mr. Handley - With the usual limit for contingencies, which made it £3,900 —The Chairman: If we don't build to the top of the tower, the cost will be about £5,000, and if we do !AIM to the top of the tower the cost will Se about £6,ooo.—Mr. Gaskell : What will be the cost upon the rates —The Chair- man said:Mr. Allen had worked out some very interesting figures. Supposing the amount spent was £6,000; the I yearly amount to be repaid principal and interest would in 30 ' years at 4 per cent, would be £347 per annum. Of course from that amount they must deduct the rent which the Board now paid and the rant the School Board would pay, which would be in all about .£l5O So ,that the increased I expenditure of the Bard would be £197. A penny rate Mr. Allen stated, would bring in £360. Mr. Ci4skell : Then there is the extra cost of furnishing. The Chairman : If y. u don't build the top of the tower you sive £9OO which would be ample for furnishing, and you would not exceed £6,000 altogether. —ln reply to Mr. Houghton, the Surveyor said the architects fees were not Included in the estimates. He thought the cost of urniehing would be about £3OO, which would briag the total cost to be £5,600 if they did not build the top of the tower.-Mr. G askell thought they ought not to exceed £6,000. If they had an epidemic in the town, which was not at all unlikely, they would have f urthef expenditure which was not provided for in the present rate.—Mr. Handley, in order to bring the matter to a head, moved that the public offices be erected, the tower being carried up to the roof, at an es- timated cost of £4,922.—Mr. Forster seconded the motion. —ln reply to Mr. Gaskell, Mr. Allen said the estimates did not include the heating of the building by pipes.—The Chairman pointed out that the design showed open fire- places on the slow combustion system for the offices, and for the hall and grand staircase, hot water—The motion WWI carried without dissent-Dr. o•Keeffe moved, and Mr. Gaskell seconded, that the matter be placed in the hands of the General Purposes Committee, with instructions to proceed with the work at once. The Board then went into com- mittee to select a site fn. the proposed infectious diseases hospital. A sub-committee consisting of Dr. O'Keeffe, and Messrs. Carey and Handley was appointed to inspect several sites for the infectious diseases hospital and report to the Board.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

THE GLAZEBROOK PRIMITIVE Misvuontm's had their an- nual treat to New Brighton on Wednesday. A considerable number accompanied them from the neighbourhood. The day was beautif ally fine, which considerably added to their enjoyment. Smoot. Iwspacriox.—The annual inspection of the Wesleyan Day School of Cadishead, took place on Thurs- day. There was a considerable muster on the part of the children. They presented a very creditable appearance, and apparently passed upon the whole a very satisfactory ex- amination. Excunstotc—The brass band of this village had an ex- cursion on Saturday to Runcorn by water and by road. It rained heavily at intervals throughout the day. One old lady had her foot severely crushed bye. plank falling on her in the boat; and a young man had a narrow escape from being drowned. The profits of the trip are to be devoted to the band fund.

div.head: RAINHILL.
div.p: RAINHILL.

- - RAINHILL REFORM CLun.—The eha'reholaers in connec- tion with this club had a general meeting on Wednesday evening, in the Liberal Club-roam, at R4inhill, Mr. Thomas lianmer in the chair, for the purpose of receiving a report from the directors. The hon. sec, Mr. Johnson, read the report, showing the negotiations that had taken pl..ce in the purchase of new premises, which had been finally completed. Mr. Johnson was re-appointed hon. sec, and the retiring directors, Messrs. W. Evans, G. W. Rawlins, and T. lian- mer, were re-elected.

RAINHILL ASYLUM 'ATHLETIC SPORTS:—Theout-door amusements provided annually for the inmates of this asylum took place on the bowling green on Tuesday, in , Presence of a large number of ladies and gentlemen, who, as usual, took a kindly interest in the proc-edings. The sports. which commenced shortly after three o'clock, consisted ed races of a varied character for bod) males and females, the successful competi ors hoing presented with prizes in the hape of wearing apparel for the females, and tabecco, snuff. I Jtc.. for the males. The asylum band wan in attendance, and everything passed off pleasantly.

div.head: LATE MR. CHARLES HADFIELP.
div.p: THE LATE MR. CHARLES HADFIELP.

The Manchester Guardian of Monday contained the follow- ing sympathetic sketch of the career of this gentleman, who was for some years editor of this journal, and who was on his retirement presented with a parse of gold by the Liberal party in Warriogton in recodnition of hi valaab e services :

' Many of our renders will have beard with regret of the death of Charles Hadfield, for many years connected with the press in Manchester and elsewhere. He was born at Glossop, in Derbyshire, in the year 1821, but came to Man- chester very early in life, and always considered himself a Manchester man, and declared to the day of his deaqi that he never felt at home anywhere else. His first contribution to journalism was, as is go often the case with ardent youths. in the shape of verse, which saw the light in the cnlumns of the Manchester Times, then the property of its editor, Archibald Pientice. He joined the advanced politicians ot those days, and was almost, or fancied he was, a Chartist. under the banner of Feargus O'Connor. Into all social questions Mr. Hadfield threw himself with energy and en- thusiasm. When young he wrote essays, and received prizes for those upon making mechanics' institutions more useful for the class for whom they were originally founded, and for the improvement of the homes of the working classes. When a free art gallery for Manchester was projected, some 25 years ago, Mr. Hadfield advocated the subject warmly in the columns of the Manchester Examiner and Times, lie took an active part in securing the Saturday half-holiday, which bad long been enjoyed by other classes of workpeople, for the Manchester building trades. He also took an active part in the movement for providing public baths and wash- houses, and in controversies between workmen and their employers put the case of the former before the public with justice and impartiality. In alliance with others engaged with trade organisations, Mr. Hadfield attempted to estab- lish an organ in the press, the title of which was Weekly Wages, a monthly publication of which he was the gratuitous editor. About the same time he accepted an offer from Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., to join tha staff of the Newcastle Chronicle, and as lecturing agent for the Northern ftefotm Union. Returning to Manchester, he became connected with the commercial department of the Manchester Ex- aminer and Times. After this he became a regclar writer for the Manchester City News, and subsEquently editor of that paper for two years in the early period of its career. He next went to Glasgow for a short time, where he was connected with the Glasgow Herald, and then accepted the editorship and management of The Warrington and Mid-Cheshire Examiner. After several years work in this position he was presented with a testimonial at a meeting presided over by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, now M.Y. for the borough, and after a period of rest and retirement he became editor of the Salford Weekly Hews, in which position he remained until the beginning of 1883. This was his last official connection with the Press, and his health, which had for some time previously shown symptoms of giving way, soon afterwards broke down entirely, and he had not since left his room. In disposition he was most affectionate, cheerful and amiable; sanguine, but without ambition. With a keen relish for social enjoyment he combined muck depth of feeling and seriousness, an,! no one who merely saw him midst "quips and cranks and wanton wiles," and taking a prominent part in all from pure gaiety of heart, could have had any conception of the depth and earnestnes of the man. Although the pen had irresistible fascinations for him, which he could no more resist than a bird can help singing—" I do but sing because I must, and pipe but as the linnets sing "—still be hated writing to order, and con- sidered such work more or less insincere. He bad such a facile pen, however, that it not unfrequently led him astray, and ptitting off some necessary and irksome work, until the last moment—for he was constitutionally indolent—he sometimes neglected to bring the requisite matured thought and information to bear upon the subject in hand. Of this tendency be was very conscious; and constantly upbraided himself for it. The inexorable exigencies and peremptory requirements of modern journalism he deplored. As a jour- 1 nalist his strength lay in his knowledge of the habits, the wants, the wishes, the foibles, the prejudices, the vices, the virtues, and the aspirations of the " working classes," and oa this subject his matter was always good, thoughtful, and suggestive. All his sympathies lay in this direction, and when he felt his end approaching he said one of his greatest regrets was that he had done little or nothing for the good of his fellow-creatures.
