div.head: OUR LONDON LBTTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LBTTER.

LONDON, TEMRSDLY. A Ministerial crisis of a very serious character, though it had no outward and visible sign by which the public could recognise it, has taken place this week. it came to pass on Monday, and was interesting as proving two things; first, how frail is the hold upon power of the strongest Ministry; secondly, how great is the power of lying, especially when persistently done. For months past, with increasing vigour daring the last five weeks, the Times has done its beat to thwart the Government in its Egyptian policy. No one would brings charge, against the Times of dishonesty for pecuniary benefit. But this great journal, as was town the other day when it fell into the trap prepared for it by the adroit editor of the Fortnightly Review, is as simple as a child. n will Mallow any bait if skilfully prepared, and the great financial houses and personages who, two years ago invested in Egyptian bonds with the expectation that British ; annexation would double their yalue, have environed the Times on all sides, from Carlo to London, from Paris to Ber- lin, and engaged its powerful resources in their behalf. Thus. the Times has opehed its columns day by day to lying rumours about Ministerial intention with respect to figypt, and has devoted for weeks its first editorial to pictaing Mr. Gladstone aud his colleagues betraying the country and dragging the name of England through the mire—in other worda, abstaining from breaking its sole= promises and pledging the credit of England an 4 the lives of British soldiers in order that the bond-holders may double their fortunes.

1 This daily dose of c tlutnny has had its effect, and even among good Liberals (at least in London) there has been an uneasy feeling as to the course of events in Egypt. On Monday night the Times was outdone by the Pall Mall Gazette, a journal which I believe to be entirely free from bondholders influence, though it has been frantically play- ing their game. The enterprising new management of this journal 'simply deSires to increase its circulation, and etruggles to provide at least one sensation per issue. On Monday it succeeded beyond expectation, though at fatal cost to its reputation as an English newspaper. It produced in its largest type, and with fullest prominence, what pur- ported to be the text of the terms of agreement arranged between France and England. These set forth with great mecision the arrangements for a loan of eight millions to I be guaranteed by England, it indicited a multiple control, and added that fifteen thousand Turkish troops—the very name of the comrnanaer being given—were forthwith to be sent to harry the tioudan.

It is known now that all this was pure and audacious in- vention. The monetary arrangement upon which the Pall Mall lavished details had not even coma under the consi- deration of Lord Granville and M. Waddington, being re- ser% ed for the consideration of the Conference. There is to be no multiple control; the term of occupation by British troops was misstated; and the despatch of Turkish troops to tue Soudan, the proposal which of all moat severely tried the loyalty of Liberal members; was the fi;mitnt of a disor- dered imagination. In jo'urnalistic circles the source of in- formation paraded by the Pall Mall Gazette is very well known. A German of considerable intelligimce and some means of information, who jointly represents in this country the Cologne Gazette, and an Austrian paper, had after the fashion of his couotrymen.‘evolved this precious "settle- ment" pneof his inner cmsciousness. He telegraphrd it to his papers in Vienna and Cologne, and then bethinking himself of the lust of the Pall ;fall Gazette for sensations, sent them a translation, which appeared improved by the reckless hand of the new editor. What was harmless enough in German papers as the gossip of a London cor- respondent became a serious matter when prominently put forward upon the honour And character of a newspaper of which, so recently as six months ago, the English press was proud.

The effect of this circumstantial lying upon the Rouse of Commons was very great. It circulated between five and half-past six, the very time when members congregate' in the lobby to exchange views. The Conservatives were naturally elate, and declared that within three weeks the Ministry would be defeated. The Liberals were correspondingly de- pressed. It seemed impossible to donbt that there must be something in a statement circulated in this portentous run- ner. If the Government bad signed such an agreement as was represented it was evidently a hopelees fight for them. The waverers on earlier votes of cencure now openly revol- ted, and the great body of the party were gloomily silent: ' but no one said a word in defence of a Government supposed I to have agreed to such a settlement. It was conceded that I they must go, and the thing most talked about was a disso- lution. Next day came the exposure of the fraud, and with that curious swiftness and completeness of movement that mares the mental attitude of large bodies of men the cloud passed away, dissolution receded in the dim distance, and to the state of perturbation succeeded a feeling of calm con- fidence in the stability of the Government. Tills has been streogthened by the extraordinary progress made by the Franchise Bill. But the episode of Monday is meworable, and is well worthy or coneideration. It thews how tickle Is the faith of public men and hew much in need of the un- swerving and the invigorating common sense of the country are members of Parliament who live in the enervating atmos- phere of London. A friend who has just returned from the United States tells me of a new development of speculative enterprise in that country. Ws have long been familiar with the pro- ceedings of the smart man who buys up theatre tickets for popular performances and sells them, at greater or less profit to the public. Some ingenious persons have now hit upon a scheme of buying up the best berths in the favourite Atlantic steamers and sell them at a premium. There is a fine opening here, for about -this time of the year there is keen competition for state rooms on the White Star, Cunard, and other favourite lines. Its natural developments, apart from speculators, are such that many of the berths in steamers now crossing the Atlantic were engaged twelve months ago.

People who read the "Arabian nights" and find much entertainment in them would be a little astonished if they knew what small proportion of the original work they hold in their hands. A little body of scholarly men who call themselves the Villon Society :hare thought it well to re- move this reproach from modern literature. A copy of the original work has been obtained, and is now being translated in all its virgin fullness. I suppose the police would inter- fere if the precious volumes were exposed for sale in the ordinary way. However that be. the Villon Society are publishing it by suhscription. There are to be nine volumes, each published at a guinea, the issue being limited to flys hundred. Subscription has baen eagerly made, and the work is going merrily forward. Of course, the book is prim' by this scholarly Society on account of its literary excellence. It is certainly not a drawing-room book.

Mr. Wilson Barrett has not been a great theatrical success on his visit to London. But he has the art of making per- sonal friends, and has done a good deal in this way since his arrival in England. The fashion set by American doctors of welcoming their Transatlantic brethren at sump- tuous feasts is spreading here. On Saturday night Mr. Toole had a very pleasant party On the stage of his theatre when the night's work was done and the curtain had fallen. The guest of the evening was the American actor, and I should not like to say at what hour on Sunday morning the proceedings terminated. They were at least not carried so near church time as was a recent sitting of the House of Commons. A very pleasant souveinr Mr. Barrett will carry back with him to the states is in the form of a little volume of sonnets illustrated with pen and ink sketches by several artists. The idea originated with Mr. Abbey, who has sketched on the fly-leaf of the wdume a charming scene. Mr. Boughton illustrates a sounet on " Love in wintar "with one of his charming female figures. Mr. Linlev Sambourne and one or two other well known artists have joined in the kindly work. Lord Dafferin before he left London for Con- stantinople was the recipient of a favourite volume thus specially illustrated, and I know he holds the book at a priceless value. The Parisians have evidently heard of Mr. Chamberlain's love of orchids, and have accordingly invented an appro- priate story. The President of the Board of Trade is not mentioned by name, but there is no other Ministre Anglais whom the cap would fit. According to the veracious chronicler of the Boulevards the Minister was the other day (Mr. Chamberlain, by the way, has not been in Paris this year) walking along the Quai de Is Megisseric, when he ob- served in a shop window an orchid of extraordinary beauty and rarity. "How much is this orchid ? " be asked the shopkeeper. "£20," was the reply. "Is it known iv France?" he asked. "No, sir," said the shopkeeper, "Is xi the sole possessor, and have not bad it 10ng.," Le Mini' ii,ve Anglais hereupon took from his purse a 500 franc rote, which he handed to the shopkeeper. Then taking the plant, he tore it to pieces, and trod it under foot. "I bay' that kind," he explained to the astonished el- "and I would rather that nobody else in F .ortope had another."

1t The question of the sale of the Blenheim House picture awaits the decision of the Court of Chancery, whose neon. wiry permission has been invited. There is little doubt that this will be given, and our Liovernment are more than half resolved to buy the pictures. Sir Charles Diake recently undertook unofficially to obtain a professional opinion upon their value. A picture dealer well known by name but not likely to be recognised at Blenheim was sent down with an introduction from Sir Charles Dilke, which obtained for him admission to the galleries. His proceedings here greatly excited the curiosity of the housekeeper. Acne. tomed to see people with more or less of interest regarding he famout pictures she bad never known one thus coreduet himself, spending an hoar over each one, prying tnto them as if looking for something the presence cif which was unsyspected by ordinary people. The nataral conclusion she came to WAS that he had felonious designs upon the pictures. She had heard of canvasses being cat out in the dead of night and mysteriously carri/d eff. These heirlooms she kusw were priceless, and the temptation cor- respondingly great. She kept a watchful eye on the stranger, and kept everybody On the qui vive through the night. abe next day the distinguished picture dealer presented himself to continue his task, and was politely INA firmly warned off the premises. It was only after personal ettninunication with the Duke that he was permitteelagain to enter the gal- leries. ,

Society still complains of the lack of opportunity of en. joying itself, which seems a little petulant considering the number of houses open every night. The principle ground work of complaint is the continued absence of the Prince of Wales. As to the absence of the Queen, that is a matter of coursa that doss not now affect the season one ray or another. But social despair is crowned by the announce- ment that there are to be no more drawing-rooms this year. that truly is Sorrow's crown of sorrow, meaning much more than the absence of opportunity to sit fur an hour or two within a line of carriages stared at by the multitude, with the subsequent privilege of fighting a way in and out of Buckingham Palace.

'Am ENFRANCHISEMENT OF WOBlEN.—During the last esxteen years Ore have been ten divisions in the Reuse of 'Commons on the question of the eLlranchisement of wornea. The following record of the results will be interesting at the present time. In 1867, for woman's suffrage, 81, against 202; 1870, 119, against 242; 1871, 159, against 228; 1872, 163, • against 244; 1873, 172, against 239; 1875, 170, against 205; 1876, 161, against 248;1578, 155, against 235; 1879, 134, against 245; 1883, 163, against 179. On Thursday. the minority in favour c, female suffmge was composed of 98 Conservatives, eight Homo Rulers, a,.d 31 Liberals. while the majority was made up of 234 Liberals, 23' Home Rulers, and 26 Conservatives. Sir Stafford Northcote and Lord John Manners were in the minority, but Sir Richard Cross, Mr. W. H. Smith. and Lord IL Churchill did not vote. A conference of delegate. and friends who approve of Mr. Woodall's ' addition to the Franchise Bill in favour of female suffrage was held on Friday, at the Westminster Paine Hotel, London, Mr. Stang- field, M.P., in the chair. Several members of Parliament were present.—Tbe Chairman said the Cabinetwere strongly against them ; but they intended to make a new departure. They had done with the academic ago, and new intended to win. The question is now one of practical politics, and those against them would N made to feel that they intended to have a voice in the Liberal policy of tin. future. Resolu- tions were carried, declining to i•cc .pt the result of Thurs- ' day night's division, as it did it settle the cl .use on its merits, and that they did ntSt re,zard at as a fair extartstien of opinion, and urging that the matter should be again rought under the nottce of boll Honda of Parliameßt.

div.head: WARRINGTON, DO YOUR DUTY.
div.p: WARRINGTON, DO YOUR DUTY.

Sir,—ln 1880 the constituents of Warrington threw off 1 the ehackles of Toryism, and put upon them the armour of "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform," by returning to Parlia- ment a Liberal member, and a firm supporter of Mr. Glad- aorta. Warringio'n electors, I understand, will soon once more be called upon to show by their votes whet!, er they will have a Liberal or Conservative member. Although I myself live outside the borough, I take a keen interest in anything that tends to the benefit of Warrington; and I should like the people once More to return a Liberal, one worthy to take the place of your Wiring member, who was retarded with honour and comes Tut With bOnour. Returned to support Mr. Gladstone and the principles of Liberalism, he has faithfully fulfilled his promises. He has supported Mr. Gladstone "through thick and thin," and proved himself a firm supporter of civil and religious liberty. Through the columns of your paper I see there are now before the people of Warrington two candidates for the representation of the borough. I have read the speeches of both gentlemen, and from these can tell which is the best man. One candidate spoke a great deal about fishing and flogging. Now as regards the flogging question, the Liberals have passed a bill for the abolition of flogging, so that is settled, unless the candidate in question should think fit to bring inet bill to revive it again, which may be possible, judging from bow be was in favour of retaining it. With regard to the fishing , question, it is better understood by the people ef Warrington than myself. But there are questions of far greater import- ance than being allowed to fish in a certain reservoir. Are you, I would 'ask, going to have a Man to represent you again who when his party was in power throLgh ther ae,;- grerive foreign policy implicated us in the mat Eterldll9 of foreign complications, from which it has taken all the .trenius of the'. Grant Old Man "and his colleagues to ex- ' ideate rie? They entirely neglected home remedial legisla- tioa. They had not time to study the elevation of Ireland. Their time war. comoletely taken up in fighting for a "scientific frontier"! in fighting the Zulus, dic. They had war to the right of them and war to the left of them, and deut behind them. Oh, yes, if you want a deficit in the Ex- chequer, send the Tories into power, for they can neither make a surplus nor keep one. Neither Peace, Retrench- ment, nor Reform may properly be given as the result of having in power a Conservative Administration. A Government that pursues "a spirited foreign policy" cannot keep the finances in a sound condition, neither Can they find time for remedial legislation. Now, as regards the present Liberal Administration, we can look to thorn for many useful measures of reform. Hardly a section of the whole community has been neglected. If we tarn to the working-classes at large, we find that the Employers' Liability Bill has been pasied for their benefit, and that it has had some effect is obvious to all thinking men. Let the working-men just look round where they are working, and they will find that far greater precaution is now taken for the prevention of accidents. As a working- man myself, I con see it by the manner in which certain dangerous parts of the various processes are protected. Then we can turn again to the Patents Bill, which is a good bill, and passed for the benefit of the British working artiz tn. By this Bill he can have his genius. his industry , and zeal protected at a far lass cost than before. This ' country has been in the habit of losing yearly about £20,000,000 by fraudulent bankruptcy; a Bankruptcy Bill has been passed to reduce this evil; and so we can go on. For the benefit of the farmers, there has been passed the Hares and Rabbits Bill, Repeal of the Malt Tax, and an Agricultural Holdings Act. For the benefit of the sailors the passing of the Seamen's Wages Regulation Bill, and there is also under consideration the Ship- ping Bill of Mr. Chamberlain. The present Government have passed a bill for the abolition of flogging in the arms- and navy; while even the friends of temperance can console themselves a little for a bill has been passed prohibiting the payment of working-men's wages in public houses. If we look to Ireland we find Me. Gladstone trying his best to 're- store peace to that unhappy country. India is doing all right, and we may fairly leave the Egyptian question in the hands of Mr. Gladstone, for be is the best man to bring us out of difficulties. I therefore appeal to the working-men of War- rington to give their votes to the Liberal candidate. There are many of us at the present time without a vote; if we have to pay just as much ae you it is all the eame, but when you sent Mr. McMianies to power we expected him to support the various measures of reform. On the Brad- laugh question, the Lind Bill for Ireland, and other im- portant measures for the benefit of the country at large, the member for Warrington *al found supporting Mr. Glad- stone. There are still many more vital questions to be answered, and if we wish to receive good legislation, let us all labour to return men to Parliament who will try to meet the increasing demands of .an increasing population, and endeavour to raiso in the social scale of life the democracy of this country. Mark your man; let it be Crosfield, and follow up the "52." Da not be led away by the men of " three F's,"—Flood, Flogging, and Fishing, but listcn to the words of the Liberal candidate, and then you will see who is fit to be the worthy member for Warrington.—Yours, &c.. A YOUNG RADICAL.

- --- Bir,—l am sure the werking-man ought to be very thank- ful to the various influential personages who so kindly and in such a disinterested manner take up the periodical "fads" that corns to the front as panaceas for all his troubles. It seems to me that there are but two avaYs in which the worker can be helped. One is for "Lad' Bonn- tifnl "to have the right and sole privilege of distributing blankets and sending orders to the coal merchant. All that is expected in return for this is that the recipient should pull his fore-lock, say "thank you, m arm," and be satisfied with his position in life. The other, and I must say the better way, is for the working-man to have a fair field and no favour. This, once granted, the rest will fol- low. As a rule it is the Tory who likes Is be the patriarch ef his district, to fuse and fume about, looking after Mrs. this, and Mrs. that, for so-and-so's child ha e got the measles All this is splendid work for the dormant talent" of the general run of Tories. On the other band, the Radicals are ' called cold and heartless, because, forsooth, they refuse to have anything to do with a patronising, policy, and simply seek to place all men on the same political footing, and leave the rest to time and their own manhood. Mr. Alfred Austin in one of the reviews seeks to lead us back to those good old days 80 dear to the old women of the Tory party. Be aimed at pointing out a way whereby the Position and surroundings of the lower classes might be im- proved. Surely a noble object. To tell the people "to re- turn to the ways of their forefathers " was scarcely suffi- cient and not worth dignlfying with the title 4. A Remedy for Social Discontent.' Rut, however that may be, it gtofobrawaCirdnitte iM o tell seems to puoss st ihbal , the tia dpyp e rJ and hn ye r Mans an: ews have got hold of such a lot of bad and expensive hibits that they could not possibly get rid of them. Amongst " the upper ten " there seems to be a great dread lest the tendency of advancing civilisation should be to break down all caste barriers. Mr. Aus,in tells us that it is what the working. man sees of the life of the upper classes that causes his dis- content—that it is in fact mere sentiment on his part to be discontented. Civilization is no empty word. Its meaning embraces the whole of life's social problems, and so long as the inventive
