brain of man fills the world with evidences of his mechani- cal skill so long shall we have the means of bui.ding op social inequalities. In 1841 Lord John Manners gave forth to the world) in poetic form his great love for the past. In ecstacy of admiration he cries out—

In many a hamlet, yet uncursed by traded Bloom faith and love all lightly In the shade, It would be quite a revelation to the teeming millions just now to have it proved that trade is a curse. ft is the general 'impression that want of trade is the greatest curse we have at present. But this scion of a noble family does intoee than curse trade with a boldness Coat is simply surmising. He hungers after "The parer faith of purer days,' when— Tile daily beadanuish welting for his bread{ Were good and,b id were all unquesti -nettled. For then It was not to our rulers known That God was mindful of the first alone.; The monks still practiced their dear Lord'aconunand. Asebmined their charity throughout the land. -, If teachings like the above are what we are to expect when ' the daysmf Crecy and Poictiers return toms. again, we ask to be saved from OVA' friends ; and we very much question ithe sanity of the late Tory Postmaster-General set:en tie cries 'Out—

Tia't wealth and commerce. laws andilea,mlng, die. But leave ma stfill oar Old Nobility. Ous nobility are gradually but certainly becoming effete. In only, a very few instances are they capable of giving evidence o even the most ordinary amoznt of intelligence. Unconsciously they they'expose their own order, and as a palliation to their own wrong doings drag in the failings ofmthers. The latest em- ample of this is Lady John Manners, who has kindly slept forward and given to the public such an expose as should most certairiy open the people's eyes, How the rich spend the hard earnings of the poor, is. most graphically sketched by this kind lady, and it will not be her fault if it remains a "mere sentiment" on the working-noon's part to be dis- contented with his position. Her ladyship tells us "the rich have fallen into the grooves that custom has followed for many years." To diminish their expenditure on superflui- ties in order to provide their poorer neighbours with oppor- tunities of earning nacessaries is "hardly possible,* bec iuse we are told with the utmost coolness "when habit has be- came second nature it is difficult to change." And what is this habit to which her ladyship refers? "New, when parties are entertained in well-appointed sporting country houses in England, or in shooting-lodges in Scotland, a succession of meals, each partaking more or less of the character of a dinner, occupies tbe attention of the guests, with brief inter- vals of rest, from morning hours till long past dewy eve." Thus we see how hard are the lives of those poor favourites of fortune compelled so live so that they may eat, their lives are a burden to then.

Her ladyship is kind enough to give us details. "Before the ladies—indeed, before most of the gentlemen—leave their beds, dainty little services of tea sad bread and butter are carried to them. Sometimes the younger prefer brandy and soda." After this our masters quietly take another snooze and come down to breakfast about ten, when "four hot dishes, every sort of cold meats that might fitly furnish a feast, fruits, cakes, tea, coffee, cocoa, claret on the side- board, constitute a satisfactory breakfast, often prolonged till within two hours and a half of luncheon." The cook's ability is severely tested by these gourmands, and for a rich man to have it said of him —" so-and-so really does you very well" is the highest of . eAcomiums. "By 10, or balf-past, dinner is generally over, coffee is brought into the dining roam, while the gentlemen smoke. It is whispered that some of the ladiee enjoy a poet-prandial cigarette. Liqueurs and tea are offered during the evening, and keep up the fiaggin4 energies till the ladies ostensibly go to bad, after a little money has changed hands at poker or loo." Poor dear fellow-mortals; just to think of their " flagging energies," after such a laborious round of daily toil. Oae can fancy how hate: must be their work. First they must rack their brains as to what they are to eat and drink, next as to whepewithal they shall be clothed. "The home-spun tweed or cintbric made by a first rate dressmaker costs from ten to twelve pounds." I wonder how much of this sum finds its way into the hands of the poor sempstress. "Many ladies at the present time, whose forttinee ginnot be considered large, spend Mx hundred a year on their toilettag." I should very much like to trace to their source a few of these in- comes. I much fear that they are the cause of many a "bitter cry." To spend "sixty guineas on a court dress is a not uncommon occurrence." Of coarse a life of this kind palls on the senses, and a sensation of being chivied, hunted, or rushed occ tsion oyeecom's ths most energetic. Notice the ladylike slang, when our attention is turned to the "Sportsman's Guide." A tone of bitterness seems to per- vade. All the best shooting is taken by men who have made "vast fortunes by commerce," as much as £4,000 be- ing paid for the privilege of "creeping on all fours" after a beast, and as much as a hundred guineas a month for a good house on the coast. Is the matter of pictures, it is to Man- chester that most of Millais' pictures find their way, "for the number of millionaires or demi-millionaires has increased greatly of late years," and "sometimes £lO,OOO a year is allowed to each son who marries, and ample dowries are given to the daughters." I beg the reader to keep in mind the fact that it is a staunch Tory whom I am now quoting—one who thinks the habit of living acquired is not to be got rid of. Her ladyship deals pretty fairly all round. Of coarse, it would not be " proper form " for her to Jell us that the manufacturers should be setisfied with less profits. and give the workmen a chance of proving that life is worth living. Instead of that she drags a highly respectable body at men to the front. "A. certain number of -brewers seem to have found in their vats the potentiality of becoming rich beyond the dreams of avarice. Distillers have extracted gold in abun- dance by their processes." Poor brewers! how hard of her ladyship to talk of their avarice, when we in Warrington know so much to the contrary! We are told that tobacco manufac- turers and soap boilers make "four times as much money" now as formerly, that as much as five pounds is spent in a day on cigars, while, of course, the extra use to which we put the tub accounts for the increase in expenditure on soap. Thank you, Lady John Manners; I hope the lesson you have taught the working-man will not be forgotten. I take It to mean that our lives are simply used as a means for providing such as you with luxuries, and that so long as you can afford to "give three guineas and upwards for a bouquet " it matters not that the "poor are hovelled and hunted together each sex like swine." and that while the wealthy soap-maker can give us a Bank Park, the equally wealthy brewer may, like the hedgehog, coil himself up showing nothing but the quills. AL roN LOCKE. June 9, 1984.

public-house as late as eleven o'clock at night showed there• WAS a duty to be performed by the constable, and was quite sufficient to account for his being in the neighbourhocd, where the affair took place. Referring to the "apology" mentioned in the letter, Mr. Cartwright had asked whether the Bench could imagine a reepsctible m an engaged in a conflict of that kind demanding an apology from a police. constable on datraa He had no right to open his mouth upon any each matter. They might iinaeine the conduct of a nn which would draw from a constable the remark that be WAS only a half-crown doctor, and it showed the impropriety of which he had been guilty in addressing a public official in the manner he did.—Mr. Swift here interposed, and can- tended that the letter Was not evidence, and all the matter which his friend Mr. Cartwright was se energetically enlarging upon was quite beside the question. 'fhe question for the Bench was "did this man strike that blow?" And if he did," Was it an unlawful blow, or was it one that the constable broughtupon —lair. Cartwright said he Was there not only on befall( of Sullivan hut aleo on behalf of the public service, and what he wanted his. friend to feel was that it wag not a case of Aseault as between man andaman, but a more grave state of . things. If his friend meant to say that any ordinary in- dividual, any citizen, had a right to go up to a police officer on duty and. do as the defendant had done, the serviee was :at an end, and that was what they wanted to teach Peter Smith. Mr. Peter Smith mast perfectly understand that he had no rigbt whatever to go to a policeman and question him as to his duties. If he allowed himself, as ad- mitted in his letter, to consent to engage in a coinneon fight, it was each a case as he trusted their worships would regard in a manner as to put such a penalty upon Mr. Smith that he and other persons might know that they interfered with constables on duty at their peril.—P.C. Sullivan was then sworn, and deposed that about eleven o'clock on Tuesday night, the 3rd inst., he WAS standing in the middle of the highway opposite Wilson's Hotel, in Bridge-etreet. The house was just closing, and as he was looking at his watch tho defendant crossed to where he was standing and said, "What are you standing here for; you have no right here at all. It would look better of you to do your duty and not he hinging about this house. I know what you are here for. Jackson's case was dismissed this moraine', and you are trying to catch him egain. I know you Sullivan, 321. If it was not for your bright buttons I would knock your neck out." tLauehter.) He could see that the defen- dant had had a deal of drink, and he told him he bat a right to stand there. He Was on duty. He advised the defendant to eo home, and witness remained there until the house was closed. As he was going down the street the defendant passed him saying "I will report you." When witneee got to the police statiox the defendant was leaving the offiee. He heard P.C. Kelly, who was in charge ol the office, say that defendant could not see the books. Wit- ness, Kelly, and the defendant then left the office, and stood near the steps leading into the office, where a crowd of about 100 persons had assembled. Defendant called out " Steal out of the way, Kelly, and I'll give him the -- hiding he ever had." Witness told him that he would commit an assault if he did, and the defen- dant replied that he did not care for a common constable like him. The defendant then pushed his fist towards his chest, and witness raised his hand to keep it off. In ex- plaining what had occurred at Wilson's Hotel, witness pointed his finger and Smith immediately said" Don't peint your finger at ins." Witness said he should if he "poked" his fist at him. The defendant said "If you do twill knock your head off." and he then struck him a severe blow on the left cheek, knocking'his hat off. He was c arrying a stick at the time—usually having OLI3 in the night—and he threw it down and closet with the defendant for the purpose of arresting him. P.C. Kelly said they knew where he lived, and he had better not lock him cp, but summons him. He then released Mr. Smith, who went to his own door. When he got there he said "I am at my own door now, and if he comes here I will knock his -- head of." Witness went towards Mr. Smith's shop, and the defendant went inside. There was a crowd of some 100 persons in the street, and with some little difficulty he dispersed them. About twelve o'c'eek the defeadent Cele° baCli to the polic9 etitiOn and Said if he whines) did aot apologise he Would repert hint in the morning; Mr. Smith was summoned on the 4th June, and witness received two summonses on the 6th June. Crose-exernined by Mr. Swift : Witness said he never used the expression " half-crown doctor," nor did he say that his " tower," so far as the police were concerned, was dead. When in the police station he did not pull Mr. Smith by the coat and tell him to go out, that he had no right there. Mr. Smith did not say " Keep your fiagers off me, as I have a right in the public part of the office, as I am laying a complaint against you." He did not push Mr. Smith against the wall of the police office, and he did not press his elbow into his stomach. Mr. Smith did not say "Mind what you are doing; although I have a big stomach there is plenty of room for you to go out." (Laughter.) He did not call Mr. Smith a swine. He said something when he closed with him, hut he did not remember what the remark was. He did not say to Mr. Smith, "The first time I am off duty I will give you a bit of my staff." —P.C. Kelly said he was on night duty at the police station on the 3rd June. He recollected Mr. Smith coming about ten minutes past eleven. When he entered he laid tt Who is 321 ?" Witness said he did notaenow. Mr. Smith said he had grossly insulted him. Immediately afterwards, when he and Mr. Smith stood at the door, Sullivan came in and said " Here's 321." Mr. Smith said " He has insulted me in the sweets." Mr. Smith then asked for the sergeant, and being told he was not in asked where the inspector was. Witness said he did notelanow, and Mr. Smith asked him to let him look at the books. Witness said he could not do that without the permission of the inspector. Mr. Smith then went to the door. and said to Sullivan "I have a good mind to knock your neck out," and then struck him a blow on the side of the head, knocking his hat off. Mr. Smith stood on the top of the steps and Sullivan below. Sullivan at once closed with Mr. Smith, and witness said "Don't lock him up. We know the man, let him be summoned." Mr. Smith went towards his own shop, and when he got to the door he said. "I am standing in my own doorway now: I have a good mind to knock your neck out." A crowd of some 30 or 40 persons assembled, and he and Sullivan dispersed them. Mr. Smith was very excited. He did not see Sulli- van hold up a stick and attempt to strike Mr. Smith. He never drew his staff. At twelve o'clock Mr. Smith again ceme to the office, and said he should write to Captain Hamersley.—Cross-examined by Mr. Swift: He had known Mr. Smith for eleven years. lie was assistant to Mr. Whit- taker for some years. and was now carrying on business on his own account. During that time the defendant had lived in immediate proximity to the police station. He believed he had assisted the police to the utmost of his power when- ever the opportunity occurred. He heard Sullivan say to Smith when he was in the office "Come out of here ; you have no right in the office." Witness said he had a right there if he was making a complaint. He heard Smith say that although he had a big stomach there was plenty of room for Sullivan to go out. At that time Sullivan was not pressing against him, and he could not say when he said it. He did not hear. the word "swine " used, and he did not hear Sullivan use any offensive epithet to Mr. Smith. He did not hear him say "The first time I am off duty I will give you a bit of my staff." He did not hear a nerson in the crowd say," Mr. Smith. shall I knock him down?" and he did not hear Mr. Smith reply "No.take no notice of him."— P.S. Waltey, who had been stationed in Runcorn for eight years, said at ten minutes past twelve—an hour after the occurrence—he was passing down Bridge-street, when Mr. Smith called him into the shop and said that he had been insulted by officer 321. He said it had taken place opposite Wilson's Hotel, and witness asked him how he had been in- sulted, and Mr. Smith replied, "lie looked into my face as I came out of Wilson's Hotel." (Loud laughter )—Witness said he would see Sullivan shortly, and would inquire into the matter. Mr. Smith then said that when he was in the police station Sullivan took hold of him by the arm and said his day was done at the Town Hall now. At twenty minutes to one Mr. Smith came to witness at the police station, and said he had come to report himself and to ask him to say that he Was perfectly soaer. Witness replied "Quite right, Mr. Smith." He could sea that the defen- dant had had a drop when he went into the shop, but he was not drunk.—Asked what other remark Mr. Smith made, witness said he had forgotten, but afterwards stepped back to the box and said Mr. Smith had told him that he did give Sullivan " a good welt on the side of the bead."—Mary Phaeton, Elizabeth Braman, Mary Salkeld, and George Halehurst gave eitence of a confirmatory character.—Mr. Cartwright remarked he had several other witnessee, but it was a question whether it was necessary to produce them Mr. Swift said he had all along felt that it was a Case Which WAS not worth while ventilating in public. He could not help feeling that it Was always better for respectable mem- bers of the community not to interfere with police officers at all, except to assist them when they were in the lawful discharge of their duty, and the best possible way of meet- ing a police officer when one could not help him was to say '• Good night," and pass on. In commenting upon the evi- dence. Mr. Swift said it seemed rather odd that Sullivan should have followed Mr. Smith down to the police station, and not lot him make his complaint without interruption. He alluded to toe discrepancy in the evidence of the two first witnesses with regard to what passed in the police office, and said he would rather put it down to the excite- ment of Sullivan in forgetting what had exactly taken place rather than upon any other footing. He argued that from the evidence it was impossible to arrive at a strictly ac- curate conclusion of what actually took place, and contended that it was not likely that the defendant in the presence of Constable Kelly, to whom he had just laid a complaint, would commit an unprovoked assault upon Sullivan.—The magistrates decided to hear the cross-sum- monses, and Sullivan was charged with having on the 3rd inst. used certain abusive amid defamatory language towards Peter Smith calculated to incite or provoke a breach of the peace. He was also charged with having unlawfully assaulted Peter Smith. Defendant pleaded not guilty to both charges.—Mr. Smith said he was a chemist and druggist carrying ou business in High-street. On Tuesday night, the 3rd June, he was leaving Wilson's Hotel shortly before closing time. It was between three and four militates to eleven. He had been in the private portion of the house. As he was leaving he sew the defendant Sullivan standing in the vestibule near the door place. He was rather startled at first, p.od said "Hallo, good night; what are you doing here?" Sullivan gave a very insulting reply. He said "You ought to be at home, and not in a hole like this. I will put a stop to such --- as you coming here." He never was so insulted in his life, and told the officer that if he had a charge against him or the house to make it. He also demanded his name, and said he should report him. Sullivan shouted after him that he was only a " half-crown " or "twopence-halfpenny doctor," and that his " tower " so far as the police was con- corned was dead. Witness at once went to the police station, where he was spoken very roughly to. While in the office

Sullivan came in, took hold of him by the coat and arm,' and pulling him beckwards from the desk towards the door said with an oath that he had no right there. Witness said' "Keep Your &tigers off. It is very questionable whether I have not right in the office. lain in the public part of the entice ;" and he demanded to see the books. The defendant gave him a poke in the stoinash—Haughter)—with his elhow as be pissed, and witness said "Mind what you are doing; although my stomach is rather a large one, there is plenty of room for you to pass, and if you do that I will knock you down." His coat WAS torn—it was an old one and not of much value—his arm was hurt, and he was thumped into the wall before he said that. When Sullivan went outside witness continued his comp:aint to Kelly. When witness went oateide he was met by Sullivan, woo put his face up to his, and ho4ding up his stick he said "You ---swine, I will give you a bit of thie." Witness was on the steps, and said he would knock Sullivan down. He could easily have done so, and he struck trim on the side of the head. Sullivan got hold of witness, but Kelly said to Sullivan 'Leave toe mart alone; we know him, and don't lock him up. We will summon him." Witness went straight to the door of his shop, where Sullivan followed him with a crowd, and he used some very violent language. The defendant again called him a "-- swine," and held his stick to hint ag tin in the presence of the crowd. Witness told him to go away, and someone in the crowd said "Knock him down, and we will jump on him." He told P.C. Kelly to disperse the crowd, and he then wrote the letter which had been placed in evidence. He wrote it while in. AA excited state, and when he went to post it he I took a stick with him, so that if Sullivan came to him again he should be defended as wall as him.— Mr. Cartwright : What time was it when you came out of Wilson's Hotel ? Refore eleven o'clock. I could not tell the esect time. I had been in the private part of the house. I was not there for the purpose of drinking. I was haying scene supper, and had some pigeon pie and two glosses of beer; th it was all the beer I had during the day —What time was it? A few minutes to eleven.—you sty in your letter it was one minute to eleven I could not tell to a minute.—Mr. Cirtwright : Then the stateineat in your let- ter is incerrect ? I could not tell to a minute or two.— Which is correct, west you say now or your letter? What I I say now.—Do I understand that you wieh to correct the statement in your letter? No, I don't.—Mr. Certweight read the portion of the letter in which Mr. Smith said it woe a minute or so " to eleven that he was leaving Wil- son's Hotel. Witaees :said he would swear to the time men- tioned in he letter. It was a question of nefibbling aeout putting a thing on piper.—Mr. Cartwright: You do not think of anything on paper then? No, not in a thing of chat sort.—Wbere woe tne police constable ? Between the two doors.—He lees on the premises then ? Yes. —Do you mean to swear that ? Yes. You heard hi.o say that he was in the road? I heard him sty many things which are incorrect.—We have it on the evi- dence of six witnesses that he was in the midale of the road. Do you mean to swetr that he woe in the vestibule ? Yes —Your letter save, "As I in company with several other gentlemen was leaving Wilson's Hotel the officer met me face to face on the footpath." Now which is correct, that letter or your statement? My statement is correct.—Then your letter is false? It is close to.—Now look here, Mr. Smith, mind what vote are doing. You are on your oath. I do not know whether you are aware of it or not, but let ins caution you. You thive already sworn that you met this man in the vestibule of this house. I swear it is so.—l want to know what you mean by saying you were leaving this house at one minute to eleven and met the officer face to face on the footpath? I swear that he was in the vesti- bule. When I say he was in the vestibule he was past the front door, and the letter is incorrect if it says that.—Very well, alit is one misrepresentation? Yes.—Now you say he grossly insulted VOGL What was, the nature of the insult? He told me I ought to be at home, and not in a " hole like that."—l ask you seriously, as a respectable now, whether you mean to say that the constable addressed you in the manner you hove spoken of? Yes.—And how many parsons were there? I could not say; they were moving abent the etNet.—Wbet else did he say? He 111,1 I Wes A tieepetiee halfpenny fleeter, acid that my tower was at an end.—What did he mesa ? I suppose he meant the late superintendent. We were neighbours, and were very friendly. —But he had never each inged words with you before, and there could be no ill-feeling? I don't know about that. I have been threatened in this court.—Then you had done something to offend the police before? No, but I have been told in this court, in the hearing of a number of respectable gentlemen, that they would do it.—De you mean to say that constables are in the habit of going about threatening people? They said it in this court, in the hearing of respect- able people.—Did you say anything to him? I told him if he had a charge to make not to insult me, but to go to the police station and lay his charge there—What charge did you think he had? I did not know. I thought he would charge me with being drunk.—Did you tell him when you saw him at Wilson's Hotel that he had no right there, and that he ought to be patrolling I never used such a word. —Did you tell him that he had no right there. I could not swear about it. I may have said such a thing.—Did you uee the words that the buttons on his coat saved his neck? Yes, down at the police station —You are a tradesman? Yes, and a professional man.---And is this a proper mode of supporting the authorities by telling a constable you would knock his neck out if it were not For his buttons? If he threatens what he will do for me I think it is. I will strike him whether he be a policeman or not.—Well, is it a fact— for this is what it CMOs to—that you would condescend to get into A common row with anyone who would make an unpleasant observation to you. Certainly not, but I am ready to get into a row with any man who insults me.— ' Edward Prescott, butcher, Bridge-street, said he was leaving Wilson's Hotel at two or three minutes to eleven on the night of the 3rd June. He had been with Mr. Smith in the private part of the house. He left the house before Mr. Smith, and crossed the street to his own house. As he did se he passed the officer guiding in the highway. He heard Mr. Smith sty to him that he had no right to stand there and he ought to move on. Sullivan cilleTi him a twopence halfpenny doctor. (Laughter.)—Mr. Certwright: The policeman was in the doorway, wasn't he? Witness: He was oaths highway.—Will you swear he was not in the doorway? I will, brit right bang opposite. (Laughter.)— By Mr. Swift: The officer might have stepped into the ves- tibule of the hotel while he was walking to his own house. Mrs. Eleanor Blythe sold she was leaving Wilson's Hotel at three minutes 'to eleven on Tuesday night, the 3tel inst., in company with her husbtnd and Mr. Grice. She and her husband went down Bridge-street, and she saw P.C. Sulli- van follow Mr. Smith into...the office, ant heard him sty to Mr. Smith that he had no Tight there. They then began to ' argue about insults, and Mr. Smith told Sullivan not to point at him, and if he did he woul•i knock him down. She saw thit Sullivan had a stick in his hand, but she did not hear him lies any offensive name exc-pt a twopence half- penny doctor. When at Mr. Smith's shop door the officer called Mr. Smith a swine, and said if he had his plain clothes on he would knock his-- neck out. A person in the crowd shouted" Knock the -- down and we'll jump on him."—Mr. Swift said he had a number of other wit- nesses, but he should spare the Bench the infliction of call- ing them after the evidence he had already procured.—Mr. Cartwright, in aldressing the Bench in defence of Sullivan, pointed out that there was no evidence showing that he had committed an assault except such as the defendant chose to allege. He thought the Bench would say, after the letter the complainant bad written, and the manner in which he had given his evidence, and the strong feeling he had shown in the box that day, that his statements were not to be relied upon. He thought Mr. Smith had showed them what class of a,gentleman he was. It was perfectly clear Mr. Smith was a gentleman who obese to take to himself c wttin ideas and views and carry them out in his own way. He held that there was nothing to show that any action on the ?art of the constable hid been of an ag.greseiva charec- ter ; and assuming that he had used the words complained of, the eonstable was only human, and he said nothing more than any man would under irritating circumstances.—After a short consultation with his brother magistrates, the Chair- man stid they were perfectly satisfied that the assault had been committed by Mr. Smith, and they- should fine him 40s. and costs. Both summonses against the officer were dismissed. The costs amounted to £4 14e. 61.—The great- est interest was taken in the case, owing to the position of the defendant, and the can't was crowded to its utmost capacity.

WIDNES LOCAL BARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board Offices, Alforde Charnhers, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present :—Mr. Gossage, J.P. (chairman). Dr. O'Keeffs ; Messrs. T. Handley, S. Sadler, E. Carey, R. Webster, D. Wright, J. Mid wood, H. Gasket!, jun., J.P., E. Manley, B. Dutton, J. E. Johnson, Allen (clerk), Copland (resident engineer), Higginson (surveyor), Dickson (cemetery in- spector).

r - - WITT-ROAD SEWER kGE.—Mr. Martley, referring to the special meeting of the Board held on the 30th ult., inquired whether the property owners in Witt-road would be charged for the sewerage of the street.—Mr. Handley said they would not.

_ GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE : Gas AND WATER CHARGES —The Gas and Water Committee reported that the rainfall for the month had been :—Gas Yard guage, 1-755 inches; Pex Hill guage, 1 570 inches; mean. 1.6132 inches. The water in stock on May 14th was 4,133,803 gallons. The committee recommended that advertisements be issued for tenders for the supply of oak scrubber boards, estimated to cost £350; that a coke cart be purchased; and also that the salary of Mr. A. Redfern be increased from £3O to £9O. The minutes further stated that with regard to gas and water charges that a letter had been received from the Widnes Alkali Company as to reduction in charge for water. It was recommended that the charge from Ist July for water per meter be OA. per 1,000 gallons, subject to a deduction of Ad. per 1,000 gallons for cash within month following Supply ; recommended that the discount for domestic supply be increased 10 per cent, for cash within first month of each quarter ; recommended, that the price of 'gas be reduced eld. per 1,000 feet from let July, viz, : Consumers below 100,000 cubic feet per annum 3s. 21, between 100,000 and 3.030,000 2s. 110., ab)ve 3000,000 2s. 81., all to be subject to a discount of 3d. ner 1,000 for cash within month following supply; recommended that gas meter rents be discontinued from Ist July —Ur. Wright moved the confirmation of these minutes. subject to the alterations that' the price cf gas be reduced 61 instead of 44, and that two-light meters be charged Is 41 per year, and that three-lighters be charged 2s 44 per year.—Mr. Gaskell seconded the proposal.—Mr. Sadler, referring to the recom- mendation to purchase a coke cart, said he should like to know how many carts the committee thought necessary for one horse, because they were always buying carts. If they would allow him, he would suggest that they buy a four. wheeler to ride about in, for they and the engineer were

constantly running about the township. He also wish( d to know if the proposed advance of salary was for increase of dunes or otherwise ?—iffr. Dutton wanted to know from the chairman of the Gas Committee whether the ratepayers had beeu. charged with any interest of borrowed money in con- nection with the gas and water plant, and if so had they got at back again? If they had not, how was it that cus- tomers had had reductions made to them first ?-41r. Carey thought that as a matter of principle the charges for gas and water should be just sufficient to pay expenses. He did not think that gas and water profits, if there be any, should ba used for the diminution of the district rate. When there was profit the prices ought to be still further reduced.—Mr. Johnson asked if the ratepayers would receive the same 'oenefits from the proposed reductions of prices as the manu- facturers 7—The Chairman could not see how a question could arise between these two people—the manufacturers were ratepayers.—Mr. Johnson said he referred to those who had a .domestic supply, and thought they ought to receive, in proper proportion, the same bene- fits as the minufacturers. Mr. Midwood thought that while they did the best they could to benefit the menu- faqurers by supplying them at as reasonable a cost as they could, the domestic supply ought to be considered in a fair proportion. He did not think that the proposals as they then stood were fair —Mr. Webster thought that each mem- ber of ties Board ought to have a balance sheet supplied to them so that they might have fully considered the matter. The Gas Cominit'ee knew nothing about the financial po- siition of their affairs ; it was all left to the Finance Corn- mittee.—Mr. Wright, in replying to the various questions which had been put to him, said with respect to the recom- mended purchase of a new cart, the GAS Committee had only purchased one cart since he had been a member of it. lie did not think there were many members of that com- mittee who had done much riding about in a four-wheeler. If they had it was done on the Board's business. The cart he mentioned was for carting coke. With respect to the in. crease of Mr. Redfern's salary, it was for increased services. He was a very good man, and it was thought the pay was scarely sufficient. As to the reduction in prices there was a slight difference between the scale for manufacturers and that for private consumers, but the committee had brought them as near to each other as they possibly could. He also mentioned that manufacturers had written to the Board about the prices, and one firm had intimated its intention of inceasing its own gas plant unless the prices were re- duced. There had been a large profit on the gas and water during the year, and the proposed reduction amounted to abmt £1,600. In reply to Mr. Duttou he said he was not aware that the Gas Committee had borrowed any money in the way slated for the carrying on or the extension of the gas works. He also mentioned that as long as the district rate had never contributed to the maintenance of the gas works they had no power to give any of the profits to the district rate. After some discussion as to the manner in which certain recommendations had been put into the committee's minutes, Mr. Webster moved, and Mr. Johnson seconded, that that portion of the minutes referring to the gas and water charges be referred back. This pro- pesal was, however, negatived, and the original proposition of Mr. Wright carried. Tile lira away COSIHITTEE.—The minutes of this com- mittee stated, with regard to Victoria-road, that a letter had been received from W. H. Kershaw and Co., thanking the committee for attention to drainage nuisance, and another asking for the flagging of parapet opposite his property, as per agreement with Legh's Trustees. Consideration of this request was deferred. A letter had also been read from Mr. J. Poole, complaining of flooded cellar, and the surveyor was instructed to attend to the matter. The property owners in private streets, who attended the Highway Com- mittee on the 10:11 January, having failed to repair the , streets as promised within the three mouths agreed upon, instructions were given to serve a further notice that if not satisfactorily repaired before the 25th June the commiteee would at once take into consideration the advisability of having them made under the provisions of the Public Health Act.—Recommended that legal proceedings be taken against Mr. W. Grace for depositing manure, Jec., and against , Mr. Baldwin for depositing timber on the highway, unless ' the obstructions are at oi:ea removed—The building plans submitted were: Plan of a house in Oakland-street for Mr. E. Tickle, approved, subject to an alteration in ashpit and privy to the surveyor's approval ; plan of three houses, flatten View, for Mr. John Rimmer, approved; plan of Ro- man Catholic schools, Appleton, approved, subject to the sanitary arrangements being passed by the Health Com- inittee.—On the motion of Mr. Midwood, seconded by Mr. Sadler, these minutes were confirmed. SEVIER/AGE COMMITTRE.—The Sewerage Committee re- ported as follows :—Recommended that the ventilating lamp at Little Brixton be placed at future level of road: recom- mended that a pipe ventilation be put up in Witt-road, Mr. Midwood as agent having kindly granted permission upon payment of Is per annum. Letter, 24th May, from It. Davies and Co., enclosing receipt for £I,OQO in full settle- ment of all claims and demands. Letter, Bth May, from R. Davies and Co., enclosing copies of letters from T. Kirk, brother, re first contract. Consideration held over. The question of continuing main sewer northward from Simm's Cross, and eastward from Kent's lamp, postponed until 13th inst at 2 p.m.—These minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Dutton. THE LATE Fins.—The Chairman said he was away at the time when the late fire occurred at Messrs. Hutchinson's, but he saw that it was reported in the local press that the floating fire eneine that had been taken by Messrs. Hutchin- son and themselves had proved to be useless. That most seriously affected him, because they were to a very great , extent dependent upon the efficiency of 'that engine as a protection against fire at their soap works. Therefore he got thair people to try the engine when it propelled water in very large quantities through a 3-inch hose over 100 yards, ' and at the end of 100 yards It threw water to the height of nearly 80 feet, not only so that it fell in a solid mass but there Wee plenty of power left to make a spray. He wanted , this to be known, because most of the works in the neigh- bourhood had found out the value of that floating engine.' There were no insurance companies that had not paid the, owners of the engine for duties done at the various fires that had taken place. The engine was as efficient now as it had ever been, or if it was now more efficient than it was when I they first got it.—Mr. Dutton was referring to the question I of the organisation of a fire brigade, when the Chairman pointed out that he had been merely explaining as to the condition of the floating fire engine. He was quite aware that the brigade did not work properly.—The matter then dropped. HEALTH COMMITTEE.—EX&GGIERATED REPORTS. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the following items :—Sankey Canal: Mr. Dixon reported that Alr„ Bal- ton (Widnes Alkali Co.) had complained about bad small from canal. Consideration deferred pending inspection of district.—Fire Engine: The-Gas and Water Cammitte hav- ing requested that this engine might be stored in the market until a suitable building is erected. Recommended that per- mission be given.—lnfectious Diseases Hospital : Letter, 15 May, from Major Cross, stating that the tints may remain until further notice free of charge —Fire at Tents: Recom- mended that a reward of £2O be offered for information which will lead to the conviction of any person not being the actual offender.—Rmornmended that the police be paid for their services 27s 61, viz : the sergeant 7s 6d and the four officers 5s each.—Pernaanent Sites, Offers Opened . Re- commended that the question Se referred to the Board, at- tention being directed to plots in Birchtield-roacl, Beacons- field-road, and two sites at Halton View.—lnstructions given to furnish the members with a list of the offers.— Varket Superintendents Report: Receipts for the month £32 3s 3d, being an increase of £l4 53 sd, as compared with April, 1883. Seven shops let and stalls have done better. The machine has been tested. Food Destroyed—Two pigs, 31b. beef and pork, 331 b. onions, 250 oranges, 18 bunches radishes, and six bunches rhubarb.—ffutehinson Street : The Chairman reported that Messrs. Bolton and Son are interfer- ing with West Bank and Peel-streets and that no plans have been deposited for the erections now being put up. Committee adjoarned to Friday next, the 6th inst., for inspection of ais- trict.—Mr.S-adler. asked how much the infectious hospital cost, and what amount of damage had been done by the late fire?— Dr. O'Keefe said that with regard to the tents and huts erected to stein the invasion of smallpox, they cost the Board —including furnishing and maintenance—something like £630 14s 4d. The loss they had sustained by the burning of the wooden structure, which unfortunately contained the tents and a great number of beds and appliances, would be about £l5O, or from that to £2OO. The value of what re- mained would be about £l5O. All the bedclothing Nv.AS, he understood, saved. He might mention that the Health Committee had thought it advieable ta offer a reward for the discovery of the perpetrators of this outrage. It was unquestionably the act of an incendiary. He didn't think it was the act of a child—except a grown-up one. He hoped they would be successful in discovering who it was in order to prevent the perpetration of such deeds in the future. They also considered that it was onlyglue to the excellent efforts of the police to give them a very little remuneration for the services they rendered. He might refer, as no ques- tion had been asked about it, to the exaggerated statements that had appeared in the Liverpool papers as to another in. vasion of measles, such as was made in the same paper some time ago, or ons of its evening issues. This statement was thoroughly exaggerated. He was going to say there was a particle of truth in it, but that assertion would be an ex- aggerated assertion too. (Laughter.) He thought it was stVed there were 400 or 500 cases of measles in Widnes. Now, as a medical man practising in the town, he had as good an opportunity of knowing of the cases of measles that Occurred in Widnes as any one. tie was in constant inter- course with his medical colleagues, and they were generally talking about what was going on, and he thought if he men- tioned that the number of cases altogether in Widnes was about 100, it would be nearer the mark than 500. He men- tioned 100 as the maximum number. He must protest against these exaggerated and of course false statements being sent to the Liverpool papers. There had been only a few deaths—he could nearly say there was scarcely a single death caused by measles—the deaths having been caused by the carelessness of the parents in letting the children get bronchitis and such like during their convales- cence. He wished that matter to go fourth by means of the gentlemen of the "fourth estate " to the public at large in order that these exaggerated reports—whoever was doing it—might n6t be sent forth in future. Dr. O'Keeffe also mentioned that the committee bad made a sanitary inspection of a great part of the township, and were glad to find it was in an excellent sanitary condition, much superior t) what it was live or six years ago. He was very glad that in every respect the sanitary aspect of Widnes was improving. (Hear, hear.) With regard to Messrs. Bolton and Son building without having deposited plans, the clerk had been instructed to write to that firm, and perhaps he had some information to give them.—The Surveyor said he had written, but Messrs. Bolton and Son had not replied.—Dr. O'Keeffe thought if that was the case they ought to take

some action. They might as well not hove any Local Board in that town if they allowed people to treat them with con- tempt, he didn't care who they were.—Mr. Carey said there was scarcely a copy of the bye-laws existing. People couldn't get a copy even if they applied for them.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved that Messrs. Bolton be requested to suspend their work until they treat the Board with the respect doe to them.—Mr. Midwood seconded. He thought the doard ought to take some action, as he did not think Messrs. Bolton had any right to do what they were doing.—The minutes were then confirmed, and Dr O'Keeffa's motion with regard to Messrs. Boltoa was also carried. FINANCE.—The Finance Committee's minutes contained the following :—Main sewer: Recommended that a fourth advance of £5,000 be obtained from the Public Works Loan Commissioners. Deposits charged to gas consumers Recom- mended that the amount for small cottage consumers be 50,, and to other consumers in proportion. Annual accounts: The following submitted and approved, and ordered to be printed as usual—Gas showing profit of £2,586 1s 11d, water profit £2,313 15s 7d, and general account a deficiency of £271 12s sd. Estimate 183.1-85 The following estimates submitted and approved—Highway, &c, £3,567 ss; hospital £249 101 ; health, £923; Finance, £1,271 85 6d; less market. credit £2B 165 31; or a total estimate of expenditure, £8,982 7s 31. Recommended that a rate at 25 per pound be laid. Property over £l5 rateable value, estimated to produce £5,494 7s; property under £l5 rateable value, owners to be allowed when paying for cottagers, 20 per cent. and empties, estimated to produce £2,513 lOs ; land, canals, dm., at one- fourth of rate, estimated to produce £675 35; private im- provements outstanding, £186; total, £B,B69.—Tbe" minutes, on the motion of Mr. Handley, were confirmed, after which the Board went into committee.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Ditton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. John Ashton presidieg. Present: Messrs. Mclntyre, Warburtoe, E. A. Wallington, Andrews, G. Whit- law Challoner R. Ashton, J. Darla webire, J. Weir, Jackson, J. Whit- law, C. Rigby, Mr. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Adams (medical officer), and Farrington (nuisance inspector). FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL CONMITTEES.—The minutes of 'these committees stated that Mr. Charles Reynolds having resigned the appointment of chairman, it was unanimously resolved that Mr. Alfred Thomas be appointed chairman of the committees for the current year. The Inspector of Nuisances read the report on the subject of the ventilation of main sewers, and recommended that ventilation Shafts snould be provided, fitted with a revolving cowl. Mr. San: croft was present in connection with the water scheme, and advised that the best course would be to ventilate the sewers by means of the gas pillars, as the heat from the lamPS ' when lighted would have the effect of drawing the foul gas from the sewer. It was decided to adopt the system of ven- tilation recommended by Mr. Bancroft, and the Committees directed that application be made to the gas inspectors for their sanction to the work being carried out. —Mr. Bancroft stated that the following arrangements had been made with the riparian owners with reference to the Frodsham Water I Scheme, subject to the approval of the Sanitary Authority, viz :—Mr. Smith Barry: Toe Authority to Pay 10 per armum for 99 years. Lord Cholmondeley : The Authority to guarantee 1,000 gallons of water per day to the Bradley Orchard Farm. River Weaver Trustees: Consent granted I on an understanding being given not to take any water other ' than from springs in Mr. Wright's field. Mr. Wilkinson: the Authority to provide a gratuitous supply of water to the farmhouse, and make a cash payment of £lOO. Knowles Trustees ::The Authority to pay MO per annum, for 99 years. The Committees discussed the scheme at considerable length and it was seriously considered whether the present water ' schema should not be at once abandoned in consequence of the demands made by the riparian owners. The Committees afterwards considered the question generally, and several alternative schemes were suggested. It was, however, thane' resolved that Mr. Bancroft again inspect the district and pre- pare a general report, for the consideration of the Commit- tees on the 20th June.—The minutes were adopted. 1 THE FEVER OUTBREAK AT SUTTON SANITARY CONDI" TION OF THE VILLAGE.—Dr. Adams, the medical officer, submitted a report on the extensive and serious outbreak of typhoid fever in the township of Sutton. Up to Friday' last ten persons were suffering froth typhoid fever. After particularising the cases, the doctor went on to say that accompanied by the inspector of nuisances, he had made two complete house to house visitations, and had issued in all cases most stringent orders and instructions with a view to preventing any extension of the disease by infection from ' those at present affected by it. These measures consisted in (1) as complete isolation of each patient as the circum- stances of each case afforded; (2) the disinfection. prompt I removal, and burial of all excreta and washings from the ; patient; (3) the disinfection of all the premises, with their , grids, cesspools, and privies whereon the disease existed ; and (4) a liberal supply of disinfectants to all infected houses. In searching for a perfect explanation of the causes of this outbreak, two classes of facts soon presented themselves to his consideration, viz.: firstly, the defective drainage and sewerage arrangements in the entiretowhship of Sutton, an examination of which disclosed the startling fact that practically speaking all the cesspools and other sewage receptacles in the village were untrapped, and thus communicate directly with the main drain of the Highway I Board, which drain is of somewhat loose construction, also discharges the functions of a main sewer for those parts of the township which are situated in immediate relation to it. Secondly, in consequence of a temporary and now remedied defect in the public village pump belonging to the I Authority, a majority of the inhabitants of Sutton had resorted for water for drinking and cooking purposes to ft pump sitnited on the premisea occupied by George Taylor, on which premises the first case of the disease occurred seven week's ago. Taylor's pump was closed, and the water had been analysed by the county analyst. As Taylor's pump was for a deep well, the analysis pointed conclusively' to recent sewage contamination, and an examination of the pump and its surroundings showed him that the possibility of surface leakage and overflow of cesspool sewage into the well was only too well established. In addition the pump is situated only a few feet from an untrapped cesspool, which was in direct communication with the main drain belonging to the Highway Board, and moreover this cess- pool was liable to occasional overflaw and consequent leak- age into the adjacent pump. An analysis of the 10 cases of fever, cons:dered in connection with a close perusal of the inspector's able and exhaustive sanitary report, drove him irresistibly to the conclusion that to the contaminated and deleterious water from Taylor's well must be attributed the serious outbreak of typhoid fever, for while that drainage and sewerage system, or lack of system, was sufficient is itself perhaps to account for the disease in those houses which were placed, with scarcely an attempt at efficient trapping, in direct communication with what was practically a main sewer, yet this theory failed to give any account of the fever arising in those houses which had no connection with or propinquity to the highway main and provisional sewer, whereas on the other hand the theory of a contami- nated water supply fully accounted for every case, for he had ascertained with certainty that every person whe had been atta'Cked by this disease in the present outbreak bad prior to their being stricken down drunk freely and continuously of the deleterious fluid from Taylor's pump. Such an epitome of grossly insanitary defections as was embodied in the inspector's able report of his survey called for prompt and efficient action, and the Authority would, he was sure, assist Mr. Farrington and himself with their utmost powers in their desire to place the township of Sutton within that Pale of security from disease, which was only afforded by effec- tive sanitation. The report concluded with pointing out the advantages of a system of compulsory notification of infec- tieus diseases. Such a general system of compulsory notifi- cation must be in store for them in a not very remote future, and he was able meanwhile merely to express his great regret that he only received his first notification of the existence of the disease in Sutton at a time when so excep- tionally large a proportion of its inhabitants were already lying under its sewerage.—Mr. Farrington reported that in compliance with the instructions of the Authority he bad submitted two samples of water from pumps at Sutton vil- lage for analysis, one being from the public pump and the other from a private one, the former was returned as being of a fair degree of purity—a water of the second class— the latter as not being a good water, the free ammonia being very high pointing to sewage contamina- i tion. ' The latter water had of late been largely used by the inhabitants owing to the public pump having been out of order; and it was highly probable that the well had be- come impregnated and polluted by typhoid germs in the I same shape or form, as up to the present no one had taken the disease but those who had used the water; and since the authority insisted upon its discontinuance no fresh cases had occurred, and he had now to ask their directions for the further dealing with the well. He had taken a sanitary survey of the whole village, and with respect to the maits drainage he could only maintain what he stated at the last meeting that it was not bad (but as to the legality of such drainage and the outfall thereto was another question). It carried off the greater portion of the sewage in a direct or indirect manner, although it was intended for the removal of the storm or surface water. There were ten untrapped in- , lets in the road, all of which were liable to become nuis- ances. The existing nuisances upon private premises in the village conid be abated at no great cost, and he had no I doubt they would be attended to when attention by notice 'or otherwise had been drawn to them. He intended to pre- sent a detailed report upon the whole of the township when he had completed the survey, and in the meantime he would endeavour to get the nuisances abated.—Mr. Wallington inquired if the water had been analysed before.—me. Far- rington replied only by Mr. Jackson'a son.—Mr. Walliug- ton observed that it was strange a public pump should be put into use without the water being analysed—Mr. Far- rington said there was no arrangement with the public ana- lyst, and he did not think the At in reference to the matter was in force at; the time.—The inspector was instructed te communicate with the Aston Estate Authorities and sag. gest the cleaning out and thorough repairing of the num!), and that the water must not be used in its present state. On the motion of Mr. Challoner, seconded by Mr. Wallingten• a committee consisting of Messrs. Lowe, .Acton, Jackson. John Bate, and Wallington was appointed to deal with the. oudareak in Sutton.—Mr. Farrington stated that a case_er. scarlet fever had occurred at Acton Grange, and Mr. Li Whitlow said the some disease had also broken out at Fres:. ton Brook.—The Chiirman read a letter front Mr. J. Jackson, of the Cedars, denying that he had informed Irlr_ Farrington that Dr. Robinson had said that Sutton was. worst drained village in Cheshire—Mr. Farrington swa!: he had mistaken what Mr. Jackson had told him he shenill;. be glad to retract the statement he made at the last meeti He had had an interview with Mr. Jack.on, and that gentl man staled that it was a lady who told him of the sanitarY condition. i The remainder of the business was not of public in- • •tereg.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE BY A RUNCORN CHEMIST. EXTRAORDINARY SCENES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE BY A RUNCORN CHEMIST. EXTRAORDINARY SCENES.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes, Mr. Charles Reynolds, and Captain C. W. Hallehurst, Mr. Peter Smith, chemist and druggist, High-st., was summoned to answer a charge of having on the 3rd June unlawfully assaulted P.C. Sullivan while in the execu- tion of his duty. Mr. Swift, barrister-at, law, appeared for the defendant and pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Cartwright, solicitor, Chester, appeared for the police.—Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk), pointed out that there had been a cross summons issued, and suggested that they should be heard together.—Mr. Swift was willing to adopt this course, but Mr. Cartwright objected, and it was decided to hear the case of the police first. All witnesses were ordered out of court.—Mr. Cartwright in opening the case, observed that there were two charges preferred against Sullivan, one of using abusive language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and one for assaulting Mr. Smith. He pointed out that these summonses against the constable were taken out after the summons against Mr. Smith had been served, and it was al ways important to notice when a counter albs- Ration was made, especially ageinet a public officer. After detailing the facts of the case, Mr. Cartwright said a letter which the defendant bad written would to some extent re- lieve them of a conflict of testimony. When their worships beard that letter read he thought they would say that Mr. Smith must be an extraordinary person. Mr. Smith Was as- sumed to be a respectable and well-conducted man, and he thought they would say after the letter that Mr. Smith was not, he was going to say a respectable man, bet at any rate not a well-conducted men, because he actually admitted that he accepted an offer to fight with a policeman on duty. A man who would do that, he thought their worships would say, must indeed be in a very remarkable state of excite- ment, and most have as a citizen a very extraordinary notion of what his duties were in supporting the police. Here was a well-known chemist and druggist, who was sup- posed to be a respectable men, who so far forgot his position as actually to accept 3 challenge to fight wita a constable on duty. He thought their worships would say that Mr. Smith had committed a gross act of interference with the duties of a police officer. It was not the police constable who was the person to have a quarrel put upon him, but tne duty which Mr. Smith should have respected which the police owed to society in general, and which he as a good citizen should have respected and supported. Whatever complaint's Smith had to make, the proper course for him to adopt was to make them to the Chief Constable, and the least he could say was that the Bench would be sur- prised at the course he actually followed. The following was the letter which Mr. Smith had written : "To the Superintendent of Police of Runcorn.—Sir, I beg respectfully to draw your attention to the misconduct of one of your constables, No. 321, I believe. As I (in company with several other gentlemen) was leaving Wilson's Hotel at one minute or so to eleven o'clock last night, the officer met me face to face on the footpath, and grossly imsulted me. After remonstrating with him for his impertinence, and demanding either an apology or his number, he savagely informed me (in the hearing of a crowd) that I was only a half-crown doctor, and that my tower as far as the pelice was concerned was dead. Astounded at such a reply, I called on my way home at the police station to inquire who the man was, and whether he was sane or not, when to my great surprise I was informed that they could not answer my question. In a moment I found the same man (No. 321) hold of my arm, informing me (in the presence of the constable in charge of the office) that I had no right in the police office (7), and requesting me to leave, which of course I I did at once. Not content with expelling me from the office, partly by force, bat chiefly by wearing Her Majesty's uniform, he defiantly held up his staff before me (a crowd of at least 50 having assembled around us), and asserted that I should feel that before long. Being as I imagined the best man of the two, I accepted his offer, and struck him lightly with my fist, whereupon he turned coward and said I was drunk. Was he? Had I not been so well known in the town I should not have thought this worth while troubling you with, but as it is I trust you well look into the matter.—Yours truly, P. An old bachelor wants to know if you ever sat down to tea, when skimmed milk was on the table, without being asked" Do you take cream " Grim Tins, THEREFORE TEAT.—" Pa, is it right to call a man born in Poland a Pole ? " "Of course, my child." "Well, then, if a man is born in Holland, is he a Hole." " What made,the mule kick you ? " they asked of a gentleman who had been sent through the roof of a barn. And he answered: "Do you think I was fool enough to go back and ask him." "Who is that man applauding so vociferously near the front ? " asked a friend of a theatrical manager on the first Production of a play in a provincial theatre. "That long- haired man with a light-coloured coat?" "Yes." "He —he's the author of the play." A HORRIBLE SUSPENSE.—" Oh! but will Heaven never relieve me from this horrible suspense? Am I to be thus tortured into my grave?" "Tortured, my dear, and how?" "My husband—my poor, dear husband! He disappeared from me two years ago, two long and weary years and I know not whether he be dead or alive." "It is indeed ter- rible." "Terrible! It is maddening.. And me with three offers of marriage on hand!" STUDYING ASTRO c(O3lY.—" There, Frances, you've caught another cold, and Pit warrant you caught it when you were out walking with Joe last night." "Oh, no, mother! I couldn't have caught it then, 'cause we didn't' go far enough to catch anything M fact; we just sat down on the stile and studied astronomy." "And did you have anythirg around You my dear ? " " Oh, yes, indeed I did ! Joe's always par- ticular about that; he won't allow me to sit down anywhere in the evening air without putting something around me." A POLICE-REGULATION —ln Germany the police-regula- Bone are very strict, and any violation of them is promptly Punished. The people have a great dread of the law. Two gentlemen happened to meet in Berlin, and the following conversation took place. "Rave you heard the dreadful neWs about Miller ? " "No; what is it ?" "He was in a boat on the river. He fell overboard and was drowned. The Water was too deep." "Didn't he know how to swim ?" "Swim! Don't you know that all persons are forbidden by the police to swim in the river?" How TO GET A START IN LAW PRACTICE.—" Well, son did you get any cases to-day ?" asked a father of a son, who had been admittea to the bar about six months ago. "No, father, none yet. lam very much discouraged." "Perhaps You don't use the proper method to get cases. You should never appear upon the streets withoat carrying in your hand a sheet of cap paper folded up so as to look like a legal document; rash about as if you were loaded down with business. When in your office and anyone comes in, be busy Writing out a deed or something, and when in court never fail to cock your feet upon the table, reach up your hair and look wiser than the judge, if you can. That's the way these fellows who succeed in law so well all do."

A good story is told of Anthony Trollope, Norman Mac- leod, and Mr. John Burns of the Canard Company, who were intimate friends, whilst making a tour in the Highlands. They arrived at an inn late at night and had supper, and, after their repast, told stories and laughed, regardless of other] visitors, half the night through. In the morning an old gentleman who occupied a bedroom just above them complained to the landlord that he had been so disturbed by the noise from the party below that he had been unaule to sleep, and he greatly regretted that such men should "take more than was good for them." "Well," re. plied the landlord, "I am bound to say there was a good deal of loud laughing and talking; but they had nothing stronger than tea and herrings." "Bless me !" rejoined the old gentleman. "If that is so, what would Dr. Macleod and Mr. Burns be after dinner ?" SOMETHING IN IT.—" What another cup of tea, Mr. Darnley ?" exclabved the landlady as he passed his cup for the third time. "I am delighted to see that you are enjoy- log your sapper." "Yes," responded Dumley, "I was quite hungry to-night, and the tea tastes unusually good." 'Not very complimentary to me," went on the landlady, with a sort of second-class genteel little laugh. "I generally make the tea myself, but to-night I was busy about some- thing else, and the cook made it. I wonder what she could have put in it." "Well," responded Darnley, as he stirred it gently with his spoon, "I should judge from the taste that She must have put some tea in it." Thus does a Western critic in the United States give vent to his views on Hamlet—a There is too much chinning in the piece. The author is behind the times, and seems to forget that what we want nowadays is hair-raising situations and detectives. In the hands of a skilful playwright a de- tective would have been put. upon the track of Hamlet's uncle, and the old man would have been hunted down in a manner that would have excited the audience out of their number elevens. The moral of the piece is not good. The acene where Hamlet sasses his mother is a very bad example to the rising generation, ma it is not improved when the dreary old ghost comes in and blows him up. Our advice to the author is a little more action, a little more gurgling taffy, and a fair share of variety business in his next piece. In the speciality arts of the play-scenes he has entirely missed his opportunities." "I'm in luck!" exclaimed a rather " loud " young man, as he stepped up to an old farmer on London Bridge recently. " I just picked it up," he said. "Why, it isn't a pocket- book! I thought it was, though." The farmer's attention had been attracted. "It's a—a--a pair o, kids!" said the lucky man, as he unrolled two gloves. "And Pll be hanged If there isn't a ring in this finger !"—and he held up the left-hand glove to remove it. "By Jingo, it is a ring!" ejaculated the old man, as the glove was being turned Wrong side out. "Certain. And you're in luck too, my friend," said the young chap, as he pulled out en exceedingly heavy plain gold ring. "You were along with me when I found em, and I'll do the c'rect thing. We'll go halves." "I'll take it," said the old farmer; and he placed the ring and the gloves in his breeches pocket. "I'm short of money lust at the present time; but come down here, and I'll bor- row it from my son-in-law." "But how much have you got With you now ? " asked the sharper uneasily. "On, never mind that! My son-in-law is a sergeant of police, and he'll lend me the full amount," replied the farmer. The lucky Man disappeared. Little Willie Cook, of Fayette Co, 0., is nearly three years old. One day last week his papa was teasing him. He stood it as long as he could, and, turning to his mother, said: " Mamma, I all the time tell papa to cern, and he doesn't don't." A tired, precious three-year old cherub of Fair Haven, 0., kneeling in evening prayer said, after having tepeated a part of the Lord's prayer: Mamma, does God know ever thing?" "Yes, daughter, " erYthing.." "Well, mamma, lam so sleepy I won't pray it all, for Crod knows she rest." ASHTON.

, This SCARLATINA EPIDEMIC.—On Wednesday afternoon. a conference of school managers and the Highway and Sani- tary Committee of the Local Board was iheld at the board- room, to consider whether further measures were necessary in order to grapple with the present epidemic of scarlatina in the township. There were present Messrs. Monbert: Grimke, Stone, C. Latham, W. Latham, Knowles, Leith- waite, and Fairhurst (members of the committee), and the following school managers: Rev. H. Siddall, Rev. Father O'Reilly, Rev. G. Fox, and Rev. El. Wilson. Dr. Hannah, medical officer of health, reported that the disease had in no way abated. The committee did not think the epidemic sufficiently serious to justify them in closing the schools, it being pointed out that the present time was inop- portune for so doing, as the annual examinations were taking place. THE ASHTON LOCAL BOARD AND THEIR OFFicitits.—A. special meeting of the Ashton Local Board was held at the office, Bryn-street, Ashton, on Wednesday a ternoon, to take into consideration the remuneration of the officers of the Board. Mr A. B. Moubert presided, and there was a good attendance of metnbers.—Mr. Galdsworth, clerk pro tem.,. at the request of the Board reported that the salaries at I present paid were—Clerk and surveyor £125, assistant sur- veyor and inspector of nuisances £BO, clerk and collector £lOO. and assistant clerk and collector £39, making a total of £344; the inspector of nuisances was appointed Junder the Public Health Act, and the Local Government Board have contributed £l5 towards his salary, which had to be deducted from the total mentioned.—After some discussion as to how the salaries should be best arranged, it was de- cided on the motion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Stone, that Mr. Goldsworth be appointed as surveyor and engi- neer at'a salary of £5O per annum.—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Knowles. that Mr. Hill be appointed clerk at a salary of £lOO a year.—lt was also resolved that the salary of Mr. Adamson be advanced 4s. a week.—This was all the public basiness before the Board.
PRESCOT.
BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians • was held at the Union Worebouse, Whistoo, on Thursday forenoon, when there were paesent Mr J T Hall (in the chab), the Revs T Chambers, J Barnacle. and T Finegan: Messrs fisher, J Lowe, W Swift, J Buckley, J Jackson. E Syder, W Birchen, J Learberbtrrow, .1 ?idler, 8 Manslo Kenwright, J Agnew, If Hnlme, R Tuson, J F Hill, W A Meadows, P LonSton, W Tvrea, T Eetock. arid S a Hartley (clerk).—The minutes of the last meeting were confirmed. WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 393 inmates in the house. against 405 in the preceding week, and 413 in the corresponding week last year. The present number was the smallest num- ber they had ever had in the house. (Eleor, hear.) There were 49 vagrants ielieved during the week, and 67 in .the correspornling week of last year. THE EMIGRATION OF PAUPER CHILDREN' TO CANADA.— The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated the 2nd inst., asking to he furnished with particulars indicated in a form enclosed in a previous letter with respect to each of the 49 orphan children the. Board proposed to send out to Canada, and also asking to be informed of the spelial circumstances which had induced the Guardians to, recommend the emigration of the girls of 12 years of age.' Mr. Hartley added that he replied to the communication. MISCELLANEOUS CORRESPONDENCE —Mr. Hartley reported the receipt of a circular letter from the Local Government Board asking for a return of the costs of indoor and outdoor relief in that Union up to Lady Day last, to which he had replied. He had also been asked to forward a return in . compliance with a resolution of the House of Commons with respect to the adoption or otherwise of the Public Libraries Act in the different parishes of the Union. He would make the necessary inquiries, and send the informa- to the Home Secretary. THE SUPPLY OF WATER TO THE WouturousE.—The Clerk read the following letter from the Local Govecument Board, dated sth June:—" I am directed by the Local Go- vernment poard to, acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th instant, enchning copies of reports which the Guardians of the Prescot Union have received from Mr. Roberts and Mr. Hanson remprcing the desirability of sink- ing a well at the Workhouse premises, and to inform you that the Board have referred these reports to their.chief en- gineering inspector, Sir Robert Rawlinson. The Board are informed by Sir Hebert that he coneurs in the opinion ex- pressed by Mr. Hanson that the supply of water should be obtained from the mains of the Corppratioa of Liverpool, or from the Corporation of St. Helens, rather than from anew well and bore-hole to be sunk on the Workhouse premises ; and Sir Robsrt Rawlinsen recommends that preference should be given to the water of the Corporation of Liver- pool as being softer, and therefore more economical for washing purposes. Moreover Sir Robret RAwlinson points Out that as the Corporation Moreover, Liverpool are constructing vast works to obtain a new supply of water from the source of the river Severn it is probable that they would be pre- pared to supply the Guardians with water at a very moderate rate, say of about 4d. per thousand gallons. A supply at this rate would be, cheaper than the cost of pro- viding the necessary well, machinery, cite., and its quality would be superior to that of well water. The Board, there- fore, request that the Guardians communicate with the Cor- poration of Liverpool with a view to arrange- ments being made for a supply of water to the Workhouse direct from the Corporation mains."— Mr. Fidler moved that Messrs. Hall, Meadows, Tyrer Leatherbarrow, and Fldler, be a committee to consult with the corporations of St. Helens and Liverpool, and Mr. Long- ton, as to their charges for supplying water to the Work- house.—Mr. Hill Seconded the moticin.—Mr. Lowe asked if there would be any expense in connection with the coin- mittee. He theught it was time that they were cutting down the expenses.—The motion was carried. PETITION FROM THE flosata—The Clerk stated that he had received a letter from the secretary to the Earl of Derby stating that he would present the petition forwarded by the Guardians of the Prescot Union against the Poor Law Re- moval and Settlement Bill.

THE SUGGESTED TELEPHONE BETWEEN THE WORKHOUSE AND ST. HELENS.—The Clerk read a communication from the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchange Company (Limited), acknowledging the receipt of the agreement I.p.tween the Guardians and the Company for telephonic communication between the Workhouse and the relieving office in St. Helens. The letter added that the rental would commence on the let of the month after the date on which the telephonic communication was op-ned.

THE REMOVAL OF CHILDREN FROM PANTASAPH In accordance with notice given at the last meeting the Rev. Father Finegan moved that the resolution passed on the 23rd august last that no children be sent to the Pantasaph be rescinded; and that the children removed therefrom be returned thereto, subject to the approval of a committee.-- The motion was seconded by Mr. Swift, and after some little discussion was passea. This was the only business of interest.

Mr. Gladstone returned to London from Hawarden on Monday, and attended a Cabinet Council. The next dinner of the National Liberal Club will be held on Wednesday, June 18th. Mr. John Morley, M.P., will preside. At Leicester, a woman and two men matched in procession to surrender to imprisonment for a week under the 'Vaccina- tion Act on Monday. SALE OF hOOTCII ESTATES.—A Lockerbie correspondent states that the extensive estates of Tinwakl and Torthor- weld, Dumfries, belonging to the Marquis of Queensberry, , and comprising 7.000 acres, with a rental of £B,OOO, have • been sold to Mr. Jas. Jardine, of Dryfolholnt, Dumfriesshirt, for £220,000. - FALL OF AN HISTORICAL COMMIT.—On Monday even- ing about half-past five o'clock, three quarters of the roof and a large portion of the Eouth gable of the Old Cockpit, situate in St. John's-place, Stoneygate, Preston, fell in with a tremendous craeh. The building had latterly been tenan- ted by Mr. Jackson, a dancing master, and his band and pu- pils were to begin to assemble at six o'clock. It is most fortunate that the accident happened at the time mentioned, as in an hour later there would have been from.loo to 120 persons in the place, and the loss of life would no doubt have been very large. It is said that this old building was erected at the end of the last or beginning of the present century, at the expense of the great-grandfather of the present Earl of Derby, who was passionately fond of cockfighting, and I fought many a main therein. On Sundays it was used as a school in connection with the parish church, And it was the duty of the apparitor to clear away the blood and feathers left from the week's combats betore the opening of the school on Sunday morning. In 1830 the place was closed as a cockpit, and the burgesses of Preston were deprived of the great diversion, the Derby family, its patrons, being then alienated by the defeat of the Hon. E. G. Stanley (the late earl) by Mr. Henry Hunt in the election of that year. Then the cockpit was utilised as a sort of mechanic's insti- tution, which took the 'fine name of "Lyceum," and after that it was the great meeting place of the temperance advo- cites; and it waa here that Dicky Turner invented the word teetotal." Speaking of drink, he remarked, in his stuttering way, that he could do "tee-tee-totally without it; aid the word became at once the shibboleth of the total abstainers. The cockpit was also the Sunday meeting place of the weavers' delegates during the great Preston strike of 1853-4, which lasted nine months; and, after the subscrip- • tions they brought from all parts of the country to support the turnouts had been counted, it was here they addressed crowded and excited meetings of the operatives. Some time ago the building was leased to a company of mineral water and lemonade manufacturers, and latterly has been used as a dauciog academy.
