div.head: ST. HELENS. ALLEGED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH: THE MOTHER CENSURED.
div.p: ST. HELENS. ALLEGED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH: THE MOTHER CENSURED.

On Tuesday afternoon, an inquest was held at the Navi- gation Hotel, Grove-etreet, off Liverpool-road, St. Helens, before the Coroner (Mr. Samuel Brighouse), touching the death of a female child, daughter of a single woman named Mary Jackson, who for a considerable time past has lodged with a Mrs. Barker, at Ravenbead, and who gave birth to the child early on the previous Saturday. In addition to the CoronerAhere were also present Superintendent John- ston, Inspector J. Whittaker, and Dr. Jardine. After the jury bad been sworn, The Coroner said: You are here to inquire into the cir- cumstances attending the finding of a female child at half- past seven on Saturday, at the house of Mary Jackson in this borough. It seems that on Saturday morning, at half.. past seven, a child was found on the bedroom floor; the I mother making a statement with respect to this child. Your first duty will be, after hearing the medical evidence and other evidence to be put before you, to say whether you think that this child was born alive; because, as some of you no doubt know, the law presumes every child is born dead until the contrary is proved. After hearing the evidence, the first question will be was this child born alive. If you are not satisfied that it had a separate existence from the mother, it will be your duty to say that the child was still-born, but if you are satisfied that it was born alive, and had a separate existence apart from the mother after being born, it will be for you to inquire as to its death, and hove it came by its death. If you can satisfy yourselves upon that point you will say how it came by its death, and if you are unable to say that you will have to return an open verdict. The following witnesses were then called:— Mary Barker, wife of John Barker, Blake's Pottery, Ravenhead, said: Mary Jackson lodged with me. She is a single woman, and has worked at the brick works. On Friday moraing, at breakfast time, she complained to me and said she was not so well. I knew she was pregnant. I had known that since three I weeks after she came to live with me in January last. She went to bed on the Friday night a little before ten o'clock. I did not, from my own observa- tions, think she was so near the time of her confinement. I next saw her between seven and eight o'clock on the next morning, when she called me. She was on the land- ing, and she said, "Have you heard me during the night?" and I replied "I have heard you, but I thought it was the castor oil makieg you sick." She thereupon said "See, it's I there," and pointed to the child which was lying covered with a petticoat. I asked her if it was dead and she said "yes." I asked her why she did not call me, and she said "I did not like as I knew you were not well." I asked her at what time she was confined, and she replied "one o'clock." I had some conversation with her, and I afterwards celled in Mrs. Glover. I asked Mary Jackson why she had not wakened me and she replied that she did not like as she was afraid of awakening the whole house. I said there was no need for awakening the whole house. I said to her that there would be a bother about it as they could not bury it because they could not say whether it was born dead or alive. She seemed to be put out about the matter and said "I am sorry I did not waken you." She said she was doing it for the beat. She is a single woman, and has no means to support herself. As far as I know, it is the first child she has had. Alice Glover, widow, residing in Old Factory-road, Ravenhead, deposed: On the morning in question I was called to see Mary Jackson, in bed about half-past ten. I delivered her of the after-birth. I saw the child, which was wrapped up in a petticoat in the bedroom. I could not see the child at all; and no one could have seen it without unwrapping the petticoat. I said: "Now. my dear child, what have you done such a thing as this for ?" She re- plied: "I was afraid to disturb Mrs. Barker, she was no., very well." "Well," I said, "you ought to have awakened the girl sleeping with you and told her to fetch her mother," but she said "I did not think I was doing wrong." I said "You ought not to have thought such a thing as that—you have done wrong," After some further conversation I told her that I would not be responsible for anything further.— The Foreman: Did she ask you to go and bury the child? —Witness: Yes, bat I said I would not. Hannah Barker, ten years of age, daughter of Mary lair- km (first witness), said: I slept ,wiCa Mary Jackscn on Fri- day night. I went first, and was awake when she came to bed. I heard Mary Jackson get up during the night, but I fell asleep, and I did not know when she came back. It was dark, and I did not know what time it was. I asked her what was the matter, and she said she did not know. Dr. James Jardine deposed as follows : Yesterday after- noon I made a post-mortem examination of the body. Be- fore dissection I examined the body and found it to be that of a full-grown, well-developed and stout child. On placiag the lungs in water I found that they readily floated.—The Coroner : Do you think this child had a separate exist- ence apart from its mother? Witness : From what I found I cannot say whether or not the child bad a separate exist- ence, but it certainly breathed, and breathed well. In summing up, the Coroner pointed out that the jury had to find whether the child was born alive, whether it had a separate existence or not, and whether or not there was any direct negligence on the part of the mother. The law imposed on the mother of the child the obligation of seeing that it had the necessaries of life and being properly at- tended to ; and if they thought there was direct negligence it was manslaughter or murder. Before they could return a verdict to that effect, however, they must be satisfied that , the mother had omitted to do something, or did something which hastened its death. If they thought there bad been negligence on the part of the mother they would have to say whether it had been wilfully and knowingly done. The jury afterwards considered their decision in private On the coroner, police' dm., being called into the room, the foreman stated that the jury had decided upon a verdict They were unable to say whether or not the child had a separate existence, but they were strongly of opinion that the mother had been negligent. They wished to bring in an open verdict and censure the mother for the negligence. —The Coroner: It leaves it to the police to do anything further they like in the future.

In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Wednesday, the Lord Chief Justice lined two jurymen £5 each for being late in returning after luncheon. On Wcdn.sday night at Ballinalty, county Tipperary, nine cows were stabbed near the udders. They belonged to a farmer who occupied an evicted farm. The election for the city of Lincoln is exciting general interest. On Wednesday evening, at the meeting in support of the Conservative candidate, Mr. Marriot, M.P., was hooted down.

_ Responding to resolutions passed at various polling dis- tricts in East Cornwall, congratulating him on his measure for the protection of seamen, Mr. Chamberlain has writteri to say he has received the resolutions with great satisfac- tion.

MARRIAGE OF A Brsuor —The marriage of the Bishop of Sodor and Man, with Miss Prodyn, daughter of Eir Dighton Probyn, took place at Marylebone Church on Wed- nesday afternoon. The ArchbiAmp of York conducted the ceremony. and there was a fashionable attendance. The trial in Dublin of the second batch of six men, accused of being privy to the conspiracy to murdec Mr. Smythe, of Barbavilla, ended on Wednesday evening in the disagreement of the jury. The prisoners are to be placed on trial again next Wednesday. &mimic LlGHT.—Colcimster is the first town in the United Kingdom which has determined on attetnpting the general use of the electric light. The arrangements have been completed, already many of the houses are illu- minated in that way, and the number is likely greatly to increase.

On Monday night the mail train from London to Brighton ran over, at Redhill, a large piece-of wood which, according to one statement, was fastened to the rail with the object of j wrecking the train. The " outrage " is variously explained; but there is strong probability that the timber fell from a goods train. THE PREMIER AND THE IRISH CHURCH.—The Premier's attention having been called by a Cornish correspondent to Lord Salisbury's assertion at Plymouth, that Mr. Gladstone ' had stated it was consequent on the Clerkenwell explosion he disestablished the Irish Church, a reply has been received ,1 that Mr. Gladstone's reference to the Clerkenwell explosion I had been repeatedly explained, and that Lord Salisbury's statement was altogether incorrect. REFORM DEMONSTRATION.—The proposed popular demon- strations in London in support of the Franchise Bill promises to assume great dimensions. Not only will the several political associations of the metropolis assist at it, but the Trades Union Council on Wednesday decided to take part in it, and to give a contribution towards its expenses. Several of the Agricultural Labourers' Unions also intend to join in the demonstration, and it promises therefore to be of a very imposing character. A London correspondent states that prominent polictical leaders will be asked to preside at the different platforms, but that the speaking will be mainly confined to representatives of the working classes. THE CHARGE AGAINST A MINISTER AND A SURGEON.— The Rev. E. J. Siverton formerly Baptist Minister at Not- tingham, and Mr. Charles Calthorp Mitchinson, described as Mr. Silverton,s physician, appeared before the Manchester I City Stipendiary (Mr. Ileadlam), on Wednesday, on an ad- journed charge of conspiracy to defraud. Mr. Silverton and the other defendant h=id been staying for some time at the Manchester Free Trade Hall, where the formet had been giving health lectures, and had advertised that, with the physician, he was ready to treat persons for a number of diseases which were specified. A number of people were in- duced to visit the Free Trade Hall, and receive certain medicine, the usual charge for which is 35s.—Mr. Taylor, who represented the defendants, argued that there was no conwiracy to defraud, and that the puffing of the medicine sold was no offence.—Mr. Headlam decided that there w. 19 no case against the defendants, and the charge was dis- missed. is LIVERPOOL OPTICIAN ACCUSED OF POISONING HIS WIFE.—At the Wallasey (Cheshire) Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, before Mr. W. Chambres and Mr. R. A. Eskrigge, Mrs. M. F. A. Craven, residing in Manchester, appeared in answ,ir to a summons charging her with libelling Mr. Ed- I ward Morris, optician, Itensbaw-s,reet, Liverpool, by accus- ing him of poisoning his wife, Rose Ellen, in letters ad- dressed to Dr. Byerly, of Seacombe. Mr. Thcimpson, solicitor, I appeared to prosecute; and Mr. Wharton, barrister, of Man- cnester, appeared for the defence. He admitted the libel, and aEreed that Mrs. Craven should be committed for trial for it, tb tt she may be able to justify her statement. Mrs. Craven was accordingly committed for trial to the assizes for the offence, whereupon Mr. Wharton ap- applied for a warrant to arrest Mr. Morris on a a charge of causing the death of his wife by poisoning her. Evidence was heard in private as to whether there were grounds to justify the issuing a warrant, and it was granted. Insp-ctor Dutton then arrested Mr. Morris on a charge of murder, and a remand was granted for seven lays, bail being accepted for him in the sum of 161,000, and two sureties et £5OO each. An application is to be mWe to she Home Office for leave to exhume the body of Mrs. Morris, with a view to a post-mortem examination.

div.p: WAR rZT SGTON. LIEZ:IAL MEETINGS —We have pleasure in announcing that arrangements are almost completed for holding a mass •Ineseting of the Liberal party of the borough in the Public on Wednesday evening, July 13th. Our readers will ohara the satisfaction we feel in stating that the Right Hon.. the Earl of Dalhousie, who, as Lord Ramsay, made such a

, gallant fight in Liverpool i few years ago, has promised te I ; attend and deliver an address. Speeches will also be made • by cur present esteemed member. Mr. J. G. MeMinnies, and also by, let us say, "the future member" for Warrington, Mr. William Crosfield, J.P. It is hoped that the President of the Liberal Association, Mr. Samuel Rigby, J.P., who has rendered signal service to the party for so many years past, will take the chair. Admission will be by ticket, and full particulars will be shortly announcad.—Turn- ir.; to the counts', we would remind our readers that there will be a public meeting at Altrincham this evening when Mr. J. S. Leadam, one of the Liberal -candidates for Mid-Cheshire, will address the electors of that portion of the constituency. Mr. G. W. Latham will Cccupy the chair. On Monday evening Mr. Leadam will address a :neeting at the Mission Hall, Lymtn ; Mr. W. Long will preside, and the proceedings will commence at eight o'clock. Mr. Leadam has a good reputation as a speaker, and we do not doubt that he will meet with a hearty reception as candidate for Mid-Cheshire. Or rnasaK or MEASLES.—During the past week an out- break of measles has been reported in Warrington. A con- siderahb number of children have been aff.cted, but it is satisfactory to know that the measles are of a mild type. The contagion has been chiefiy felt at Town-end and Sankey-bridge, at the fermer of which places' it is said, St. Peter's School has been in consequence closed for the holi- days somewhat earlier than they would otherwise have

been. - ANTIV,'EP !INTERNATIONAL ESHIBITION —Mr. Voisey, secretary of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, teas re- ceivel extensive particulars of the proposed Interitational Exhihition to be held in Antwerp, in 1885. There lb an ac- companying.circular from Mr. P. L. Simmonds, the British Commissioner, pointing out toe unexceptional facilities" wh!ch are being offered to British exhioitors—the chief point being that they will not he called on to nay anything for the "outlay connected with the working of the *British Commission." THE PROVINCIAL ASSEMBLY of Presbyterian and Unitarian ministers will meet at Warrington on Thursday next, the 19th inst. In the morning a religious service will be held in Cairo-street Chapel, and in the afternoon, at two o'clock a business meeting will be opened with an address by the Rev. Russell L. Carpenter, B.A. At half-past four on the same afternoon tea will be provided at the Lion Hotel, and at six o'clock a meeting will be held in tha Co-opera- tve Hail. The chair at this latter meeting will be occupied by Mr. W. Long, ant addresses will be delivered by the Revs. R. A. Armstrong, 8.A., John Dandy, and Mr. Charles W. Jones. THN PARISH CHURCH STRUCE BY LIGHTNING.—A severe storm, accompanied by thunder and lightning' passed over Warrington and the neighbourhood on Saturday, causiug considerable damage in various parts of the town. In the afternoon there was a heavy downpour of rain for about an hour, and the lightning was very brilliant. The violent peals of thunder seemed to shake the houses to their foun- dations, and numerous windows were damaged. The par'sh chnrch was struck by the lightning aud sustained consider- able damage. The editize was visited by the apparitor, who found it full of smoke and dust, and when this had cleared away it was discovered that it had been caused by the gas piping having boon wrenched from the walls for several yards, and reduc ol to atoms, which sparkled on the floor amongst the plastering that had been stripped off and re- duced to powder. On the north side of tho tower, near the corner, a portion of stone was dislodged, and on the wet &de of the tower a hole several inches deep and about two feet six inches across was made in the very centre, the stones being driven along the entire length of the roof to the west end, where they fell to the ground. It is supposed that the lightning conductor was defective. WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—A. sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before the judge, Mr. W. Wynne Fforilkes.—The only case of interest was one in which Jos. Heywood, builder, Moore, sued Peter Rowlands, a retired former, also of Moore, for the sum of £8 Os. 101. as bilance of an account due for the erection of a stable.—Mr. Ridg- way appeared for plaintiff.—Mr. Browne defended, and said that extra work had been charged for whatsboald have been included in a contract entered into by the two parties to the action. A contract, Mr. Browne said, was entered into origi- nally for £B, for the builling of a two-stalled stable, a coach-house, and loft, but afterwards the price was increased to £lo.—Altor bearing the evidence, his Honour said that be thought there were one or two reasons why he should believe the story of the plaintiff. One might almost assume that both plaintiff and defend ant knew pretty well what they were about. One was a joiner and the other was a farmer. The joiner knew what the cost of material and labour would be, and the farmer must also from his expe- rience have known what such Imildings were likely to cost. The defendant would not say VI cross-examination whether it was a great deal of work to get for £lO, but did say that be was satisfied to get it for that amount. Was it likely or probable that a joiner would undertake to build a coach- lion 32. a two-stalled stable, and a loft, for £lO. The defen- dant admitted that there was a conversation aboatthe build- ing being like another one that was mentioned. After some pressing he said that conversation took place after the con- tract was entered into, and then he distinctly contradicted that, and said that he did not know whether it was before or afterwards. That was an important circumstance. He (the judge) felt convinced that the plaintiff's recollection was the right one, and be must give judgmest against the de- fendant for the amount claimed. Wynne Ffoulkes, County Court Judge, has given judgment in the actions brought by Mr. Brinier Sheridan. of Warrington, ageinst his late manager Mr. Coli, and Miss St. Clair, a leadlng member e Mr. Cole's company. The actions were brought against the defendants on the ground of their having, on the 4th February last, at Leigh, unlawfully re- presented a drama, originally entitled ‘• Grelley's Money," without the written consent of the plaintiff, who claimed damages and an injunction to restrain the defendants further representing the drama in question. His Honour gave a lengthy judgment, and quoted numerous cases with reference to copyright of works. He did not think that "Love and Hate," which was the title ot the piece which Valuta claimed to have been pirated from " Grelley's Money," came under the category of abridgements. " Love and !date ''did not bear the same name, nor did it curtail dialogue', or omit portions of them, but left out whole scenes and acts of the play it was alleged to abridge nor did it profess in terms to be an abridgeMent, but an adap- tation. It Was much shorter than "Grelley's Money." but the narrative, dramatic effect, impressions and scenes were identical with those of certain distinguishing d hemedn by sothbe- and material parts of "Grelley's Money," and he was therefore of opinion that "Grelley's imitated andbaborrow stantially and materially defendants ln " Love end Hate." The copyright was clearly asaigneti to the plaintiff, who purchased from the author, p 4, Ross, the sole right of the drama for the provinces. Ross reserving London to WIDOW. With regard to the fact of the drama having been revised by Mr. Cole for Mr. Sheridan when in his employ, his Honour said that it was clear to him that Rosee drama was the material source of Cole's revised version. It was Sheridan's drema that furnished everything that vrent to make up the revised version, and Sheridan gave it those finishing touches which settled its final stamp and character for representation on the stage. The vereion was written under the orders of Sheridan when Cole leis in his capacity of theatrical manager and assistant, and with materials furnished by his master, nor was that employment other than germane to h's duties, the case differing altogether !rem a contract to write a play for an agreed price or money compensation. It seemed to him impossible to say that the originality of this version of Cole's flowed independently from the mind of Cole, when the material for it was from .13berida0, whom was the controlling mind. If so. the pla- giarism of Gralley's Meney " was established, and he gave Judgment for the plaintifft granting the injunction in the tams asked for.

Mr. Gomel!. BUTTERMARIGE'T-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.— On Sunday afternoon anniversary services in connection with the Buttermarket-street Wesleyan Schools, were held in Bold-street Chapel. The pulpit was occupied morning and evening, in the aosence of the Rev. George Dickenson, by the Rev. E. Lloyd-Jones, a former minister of the cir- cuit.Phere were large congregations. The Rev. F. Luke Wiseman, B.k, of Didsbury College, conducted a children'e service in the afternoon, and this was also well attended. The collections of the day were in aid of the school fund, and amounted to £45. The organ was presided over by Mr. G. S. Pendlebury. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—FoI week ending Saturday, • June 7th, 1884. The mean temperature was 439 Fahrenheit, and therefore lel degrees colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 67 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 3rd met, and the minimum temperature 29 Fahrenheit on the let inst. The rainfall measured 1 inch. The general direction ef the wind wee westerly. Divine the week, which was the 23rd of the current year, 34 births and 16 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 137 per 1.000, against 15 8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 95 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from measles, 4 from phthisis, 1 from old age, 3 from brain disease, and 3 from lung diocese. One Case of smallpox and one of typhoid fever were repea- ted under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.— JOAN IL GORNALL. medical *Meer of health. A DRINKING CLUB. Yesterday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, an elderly woman named Bridget Burke was charged with using languaze calculated to pro- voke a breach of the peace towards Martin Ward.—elr. Yearsley, who appeared for the complainant, a labourer in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Company, who lives in lodging. in Fonedry-street, said that the defendant, to- gether with some neiehbours living in the Same locality as the complainant, were in the habit of " clubbing " to- gether for the purpose of drinking, and an boat!le froiig was raised against those who refused to join, which feeling ultimately resulted in a row. The wife of the man with whom complainant lodged had refused to join in the orgies of these people, and on the 10th inst. the defendant black- guarded this person and accused the complainant of being improperly intimate with hen—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for ail months, herself in £5 and one surety of. £5. THE MAYOR OF WARRINGTON ON "STRIKES."—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, a man named Daniel Fairbrother was bound over in his own recognisances to keep the peace for six months for having used threats to a person named Thom as Whitley.—From the evidence ad- duced it appeared that the parties were wiredrawers, and that during the strike the complainant went to work. The defendant alleged that the complainant received some club money and then afterwards went in to work, and that had he not done that the feeling against him would not have been "half so bitter."—The Mayor, who presided, said that it was a monstrous thing that in this country a man could not be permitted to sell his labour as he pleased. Every man bad a right to strike if he thou'ght fit, but he had no TlVltto dic.tatt t. 2 "tt",M II Wee MonetrOne that such things were tolerated. A men had a right to ask !Or Wilit stun of money for his labour that be pleased to ask, hat another man had no right to dictate to him, or coerce him against his wish. "The Cot:Timor Tara LOYE."—At a time when the newee papers almost daily record, under the ominous heading "Breach of promise," cares in which swains, having plighted their troth to confiding maidens, have after all ungallantly and unfaithfully taken the advice which Punch so concisely conveyed in the word "Don't," it is pleasing to hear of an ardour in lovers which many people believe was only to be seen in the poetic days when women were all beautiful and men all true. On Whit-Monday a youthful couple, eager to bring to a close the period of their eeperate existence, made their way, accompanied by. the customary retinue of a wedding party, to Wycliffe Church, Warring- ton. On arriving there, however, it was fonnd that, with the impatience of those who have loved well, they had in- deed taken time by the forelock, and had not allowed the time prescribed by law to expire before their desires could be consummated. This formidable "cease and impediment" could not, of course, be evaded, and consequently the nup- tials had to be postponed. It is pleasing, however, to record that on Monday bet the devoted two were made one, and have, it is said, gone to reside at St. Helens where, to quote the words of the novelist, it is to be hoped they will " live happy ever afterwards," THE OTHER SIDE OF THE Quasrmer.—Chargeg a wife. boating are not infrequently heard before the Warrington borough Bench of magistrates, but yesterday a charge of an opposite character, in which a men summoned his wife for assaulting him. was investigated.—The complainant was George Ball, a file cutter, and the defendant, Catherine Ball, hie wife, who was charged with assaulting au 4 beating her husband on the 8•11 June.—Mr. Davies appeared for the complainant, and characterised the case as a very sad one. Plaintiff was the husband, which was rather unusual, but sometimes the hudeand had to lee very careful as to how he dealt with his wife, especially if she was a person of drunken habits. These parties hart been married 18 or 19 years, and had five children. The woman had been an habitual drunkard for 11 or 12 years. It wait not the first time that she had appeared in that court, and be thought that the officers of the borough would be able to say whet sort of a character abs was. She PTAS totally unflt to take care of her children. The husband had gone to his father, offering to allow his wife a separate sum for her mainten- ance, and to keep the children, but she would not let him alone. He was willing that the Board of Guardians snould fix a sum to be paid. The assault was committed by the defendant rushing into the Bay Horse Inn, where complain- ant was occasionally engaged to serve customers, and striking him a violent blow on the head with her umbrella. She had alsa abused him, and threatened what she would do to his mother.—Defendant said that her hueband had left her destitute, and consorted with low women.—She was hound over to keep the peace for six months, in two sureties of £lO each. ROAD CONSTaUCTION AT NEWTON•IN-MAKERVIELD the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, on Thursday, the case of the Newton Improvement Com- missionere v. the Justices of Lanceshire was resumed before Mr. Justice Mathew and Mr. Justice Day, sitting as a divi- sional court. This case raised the question whether the justices aS the county authority ought to contribute out of the county rate a half of the expenses incurred by the Newton Improvement Commissioners in maintaining and re- pairing that portion of the (old Warrington and Wigan turnpike road which passes through the township and district of Newton-in-Makerfield. The plaintiffs' case was that in 1877 the road in question was disturnpiked and became a main road, that under the High- ways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act, 1878, the county authority must contribute one-half of the cost of its mai:i- -t-mance, and that the part of the road which passed through Newton was a portion of the old Warrington and Wigan turnpike road, and was partly repairable out of the county rate. The defendants, on the other hand, subnaitted that the portion of the read which was within the district of Newton was cut off and disturnpiked in 1855, when the Newton Improvement Act was passed, and became a street within the district, that it had since been repaired by the Improvement Commissioners, and that ' therefore the county were not liable to captrinute anything towards the cost of its maintenance.—lvir. Justice Mathew, in delivering judgment, said that the Newton Improvement Act of 1855, which dealt with a portion of the Warrington and Wigan turnpike road, was not a ceseor within the mean. beg of section 13 of the Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act. 1878. It did not cause that part of the road within the district of Newton to cease to be a portion of the turnpike road, and therefore the whole road came within the Act of 1878, and the plaintiffs were entitled to receive out of the county rats one-half of 'the expensee in- curred by them in repairing the portion of the road within their district —Mr. Justice Day concurred.—Judgment for plaintiffs accordingly. NEW lON RACES. LETTING OF BARS lOW BOOTH SPACES —On Monday at noon, a large number of persons assembled in the neighbourhood of Newton Common to witness the annual "letting" of the bars and booth spaces in view of the races next week. The auctioneer was Mr. Councillor Sutton, of Warrington, and there was also pre- sent Mr. J. E. Pardey (stewardto W. J. Legh, Esq ), in addi- tion to several publicans from Manchester. Warrington, tee. The restriction of the races to two days instead of three as formerly, seemed to bave influenced the atten- dance of the "bidding " community, and as a consequence there was on the whole little compe- tition for either the bars or booth soacee, many of which were re-let to last year's tenants privately. In the course of the "sale" Mr. Pardey intimated that if the old tenants thought they would be able to get their bars or tents back for a lees sum than last year by waiting a few days they would find themselves mistaken. He (Mr. Perdey) would keep them shut first, he would not let them go at a penny less. The brick bars were let to the following persons : No. 1, Mrs. Prescott, Warrington; No. 2, Mrs. Clough, Manches- ter; No 3, Mr. E. Badley, Warrington; No. 4, Mr. Thos. Hayes, Knott Mill, Manchester ; No. 5. Mr. Johnson, Old- ham; N 0.6, Mr. Davies, Liverpool; No. 7, Mrs. Clough, Manchester; No. 8, Mr. Wm. Berry, St. Helens. The booth races opposite the Old Swan and entrance to the Grand Stand were taken as follows :—No. 1' James Holden, Manchester; No. 2, Jos,eph Shillcock' Warrington - No. 3, Joseph Shillcock ; Nos. 4,5, and 0, not taken : No. 7 (near paddock), Mrs. Kearns. Raiford, Manchester- Nos ee 9, and 10, not taken: No. 13 (near ttie brick bore on Haydock-road), Mrs. Prescott, Warrington ; and Na.'l4. Mr. Samuel Hurst, of Salford, Manchester. This concluded the proceedings. after which Mr. Sutton informed the par • ties who had taken the bars and booth spaces that those who wished to get their licenses would have to apply at the Petty Sessions at the Town Hall, Newtnn, to-morrow (Sat- urday) morning at ten o'clock.

As most of our readers know, the system of sani- tation which has been adopted in Warrington is what is known as the" pail and tub system"; and under present ar- rangements the only mode of conveying, the contents of the pails and tubs to Hie Longford DeprY: where it is dealt with is by, vans. This expensive and otherwise not altogether unobjectionable mode of carriage is, it is pretty generally admitted, a somewhat serious defect in a system which, on the whole, seems to find more favour amongst enlightened sanitarians than almost any other method of sewage removal. In Warrington, for instance, the vans used each take 24 pails, the nett liquid contents of which weigh only from seven to nine cwts.; after heing filled they have to traverse a long distance to the depot and back, so that it is evident, without saying anything about the offense the ungainly vehicles with their enal-odirous loads may cause—that the horse and minuet labour will form a very prominent item in the Cor- poration exoenses of the year. It is obvious, therefore, that any agency by which this defect may wholly or in part be remedied would be a very great improvement in sanitary appliances. With a view to demonstrating that excreta can be conveyed or rather propelled to Longford depot from central depe;ta in the town by mechanical means, viz, on the "Shone" system, which is at present in else in connection with the low-lying drains in Latchford, this experiment was arranged by Mr. Longdin, the borough surveyor. In Gas- strew, adjaining the Gasworke,a tank had been placed capable of holding about 800 gallons which represented the contents of about 300 reeils or 13 van loads. This tank was so placed that the material which it contained could flow into an ejector through a hose, and arrangements had been made by which the ejector when full could force the excreta into iron main pipes. The total length from Gas-street to Longford is 1 miles, and the height to the storage cistern that would be required at Longford lies at an eleva- tion of 20 feet above the ejector. Therefore in order to test the power of the ejector to propel its load of sewage along a drain 11 miles in length and to the height of 20 feet, the pipe with which the ejector was connected was erected perpendicularly to the height of 42 feet U inches above the ground. this additional height not only allowing for the rise of the ground from the site of the experiment, but also leaving an ample margin for any (fiction which might retard the flow of the sewage along a drain a mile and a half in length. The ejector, it is necessary to explain, was supplied with compressed air from the engine in the gas works, which is at present need to work the Latchford sewerage system. As soon as the gentlemen who had been invited to witness the experiment had assembled, the con- tents of the pails which had been accumnlated in the tank were allowed to flow quickly into the ejector, which was no sooner filled than it automatically and rapidly discharged the excreta into the pipes. The excreta then was as rapidly impelled up the ascending pipe, and, having come down the descending pipe was emptied inta a partly-opened sower, along which it was soon lost to sight. The ejector was again filled in the acme manner and the same process took place, and afterwards it was filled slowly to demonstrate that the apparatus would accommodate itself to discharge just as the material was b-ought by the vans to the receiving task, so that no excreta need be stored at the central dep6t. It may be mentioned in order to make clearer the peculiarities and advantages of this proposed method of removing ex- creta from the precincts of the town, that if it were adopted one or more depots for the reception of the vans would be formed in the town., At each of these depots there would ' be a tank and ejector similar to those which were used at the experiment we have described, and into these tanks the • contents of the pails brought by the collecting vans would be emptied. , The tank would be emptied into the 1 ejector, which would in the manner described I.let its contents into iron pipe% laid beneath the streets wbiCh Would connect the ejectors with Longford depart. In this way' the • material which is at present conveyed all the way to Longfo.d in slow-moving vans, would be Propelled in a few teconds along the pipes to the depot. It is evident that a system of this description if in successful operation would in a most effective manner remedy the defects in the pail and tub system to which we have alluded. The vans would then chi-fly be need for the purposes of collection, the discharging depot or depots in the town rendering the long journey to Longford and back unnecessary, whilst the fact of the excreta being shot rapid- ly along hermetically-sealed pipes beneath the ground would obviate all nuisance caused in transit. After the experi- ment had been made the nature of the machinery need was explained by Mr. Longdin to those present. and a general opinion seemed to be held. that the process pceeessed all the advantages which were el tinted far it.—Alderman Burgess, in the mime of a few remarks, said he thought that by that system they would accomplish what in his judgment was of much more consequence than the economy Mr. Longdin had been speaking of, and that wee that from the terminus of the borough boundary they should cease to be a nuisance to anvlarcly by having to send their vane through the dis- trict of the Rural Sanitary Authority. (Hear, hear.)—Af toe cores water bad been discharged through the pipes by the ejector in the same way as it had discharged its pIeVibLIS , contents, the company of spectators disputed.

At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Thompson and 4 jury, an action was partly heard in which Mr. Thomas Boardm-an, who occupies the Dairy Farm, Rainford, under Lord Derby, seeks to recover £32,'" value Of cow which died from the effects of drinking water from the Rainford Brook, &ilea had been contaminated by the water discharged from the slack-washer of the Rainford coal company." There was also a further claim of Rd Is ed for an- alysis of the said water, and V. 74 6d for veterinary surgeon's fees for medicines, professional attendance, and post mortem examination, making the total claim £l2 m.—)fr. Swift, barrister, Liverpool and St. Helens, appeared for plaintiff, asd Me'. 1,11:11 I holland, Liverpool, defended.—lt appeared from the opening statement of Mr. Swift ;pat the Rainford Brook is a natural stream and a general watering place for cattle belonging to farmers of the district through which it passes. The defendant company's works are situate some little die- tancs above plaintiff's farm, and up to January last there was no cause for complaint,as the water flowed in a tolerably pure and unpolluted state: On the 14th January, however, Mr. Boardman noticed that the water had become very much discoloured, and he went to the colliery to-ascertain the cause. Re there found the defendants had-commenced a new procese of treating their slack, and were washing it in a trough, the refuse from which they sent down a ditch and into the stream. This blackened and polluted it, and gave it the aopeatance seen by the samples produced in court. Plaintiff and Mr. Greener were both members of the Rain- ford Local Board, and plaintiff said that while returning from a Board ifleeting Mr. G,eener informed him of what the company intended to do, and said, "'lf it did any harm they would fence it off, and make drinking places for the cattle." On the 15th January plaintiff' Saw Mr. Greener, reminded him of the conversation, and said that if anything went wrong with the cattle he should certainly compensation, and- Mr. Greener agreed that it was right. Shortly afterwards nettle which hit hitherto been healthy, became ill, and a veterinary surgeon was called in. He attributed the illness to the polluted state of the stream, and samples of the water were , taken from time to time and sent to gentlemen who were who would be called as•witneeses. On the 15th March one of the cows died, and on the following day two veterinary sur- geons made a post•esortene examination of the carcase.—Mr. Swift said the first thing the jury would have to consider was: Did the company pollute that water P and secondly : Did the pollutod water of that stream injure the cow 7—Mr. Mulholland said the defendants admitted that for some weeks dated from about the 10th January they did use the s•ream for the purpose of carrying away thAr slack-water. But they contended that it did not cause injury or death- to the cattle —Plaintiff having corroborated the opeoint State- ment of Mr. Swift, Mr. W. ii. Reughsedge, M.H.CY.S., said the cow was suffering fromgeneral debility and loss of appe- tite, and irritability of the stomach, no doubt caused by drinking water from the brook, in which he had ven par. tides of coal floating down. He had examined the excreta of the cow and found pieces of coal exactly the same as ho • bad seen in the brook. In his opinion, that was the canoe of deatb.—Cross-examiwed : He found apiece of wire and a nail in the sminach of she animal, but that was a common thing and did not in, the slightest degree accelerate the death of this animal.—Mr. T. 8.. Stone, m.R.c.v S., of Newton- ie-Mltows, who assisted with the poet•niortene was also of the opinion that the slack-water had caused death. Re did .no 4 cooieo the nail in,the atom lob. If he had found a nail competent to andvse them and state their constituents, and penetrating the coat of the stomach he should have said it, would have materially assisted to cause death, but be found nothing of the sort, nor any symptoms wnich would attend such penetration.—Professor Williams, of Edinburgh, having expressed the same opinion as to the eause of death being due to the slack which had been taken into the stomach. the Court adj.-Ahmed until the SOO inst.

LATEST NEWS It is stated that the Claimant is due for release on license on October 24th. A boy Rained Trainor was killed at Elswick Colliery, New castle, yesterday, by falling down the shaft. Last night's Gazette notifies that the State apartments at Windsor Castle will be closed on and after, Tuesday next, the 17th instant. Sir Hardinge Giffard and Mr. Warton have undertaken to ' move the rejection of the bill to abolish actions for breach of promise of marriage. At the sitting of the Primitive Methodist Conference at Henley, yesterday, it was resolved to hold the next year's Conference at Reading. The Gazette announces that the Queen has conferred the dignity of Knight of the United Kingdom on Mr. Samuel Davenport, of Australia. Yesterday Mr. Richard Hall (Conservative) and Mr. Jos. Ruston (Liberal) were duly nominated for Lincoln. The polling is fixed for to-day. It is expected that the first vote which Lord Tennyson will give in the House of Lords will be in favour of the Aecond reading of the Franchise Bill. Mr. Bright, who has been staying at Llandudno for the past fortnight, left that place yesterday morning for Roch- dale, the right hon. gentleman's health being quite restored. The Staffordshire nailer, yesterday afternoon agreed to accept 10 per cent, reduction of wages, thus averting a strike. The reduction applies to spike and large nails. Major Marindin, tha Board of Trade inspector, yesterday held an inquiry into the Sevenoaks railway collision. The proceeding lasted six hours, and Maj..tr Marindin will re- port to the Eoard of Trade in due course. In the cricket match of Nottingham County v Austra- lians, at Nottinghatn, yesterday, Notts made 137 in the second innings, leaving the Australians 177 to win. They had made 11 without losing a wicket when the stumps were drawn.

The screw steamer Lame, of Newry, was wrecked off Wexford coast during a fog yesterday morning. The crew and passengers were saved. The vessel was owned by Mr. Felix O'Hagan, of Newry. and was engaged in purchasing fish from boats along the Irish coast. THE HIGHLAND CrtorrEns.—At the annual meeting of the Highland Land Law Reform Association, field in Lon- don, lent night., it was stated that thirty branches had been established in the Highlands. It was resolved to hold a public meeting in Exeter Hall, to support Mr. MacPherson's motion respecting the evictions of the crofters. Serarox DISEASE IN THE Dag.—Salmon disease of an es- pecially destructive character has shown itself among the salmon in the upper reaches of the Dee in North Wales. As many AS half a score of salmon are daily picked out of the water dead. Anglers describe the disease as a kind of itch, produced by the low and heated condition of the water. THE ACTION AGAINST Mn. BRADLAIIGIL—The trial at Bar of Mr. Bradlaugh to recover penalties to the extent of £2,500 for alleged illegal voting in the House of Commons commenced before Lord Coleridge, Justice Grove, and Baron Huddleston, on Friday. The prosecution was insti- tuted at the instance of the Attorney-General, with whom bir Hardinge Giffard appeared, while Mr. Bradlaugh con- ducted his own case. The Attorney-General, in opening, said the questions to be considered were questions of law rather than of fact. He stated the circumstances under which Mr. Bradlaugh sat and voted on the 11th February, and contended that the hon. member did not take and sub- scribe the oath in the proper form, and, therefore, he Wag liable to penalties for voting. The first main question was whether Mr. Bradlaugh had properly taken the oath, and the second, when he went through this form, whether he was a person who could come within the meaning of the statute to" make cath."—Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., deposed that he was one of the members who introduced Mr. Brad- laugh on the 11th February, and the book that gentleman kissed was handed witness. EHOCKING FATALITY IN LIVERPOOL. About half.past nine o'clock on Friday morning, as a cot- ton porter named Hugh Woodside, sixty yeara of age, who resided at 48, Ulleswater-street, Breck-road, was passing along Vaudries-street. the coping stone from one of the warehouses in the street fell upon him, fracturing Loth thighs and injuring his back. He was taken by the horse ambulance to the Northern Hospital, but the man died about half an hour after admission. An inqueat will in laela nu the body.

THE SOUDAN, &C.—Lord Fin Memitc 0, replying to Mr. Asinnead Bartlett, said he had nothing to add with regard to the evacuation of the Boudan in seddition to the statement made by Lord H irtington on the Vote of Censure. Reply- ing to another question, the noble lord said no intelligence regarding the reported capture of Berber and the massacre ott the garrison had yet been received at the Foreign Office. He could not then state the number of Earopeans in Rtrber but he would make inquiry. , THE FRANCHISE BILL.

Mr. ALERT GRANT moved a new clause to provide that the elections before January, 3587, should betaken as hereto- fore, unless Parliament should determine otherwise, not withstanding anything contained in this Act. He defended this clause, and said it would insure the bill not coming into operation until the Redistribution Bill was passed. If that boll was passed next year it would be very easy to alter' the date.—Mr. Crmatsrosit opposed the clause as it could not effect the object intended, as it gave two yeses, during which the Redistribution Bill might be passed. He con- tended that it was not possible for the House to pass vast enfranchising Act like the present and then hang up the scheme for an indefinite time. There was a probability of redistributiou being raised next year, and more than a pro• btbility in human affairs they could not have. Govern- ment had promised to deal with redistribution next session, and, that promise would be fulfilled if they emained members of the crown. It would be impossible for the overseers to get the new list ready for the present Act taking effect on Ist January, 1885. Therefore the Government proposed the let of January, 1881, for the new constituencies coming into operation Lord G. HAMILTON objected to the proposal of the Prime Minister. It was no concession, and the only proof the Government could give of their sincerity was to withdraw the present bill, and introduces new one.—The ATTORNEY- GBN.ER&L insisted that the concession made was substantial, and left full time for passing the Redistribution Bill next year.--Sir M. BEactrsaid the concession of the Premier did not remove his objection to the bill.—Mr. Arnold and Mr. Goschen advised Mr. Gray to withdraw his clause.—After a abort discussion the clause was withdrawn. Viscount FOLKESTONE moved a new clause providing that every person convicted of offences against the person or property should he excluded from the franchise for a term of years laroportionate to the nature of the offence Mr which such person might have been convicted. For offencee- other than felony the suspension should be for seven, and for felony 14 years.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL opposed the claufse:—Mier some discussion the clause was negatived. Mr. BRINTON moved a new clause providing that convic— tion for felony should disqualify an elector for voting for twelve months.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL opposed the clause. He thought it harsh and unjust to disqualify a man for a venal offence.—Mr. A. BALEoLIa supported the- clause, as, according to the Attorney-General, it was a greater crime to be poor than criminal.—Mr. MACFARLANE supported the clause.—Mr. GLADSTONE said, looking at the clause in all its bearings, and not as a Government question, ho could not vote for it.—Mr. T. Comma could not see why a pauper should be disqnalified, if the convicted felon was- not to be placed in the same position.—Sir R. Coss- and Mr. PELL supported the clause.—Viscount FOLNE- STONE would vote for the clause in order to amend it.— Mr. kliegs objected that a felon, directly he returned from penal servitude, should be placed.on the register.—Mr. C. Law's thought it should be known throughout the country that the Government thought convicts capable of being placed on the electoral roll from which women had been ex- eluded. On the division there- were for the clause, 134; against 178.—0 n the motion of EARL PERCY progress was reported and the further consideration of the bill in committee was fixed for Monday.—The bitting was then suspended. THE CLAIMS OF AN lievennon.—The House resumed at 'nine o'clock.—Mr. MacFAttwoes called attention to the 'claims of Mr. Lynal Thomas, agains• the War Department. Mr. Thomas had invented a 7-inch rifled breech loader which was practically the gun now in use in the Royal navy. He received a promise of his expenses in demonstrating his in- vention, but, his gun having been practically appropriated, his expenses were refused him. He moved for a Select Committee to-inquire into the subject. Mr. R. LEAEE seconded the motion, and said it was dishonest to withhold the expeases which were Mr. Thomas's right, especially as he had recovered a verdict for £9,000 which on appeal had been set aside on purely technical grounds.—Ctilon.l NOLAN I supported the motion bat proposal for Select Comiaittee was rejected by 42 to

EARLP,'STOWN. THE REV. H. E. SMITH, curate of St. John's Church, who has been ill since suoday week, has been ordered by his medical attendant to another fortniyht's absence from duty.

ANTI-VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN.— On Wednesday evening a preliminary meeting of persons interested in the abolition of compulsory vaccination, met at the Good Tem- plar lodgeroom, Bridge-street, and discussed the advisa- bility of calling a public meeting upon the subject. It was decided to hold a meeting, and the arrangements were left in the hands of a committee appointed for the purpose. TEMPERANCE MISSION.—Under the joint auspices of the Gospel Mission, Blum Ribbon Army, and the Good Templar. Lodge, a special temperance mission was conducted in the Co-Operative Hall, Earle-street, on Sunday, Monday, and luesday in the present week. On the first named day ser- mons were preached by Mr. R. W. Duzbury, of Oldham, and on Monday and Tuesday evemings large numbers of persons assembled to hear addresses from that gentleman. On Mon- day evening the chair was occupied by Mr. deorge Clarke, and on the succeee:lng evening by Mr. Joseph Cordinglv. The proceedings were interspersed by numerous musical selections.

LIVERPOOL FOOTIALL ASSOCIATION AND THE EARLES- TOWN CLIIE : PRESENTATION OF MEDALS.—The annual g neral meeting of the Liverpool and District Footoall Asso- ciation was held at the Neptune Hotel, Liverpool, on Thurs- day evening, for the elecdon of officers, passing of accounts, ikc. Messrs. Y. Hastie and J. Duahury represented the Earlestown Club. A pleasing feature of the proceedings was the presentation of a silver challenge cup to Evertor], and gold centre medals to each of the players in that team as the winners of the last season's competition. The representatives of the Earlestown Club were afterwards . . .
- presented with handsome silver medals as the runners-up for the trophy. The presentation was made by Mr. .1. flould- ing, J.P., of Liverpool, who commended the two teams for

their play, and congratulated the Association upon the advancement and progress they had made during last season.—Me. leuxbury responded on behalf of the Earles- town club, and in doing so stated that though they had not had the honour of winning the cup this year it was no reason why they should be downhearted, but rather stimu- lated to put forth further energies to achieve that distinction in the future; and he hoped they would accomplish it. The appointment et officers was then pro- ceeded with, and the election of the committee created considerable interest, RS 22 candidates were nominated for thirteen vacant seats. The voting, which was by ballot, was as follows, only two representatives from each club being allowed to vote :—T. Evans (Everton), 91 votes; Hull (Ramblers), 18 ' • Earle (Ramblers), 17; Sloane (Bootle), 15 , Lemont (St. Peter's), ; Dusbury (Earlestown), 13 ; George (St. Mary's), 13; Grant (Stanley), 13 ; Dovey (Stanley), 9; Herd (Bootlej, 7; Edwards (Tranmere), 6; Stele' (Anfield), d. These twelve were declared elected, but for the thirteenth vacancy Blackie (Haydock Temperance F.C.), Holmes ()Infield), and Briggs (Southport) tied with five votes each. On being again put to the meeting Briggs was elected by a large. majority, Blackie only receiving two votes, and those were from the two Eerlestown representa- tives. Proposed alterations to several rules were afterwards discussed. Tna DHATH OF Mn. W. H. DAGNALL.—The remains of Mr. W. H. Degnall, of Cross-lane, Earlestown, whose deatb we recorded last week, were interred in the graveyard at- tached to Wargrave Church on Saturday afternoon; the officiating clergyman being the Rev. Canon Whitley. The general esteem for the deceased gentleman and the sincere sympathy for the bereaved family was evidenced by the large attendence of friends and representatives of various organisa- tions. The funeral cortege left the late residence of the de- ceased shortly after half-past three, and notwithstanding the rain, which fell almost in torrents throughout the after- noon, many sympathisers assembled on the route to the church to witness the procession. In front of the hearse and mourning coaches walked nearly 100 members of the Druids' Order ; several representatives of the Earlestown itna Dietritt Liberal Club, and other friends of the deceased who had gathered to pay their last tribute of respect. Messre. T. and T. Vicars' (with which firm Mr. Dagnall had had a life-long connection) were represented by two of the Messrs. Vicars. The remains were placed in the same grave as those of the deceased's wife and a son, and the accompanying service was impressively conducted by the Rev. Canon 'Whitley. Numerous wreathe were subse- quently placed upon the grave, some ot which bore the fol- lowing inseriptieee t-ee" In etTeettopate remembrance and Wren et aefeeia i teir late met:lager, from die employes of Messrs. T. and T. Views, Earlestown works" (two wreaths); " In affectionate remembrance and token of esteem froM the Liverpool and Earlestown offices of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars ;" and "With sincerest sympathies, W. E. Lirge." In the course of a prayer at the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Cross-lane (which the deceased with his family had been in the habit of attending), on Sunday evening, the Rev. G. Smith, of St. Helens, said : We pray to-night for one family especially, Let Thypresence be with those that , are left; with those that Thou has spared without father, , without mother. Thou who are a father to the fatherless , care for them; guide them through all the difficulties and temptathms of life, and noey the children thus left feel that they are not left without a Father in heaven. May they , grow up to love whatever is good. Hear us in these our prayers; knit us together, give us more of the spirit of eherity, and more of the spirit of unity, through deems Christ our Redeemer. THE STRAY CHILD AND THE NIZGLECT AT THE LitxaPcot Wortxtrousx.—At the meeting of the Workhouse Commit- tee, on Thursday, a letter was read from Mr. George Hilton, 29, Rethhone-street, Earlestown, ceiling attention to what I he considered a case of flagrant neglect on the part of the sverkhouee officials. He said that on the 24th of May his eone Joseph Hilton, six years, strayed from his home, and af;er wandering about was ultimately picked up by Police- cons`ahle 1097, of the Liverpool police, and taken to the workheuse the same night. The lad eupplied his name and address, which was evidenced by the entry in the union book. Notwithstendlng this he was not advised by the officials until the sth instant, nearly a fortnight after the lad's admissiorf to the house. He considered this a down. right piece of gross carelessness on the part of someone, and he should he glad if the vestry would look into the matter at once. Further, he had to pay 6s for the keep of the boy, but had he been advised in a proper manner no doubt the charge would have been considerably less. Owing to tfre netrlect he had been put to a vast amount of expense and anxiety, and he should like to know what re- compense they were prepored to make. He thought they shoule refund is portion, Benet all, TA the 6s. In conjunc- tion with the letter reports were produced stating the result of the 'inquirer whith had been made. It appeared that the child was found by the police officer Wearing at the Dingle the same night, and was taken to the workhouse, where he was admitted. Mr. nagger' tho vestry clerk, explairted that it was usmal for one of the oficsrs named Wood, to take charge of such cases, but at the time when the child was brought to the remade:rase he was ebsent through Mines, and the matter was overlooked by the officer who was tempor- arily in hie place. Ties discovery therefore was not mode until a number of children were being passed for the indus- trial schools, and the father of the boy was immediately written to, and the boy taken from the workhouse on the following day. Mr. P. Smith said it was a most cruel cir- cumstance for the child to be in the workhouse for a fort- night without the father being cenainueicated with. Mr. Haggar. the vestry clerk, said no doubt everybody would sympathise with the father under the circumstances. It was agreed to return ,the 63 to Mr. Hilton, and to express-regret at the occurrence.

A HORSE KILLED ON THE ItattwaY.—lß the early hours of Sunday morning, two colts 13-longing to Mr. John Hes- keth, farmer, Roby, broke out of their stable, and one (a two-year-old; strayed on to the railway station platform. It is conjectured that an express train, approaching from the direction, of Iluyton,frightened it, so that it olloped along the platform until it came in coll:sion with the bridge which crosses the line with such force as to break its neck, when it fell dead across the metals. A gentleman residing near the staldon, who was aroused by the noise, proceeded to Huyton and had the line blocked until the rail was cleared. The horse was only just being put to work, and waa valued at between £".10 and £5O.

Twit Sim. CANAL Bmt..—The Select Committee of the House of Lords on tais Bill have reported the measure. The report is as follows:—" The Queen's consent signified, and Bill reportel specially from the Select Committee, with amendments." Toe Bill now awaits the third reading. The evidence gi-ren in behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board before the Ship Canal Committee- had drawn a sugges- tion from Mr. J. Cross. civil engineer, Widnes. Assuming that the Mersey Dock Board will remain content with exist• ing conditioae of depth and tide-flow over the Mersey bar, Mr. Cross lea opinion that this inertness will not long re- main satisfactory to the great Atlantic steamship owners, "who now calculate a passage by minutes, and will not sub- mit to being kept for hours waiting for water to cross the bar." Theo, As a remedy, comes the proposal to turn the Dee into the Mersey by widening and deeping the Ellesmere Port and Chester Canal. By the additional outflow thus seeured. Mr. Cross expects that in a short time therwwould be a material lowering of the sandy deposits which now at times virtually block the estuary against the largest steamers. The undertaking, it is claimed, possessee advan- tages of ecenomy and easy construction; as there aro nO en- gineering difficulties. Mr. Cross suggests that the lower pertion of the Dee estuary, thus robbed of its water, might be barred by an embankment, which would not only permit the recovery of the large tract of waste laud SO enclosed, but would furnish, with the M'ersor Tun- nel, a direct line of railway from Liverpool to Holyhead.— On Wednesday two important public bodies in Liverpool had the Manchester Ship Canal Bill under consideration, and in each case it was resolved to continue the opposition to the project. The Council of the Chamber of Commerce, at A lengthy meeting, adopted a petition against the Bill, princip By on account of the great injury to Liverpool which is expected to follow the ereetion of training-walls in the upper estuary. The petitioners suggest that no guarantees to be given beforehand should be accepted, for if, as they fear, the novigation should be closed to large ships and nteamees. the guorantees would be "necesaarily inadequate In the face of a national calamity." This pe- tition is to be circulated amongst Lancashire Chambers of Commerce. t a meeting of the City Council, Sir W. Forwood recounted the experience of his colleagues and him-! twit before the Lords' Committee, and said they had spent £3,000 in fruitless opposition to the Bill. They " hoped to Co strengthen their coo before the Commoias as to secure the rejection of the measure," and (lid not anticipate that more than an additional £2.000 would be required to do it. Power was given to the Parliamentary Committee to ex- %pond that sum and to renew the opposition hews the Select Committee.

NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH OPENING OF TIII; NEW ORGAN.—The opening of a new organ at the Congre- gational Church, Crow-lane, was commemorated by special services on Sunday last, and by a " recital " on the now irt-- strument, on Wednesday evening. The organ is a fine one, and excellent in every respect. It has been erected by Messrs.,Tharuld and Smith, of Manchester, to the epecifica- ti of Mr. F. W. Blacow, of Manchester, at a cost of £750. Towards this seam nearly £650 has been realised. ns The instrument has three manuals and independent pedal organ, and con-twine in all, 1,490 pipes. Tbere are four double-action composition pedals acting on the stops of the great organ, and 'war to the swell; also pedal to act on great to pedal coupler, The balance-pedal is applied to the swell shutters, and the whole of the metal pipes are of spotted metal of superior quality. The tuning is "Equal temperament." The pedal-board is slightly concave, with radiating sharps. There was a very large attendance at each of the services on Sunday, and the collections ombehalf of the organ fund realised the sum of £35. The preacher was the Rey. James Allatt, pastor: and Mr. F. W. Blacow (oraaniet. of St. Clement's Church, Broughton, Manchester,) presided at the new instrument. The church was nicely filled On Wednesday evening, when Mr. ..E Kendrick Psrne (orgasist, of the Manchesttr Cathedral an Town Hall) gase a recital- The programme included some of the best pieces from the works of Beethoven, Haydn, Bath, and other composers, and. the performance of Mr. Pye met with a hearty appreciation_ appreciation- In announcing the collection,.the Rev. James Allan ascended the pulpit, 4:aid said he desired to thank the friends connected with oner churches for the kind and even generous way in width they had met their appeal for aid. He was also requested to say a few words with the view of obviating some misconception which secured to have arisen in some minds. He wished to say that the organ was not a presentation organ: if it were so they should not have appealed for sny help on that or any other occasion. Some few years ago three or four friends made-them a generous offal- of a sum of money for cur - chasing an organ if the congregation rained among them- selves-the sum of £250. This was regarded in the light of a challenge, and they took the matter mo with the result that a ehort time ago they, felt justified in proceeding with the work. The whole of the money was not yet raised, and' he again appealed to their friends to kindly assist them. The collection realised this- stun of £l6.

A tiger-cat last week escaped from a menagerie at Comrie, Perthshire, and prowled about the district to the general alarm until Wednesday, when it was captured in a barn. Steps are to be immediately taken for enlarging the observatory at the Summit of Ben Nevis, which has ren- dered good service to meteorological science since its opep- ing in October last. At Old Traffortl, on Wednesday, Lancashire lost the match with Kent by seven wickets. Marylebene defeated Cambridge University, having lost only two wickets in get- ting the 76 runs required. Mr. Pugh, M.P. for Cardiganshire, and Sir M. Lloyd, Bart., are withdrawing from the County Liberal Association, ard the former will vacate his seat in Parliament rather than support disestablishment in Wales. A watcher named Newton was shot on Tuesday night during an affray with poachers on Lord Londesborough's estate, near Scarborough. He is in a precarious state. A poacher named Pearson is In custody. A Paris correspondent says Prince Henry Von Henan, son of the Elector and Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel, and grand-nephew of the Emperor of Germany, hag been re- ceived into the Roman Catholic Church, by the Papal Nuncio, in the Chapel of the Nunciature. At the annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches at Haslingden, on Wednes- day, it was reported that the membership of 107 churches in the Association amounted to 17,014, as compared with 16,630 in the year 1883. CORPORATIONS AND UNIVERSITY EDFCATION.—The Select Committee to which was referred the question of the South Wales University College decided on Tuesday to insert clauses in the Cardiff Corporation Bill enabling the Corpor- ation to contribute £lO,OOO towards the College. STARVING I CHILD—At Killarney petty sessions, on Tuesday, Patrick and Mary Sullivan, owners of a consider- able amount of house property, were committed for trial on the charge of manslaughter of their infant child, whom, it is alleged, they starved to death. A large varnishing shop at the works of Mr. Alfred Bul- lows, Long-street. Walsall, buckle manufacturer, which was opened so recently as Monday, fell in on Wednesday even- ing, burying several women who were at work. Three were seriously injured. The building was above tke yard, and was supported upon girders. The motion for an attachment against Mr. O'Brien, M.P.. for contempt of court, came before the Common Pleas Court, Dublin, ou Wednesday. Chief-Justice Morris said the motion would be granted, but an attachment would not issue unless the abjectionable articles were repeated ; Mr. O'Brien to pay costs. In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Wednesday, a Hack- ney baker recovered from the proprietors of the Bakers' Record 40s damages for libel. The libel consisted in a pub- lished report of a meeting of a trade association at which the plaintiff was abusively spoken of because be thought fit to sell his quartern loaf at 5d when the association had "ar- ranged that the price should be lid." CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION DEPARTMENT.—The vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Howard Vincent, Director of the Criminal Investigation Department, is about to be filled up by the appointment of Col. Dillon, Chief Constable of Hertford, as Assistant Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, with special supervision of the Criminal Investiga- tion Department. WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE—At a meeting of the Board of Conciliation and Arbitration in the North of England Finished Iron Trade, at Darlington, to consider a 10 per cent. reduction in wages, the employers agreed to a resolu- tion fixing 21 per cent, reduction from the 28th inst. to September 28th, during which time an effort is to be made to arrange a scale. DYNAMITE HOAX eer Levertooote—The fact that a snuff canister containing steel filings, and having a fuse attached to it, was found near the railing of the Liverpool Town Hall on Monday, showed that some foolish persons consider the dynamite outrages a fit subject for joking, but the hoax also eerves to show how imperfectly the Liverpool Town Hall is being guarded. DOMESTIC TRAGEDY NEAR BOLTON.—At Farnworth, near Bolton, early on Sunday morning, John Boyle, who was for- merly a beerhouse keeper in the town, but who absconded some months ago, stealthily entered the house of his wife and attempted to murder her. He also attacked with an axe two servants who came to his wife's help. Boyle afterwards committed suicide. Two of the women are in a dangerous state. A YOI7NG THIEF.—Pat Birmingham, on Wednesday, Mary Rose, six years of age, was convicted of picking pockets. She and her sister, aged eight, stole a purse containing 35s from a lady in a grocer's shop on Saturday; and on Tuesday she stole a second purse, containing Bs, from a lady going into the board school she attends. The last purse was found secreted in her bosom by the teacher. The two children were remanded for inquiries. THE DYNAMITE OCTTRAGES.—It is stated that although the Home Secretary and officials of the new political depart- ment at Scotland Yard have but little belief in the practical utility of offering a reward for the capture of those con- cerned in the recent dynamite outrages, they regard with no small amount of favour a proposal to place a considerable sum at the disposal of the police authorities to be used with secrecy and discretion. At the Hanley Police Court, on Wednesday, Dinah Par- sons., who had been twice previously convicted, was fined £lOO and costs for having an illicit still in her possession, and, in default of payment, was sent to gaol for four months. The Bolton Town Council on Wednesday adopted by 27 vetes to 17 a motion that the Chadwick Museum should re- main closed on Sundays. In a code of regulatiens submitted by the Parks Committee there was a rule for keeping the Museum open on the Sunday. Tax CAPTIVE CREW.—Official correspondence respecting the imprisoned crew of the Nisero was issued on Tuesday. Lord Granville, writing Count Bylandt May 31st, regrets that the Netherlands Government has refused English medi- ation in Acheen, and points out that the affair has created painful anxiety and a growing agitation in this country which the English Government view in a serious light. Lord Granville again presses mediation, and says England will send a mission to Kenala to open negotiations if the Netherlands will restore the freedom of trade. THE MAORI KING—The Maori King on Saturday and Sunday suffered from inflammation of the eye, and had also contracted an attack of ague. He was therefore kept in- doors. The Maori chiefs visited St. Paul's Cathedral on Sunday, and attended the afternoon service. They relished music, but went to sleep during the sermon. They were followed back to their hotel, according to one authority, by "half the boys in London." On Monday the Maori King was visited by great numbers ef people, and at night the King occupied the royal box at Drury-lane Theatre. On Tuesday, along with his secretary, he visited the Zoological Gardens, previously paying a visit to Westminster Abbey. THE DOWNTON RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—CoIoneI Rich held the Board of Trade inquiry at Salisbury on Monday into the recent railway disaster at Downton. After hearing evidence, Colonel Rich remarked that it was certain either the driver was too hard or the road was too weak. The road, however, certainly seemed very good, and he should not be afraid to run an engine over it at the rate of 40 miles an hour.—Mr. Colson, assistant district inspector, stated that the line had been lifted, ballasted, and re-sleepered about three weeks before the accident. He went over the line four days previously, and could find no fault in it..—This concluded the evidence, and Colonel Rich visited the scene of the acci- dent, accompanied by several prominent officials of the South-Western Company. CO-OPERATIVE WHOLESALE SOCIETY.—The quarterly meeting was held at Manchester on Saturday, under the presidency of Mr. J. T. W. Mitchell, of Rochdale. There were 353 delegates present, representing 153 societies. A resolution affirming the desirability of erecting a corn mill on the banks of the Tyne was negatived, while a second resolution, moved on behalf of the Heckmondwike society, recommending the appointment of a special committee to consider the committee's fees and fares was agreed to unanimously. It was also agreed to erant £5O towards the expenses of the Derby Congress. Messrs. T. Hall (Brad- ford) and J. Stansfield (Heckmondwike) were declared re- elected on the General Committee, and 15 societies, with 2,754 members and subscribing 282 £5 shares, were admitted into the federation. SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION: Two MEN Kreeme.—An alarming railway collision" occurred on Saturday at Seven- oaks Station, on the South-Eastern Railway, between two goods trains. While the Continental goods train was taking in water at Sevenoaks, the fast goods train from Deal dashed up, crashing into the other train, wrecking several of the rear carriages, and sending the remainder, to the number of thirty, a distance of about a quarter of a mile, so great was the shock. The driver, stoker, and two guards of the Con- tinental train fortunately escaped unhurt, but the driver and stoker of the first engine of the Deal goods train were killed on the spot, the body of the former being jammed between the first and second engines. The driver and his mate of the second engine escaped with slight injuries, being thrown underneath their engine, while two guards of the same train sustained only a few cuts. THE RAILWAY EXTENSION INTO WALES FROM CHESTER. The petition of the Mayor, aldermen, and citizens of Chester against the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway (Chester to Connah's Quay) Bill, and the River Dee Commissioners, praying to be heard in the Lords against I the bill, sets forth among other matters that the pier on which the railway is to be carried over the Dee will take a considerable width out of the navigable channel (which is here only about 80 yards wide), and will oppose serious re- sistance to the flux and reflux of the tide along the navi- gable channel, and prejudicially affect the scour of the river, whilst it will also injuriously affect and endanger the artifi- cial banks and bed of the river. It is urged that a railway with a swivel bridge across a tidal river can obviously not be made available for passenger traffic unless the bridge is to be permanently closed, as passenger traffic to pay, must run at stated hours; whilst, on the other !amid, the require- ments for opening the bridge must vary with the tides, and in the circumstances of the river Dee must be Prolonged at certain states of the tide. All the circumstances and sur- roundings of this proposed bridge would be fatal to the use of the river for trade. It is also alleged that the bridge is badly devised in an engineering point of View. The petition is signed by the Mayor on the part of the city, and by some influential members belonging to the River Dee Commis- sioners.
